findings.claim: Jan 1, 2027 CR26 mandatory: "the legacy Rev 5 path closes for new authorizations"
findings.problem: The deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml) attributes no Rev5-path closure to Jan 1, 2027 — the cr26-mandatory event covers only 'existing Rev5 Certifications must adopt; ConMon evidence machine-readable KSI'. A separate registry entry (fedramp-rev5-last-applications) says FedRAMP stops accepting applications for new Rev5 Certifications on Jun 11, 2027. Attaching the Rev5 closure to Jan 1, 2027 contradicts the registry by ~5 months. (The same wrong clause also appears in federal-aan-conmon-gap-roadmap.md line 103, which contradicts its own line 105 — the error propagates from there.)
findings.fix: Change the table cell to match the registry: on Jan 1, 2027 existing Rev5 Certifications must adopt CR26 and ConMon evidence must be machine-readable KSI; new Rev5 applications close Jun 11, 2027. Also fix the same clause in the roadmap so the two documents agree.

findings.claim: "The fully-sourced timeline is the ConMon Gap Roadmap (the single source of truth for dates)."
findings.problem: aan-authority-deadlines.yml declares itself 'the SSOT for every binding federal date the series cites' and is the enforced gate (check_authority_deadlines.py). The brief designates a different document as the single source of truth for dates, creating two competing SSOT designations — and the roadmap it points to currently carries the Jan 1, 2027 Rev5-closure error, so the designated SSOT disagrees with the enforced one.
findings.fix: Point the SSOT designation at aan-authority-deadlines.yml (the gated registry), and describe the ConMon Gap Roadmap as the narrative/fully-sourced timeline derived from it.

findings.claim: "ServiceNow Government Cloud is FedRAMP High coordinating a Moderate boundary (a conservative delta)."
findings.problem: ServiceNow Government Cloud's FedRAMP authorization level is an external-product claim not verifiable from any in-repo SSOT (not judging it true or false). The parenthetical 'a conservative delta' is an unsupported inference — a High authorization of the provider does not by itself establish that inheriting into a Moderate boundary is conservative; that is exactly the AO determination the decision item requests. Note the High mention itself is the baselined occurrence (count 1 in aan-high-claim-baseline.yml) and the spine's Vol VII comment directs 'refer as authorized' rather than by level.
findings.fix: Verify ServiceNow Government Cloud's current Marketplace status against the FedRAMP Marketplace before circulation; either drop '(a conservative delta)' or state it as the assertion the AO is being asked to accept, and consider following the spine's 'refer as authorized' convention.

findings.claim: Controls "cannot be satisfied by a perimeter architecture at any budget" / "Spend does not fix it... regardless of tooling budget" (lines 20 and 77-80)
findings.problem: Unfalsifiable absolutes ('at any budget', 'regardless of tooling budget'). The brief does sketch a mechanism (tools measure a gap they cannot close) and the series body argues the structural case, but a hostile reviewer can dismiss the absolute form as rhetoric since no in-file citation carries it.
findings.fix: Anchor the absolute to the supporting analysis (e.g. 'see the pattern-mismatch analysis in Vol 0 Book 00') or soften to 'cannot be satisfied by tooling additions to the perimeter pattern'.

findings.claim: Vol I Book 01 closes 16 NIST controls (headline at line 712, prose at 718, 'Controls closed: 16' at 745, repeated in the Control Count Comparison table at 1089).
findings.problem: The number 16 is immediately followed by an enumeration of 18 items (22 distinct control IDs; 17 distinct base control numbers when enhancements are folded in, the convention the series' 34-count uses). No counting convention yields 16 — the claim contradicts its own list, and the table above it has 18 rows.
findings.fix: Recount under one stated convention (17 distinct base controls, or 18 table rows, or 22 IDs) and update every occurrence of '16' including the es-fig-01 alt text and the summary tables.

findings.claim: Vol I Book 05 closes 12 NIST controls ('Controls closed: 12' at 852; heading at 817; repeated at 1091).
findings.problem: The parenthetical list at line 852 has 13 entries, the closure table has 13 rows, and folding enhancements to base controls gives 15 distinct numbers. 12 is unreachable under any convention. Together with the wrong '16', the Control Count Comparison total row (16+7+12+7 → '34') cannot be reconciled column-by-column even though the 34 union itself is correct.
findings.fix: Recount (13 rows / 15 base controls) and propagate to the heading, the summary table, and the es-fig-01 alt text.

findings.claim: 'FedRAMP 20x Consolidated Rules cover all 29 CR26 KSIs' (1181); same conflation at 615 ('the 29 active FedRAMP 20x CR26 KSI rules'), 670 ('29 CR26 Rules' table caption), 980 ('all 29 CR26 KSIs evaluable'), 1167 ('all 29 CR26 indicators'), 1177 ('All 29 CR26 KSIs are now evaluable').
findings.problem: The file's own KSI-count reconciliation callout (~line 647-659) states the 29 rules are the series' INTERNAL decomposition, not the CR26 catalog, and that CR26 has 46 indicators of which only 19 are explicitly mapped. Calling the 29 'CR26 KSIs/indicators/rules' asserts exactly the equivalence the reconciliation disclaims — a hostile ISSO reads line 1181 as claiming full CR26 coverage that the same document says does not exist (19/46 mapped).
findings.fix: Replace every '29 CR26 KSIs/rules/indicators' with 'the 29 rules in the series' internal KSI decomposition' as the exec-summary block (line 167) and Conformance Adapter section already do.

findings.claim: Conformance Adapter row: '29/29 of the series' internal KSI decomposition mapped (not the ~56–63 CR26 indicators)'.
findings.problem: The file's own reconciliation note (line 651) and the committed AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md put the CR26 indicator count at 46, not 56–63. The stale ~56–63 figure contradicts the document's own SSOT-backed count three hundred lines earlier.
findings.fix: Change '~56–63 CR26 indicators' to 'the 46 CR26 indicators' to match the reconciliation note.

The same four books are also absent from the 'NIST Control Closure — Vols III–IV' table (lines 955-966), though that omission is partially explained by the extension-books note at line 79.
findings.fix: Add the four extension-book rows to the master designation table (and consider a row or footnote in the Vols III–IV closure table).

A 3PAO would reject a closure claim for a withdrawn enhancement.

findings.claim: '34 distinct NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 controls' (line 142) and 'approximately 55 additional controls' (line 150) presented as parallel figures.
findings.problem: The two numbers use incompatible conventions: 34 reproduces only as distinct BASE control numbers (enhancements folded in, per the line 1098 note), while 55 reproduces only by counting every enhancement separately (11+8+9+12+15 across the Vols III–IV table). A reader summing them ('~89 controls') gets a number with no meaning, and an assessor recomputing either under the other convention (six tracks = 41 IDs; Vols III–IV = ~30 base) finds both 'wrong'.
findings.fix: State the convention next to each figure (e.g., '34 distinct control numbers, 41 including enhancements' and '55 controls and enhancements'), or normalize both to one convention.

findings.claim: OSCAL AP row: '10 themes, 32 CR26 controls'.
findings.problem: The '32 CR26 controls' figure cannot be reproduced from anything in this file, the spine, or the reconciliation framing (which counts 46 indicators / 29 internal rules / 19 mapped). 'CR26 controls' is also off-terminology — CR26 defines KSIs/indicators, not controls — so the cell reads as a stale artifact of an earlier schema.
findings.fix: Recompute from the actual emitter output and restate in consistent units (themes/indicators or NIST controls, not 'CR26 controls').

findings.claim: 'The assessment tool confirms what the architecture already guarantees.'
findings.problem: 'Guarantees' overstates: the surrounding text describes mechanisms that make compliant configuration the steady state, but nothing in the series can guarantee a near-clean SCuBAGear report — the same paragraph's 'should return a near-clean baseline report' is the defensible form.
findings.fix: Soften to '...what the architecture is designed to produce' or similar.

findings.claim: "As of May 4, 2026 FedRAMP uses 'FedRAMP Certified' with impact classes: Class C = Moderate, Class D = High."
findings.problem: Per the deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml), 2026-05-04 is the date of the CR26 PUBLIC PREVIEW (source: fedramp.gov/2026-05-04-public-preview-consolidated-rules-2026); the Consolidated Rules were launched 2026-06-25 and do not become mandatory until 2027-01-01 (cr26-mandatory). Attributing adoption of the nomenclature to the preview date misstates when the terminology took effect.
findings.fix: Cite the CR26 launch (June 25, 2026) as the point the nomenclature entered use, or phrase as 'introduced in the May 4, 2026 CR26 public preview and launched June 25, 2026; mandatory January 1, 2027.'

findings.claim: The §3 table presents 'Class C (Moderate)' / 'Class D (High)' as each product's 'FedRAMP status (verified 2026-07-08)', e.g. Splunk 'Class C (Moderate) (2019)' and ThousandEyes 'Class C (Moderate) — ATO 2026-03-05'.
findings.problem: Per the deadline SSOT, the FedRAMP 20x Class B+C certification pipelines do not open until 2026-08-31 (fedramp-20x-class-bc) and Class A not until 2026-08-03 — after the claimed verification date of 2026-07-08. Authorizations issued in 2019 or March 2026 are Rev5 Moderate authorizations; on the Marketplace as of the verification date they would not read 'Class C'. The table retro-translates Rev5 statuses into 20x class letters and presents the translation as the verified status. A hostile 3PAO would say the 'verified' statuses cannot be reproduced from the Marketplace as labeled.
findings.fix: Record the actual Marketplace designation at verification time (e.g., 'FedRAMP Moderate (Rev5 Authorized)') and add the Class C/D mapping as an editorial translation in the §2 nomenclature note, not inside 'verified' status cells.

findings.claim: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN row: FedRAMP status = 'Cloud-hosted SD-WAN Manager carries a FedRAMP authorization (verify level/CSO on Marketplace)' yet disposition = '✅ / ↪️ Chosen'.
findings.problem: The §2 disposition table says ✅ In scope requires a Class C (Moderate) authorization with the CSO / Marketplace ID recorded. This row grants the ✅ disposition while explicitly stating the authorization level and CSO ID are unverified — the only pre-filled product that violates the instrument's own hard scope rule, and it is the 'Chosen' SD-WAN. A reviewer would ask why the flagship selection bypassed the gate every other product was put through.
findings.fix: Either verify and record the SD-WAN Manager level + CSO ID like the other rows (dated 2026-07-08), or move the cloud-hosted component's disposition to ⚠️ Flag pending Marketplace verification (keeping ↪️ for the on-prem WAN Edge gear).

findings.claim: Vendor FedRAMP statuses in §3 and §6: SailPoint ISC Moderate (CSO FR2001938710A); ServiceNow Government Cloud High / DoD IL-4; Splunk Cloud Moderate (2019) + High, Splunk SOAR Moderate; Riverbed Platform for Gov High-only + SteelHead as non-FedRAMP gear; Atlassian Government Cloud Confluence Moderate (Mar 2025) and commercial Confluence not authorized; InfoBlox DDI Moderate (CSO FR2017257053); ThousandEyes for Government Moderate ATO 2026-03-05 (CSO FR2523656707), FIPS-validated; Prisma Access Moderate / Prisma Cloud High-only; Wiz High; Tanium Cloud Moderate (FR2110342613).
findings.problem: None of these product-authorization facts are reproducible from in-repo SSOTs; sources are vendor blogs and Marketplace URLs (lines 253-263), several of which are marketing posts (Riverbed, Wiz, Palo Alto, ServiceNow press release). Authorizations change; the whole §3 disposition logic and §5 flag list derive from these claims. Not judging them true or false — they require Marketplace re-verification at decision time (which the document itself acknowledges).
findings.fix: Keep the existing 'verify on Marketplace at decision time' caveat and the 2026-07-08 verification date; where possible replace vendor-blog citations with Marketplace product URLs so each status has an authoritative source.

findings.problem: There are no Volume VI rows above — the discovery tables cover Volumes I, II, III, IV, VII, VIII, and IX only, and the same callout says Volume VI needs no separate intake table. Pointing the reader at nonexistent 'Volume VI rows' is self-contradictory.

findings.claim: "actuation is platform-native (privileged access, patching, posture, and detection are performed by each platform's own stack), while governance and evidence are unified"
findings.problem: The prose assigns detection to the platform-native actuation side of the doctrine split, but the same file's volume-map figure (line 53 alt text) and books table (line 64) place Book 06 SIEM/XDR Detection on the UNIFIED governance-and-evidence row, describing it as 'analytics and response over the evidence lake.' The Executive Summary doctrine (Vol 0 Book 00, 'Governance Is Unified' section) likewise puts SIEM analytics over the unified Sentinel/Log Analytics lake on the truth-plane side. A reviewer would ask which side of the split detection sits on; as written the paragraph contradicts the figure two lines below it.
findings.fix: Drop 'detection' from the platform-native parenthetical (or rephrase to distinguish platform-native sensing/EDR from unified detection engineering over the lake), e.g. '(privileged access, patching, and posture are performed by each platform's own stack)' so the prose matches the figure's row assignment for Book 06.

findings.claim: "This series-wide master table below is still the hand-maintained superset — it indexes all 146 controls, including the books the spine has not yet back-filled" (repeated at line 108).
findings.problem: The master table is NOT a superset of the spine. Three spine-closed controls are absent from the 146-row master index: AC-2(3) (Disable Accounts), AC-2(4) (Automated Audit Actions), and SA-9(2) (Identification of Functions, Ports, Protocols, and Services) — all closed in book-sn-saas (Vol VII Bk 06) per aan-compliance-spine.yml. The arithmetic exposes it: the appendix (line 351) says the spine closes 53 of the 146 indexed controls and lists 96 not-yet-closed, but 53 + 96 = 149, not 146; only 50 of the 53 spine-closed controls actually appear in the master.
findings.fix: Add master-table rows for AC-2(3), AC-2(4), and SA-9(2) (Vol VII Bk 06), update the 146 total to 149 everywhere it appears (lines 46, 69, 301, 351), and rerun render_crosswalk.py so the appendix arithmetic reconciles (53 closed + 96 open = 149).

findings.claim: "the one genuinely new control number they [Volumes VII–IX] add is CM-5" (also line 95: "With one exception (CM-5, new in Vol VIII), these volumes re-close control numbers the architecture volumes already own"; and lines 306–309: "add only one new distinct control to the series total (CM-5) ... The series total moved from 145 to 146 for exactly that reason").
findings.problem: Contradicted by the spine: Vol VII closures in book-sn-saas add AC-2(3), AC-2(4), and SA-9(2) — control numbers no architecture volume closes and which the master table doesn't even index. The claim is only 'true' relative to the master table because those three controls were omitted from it (finding above). The '145 to 146' delta is also irreproducible from repo data.
findings.fix: Revise all three passages to name the four genuinely new control numbers (CM-5 plus AC-2(3), AC-2(4), SA-9(2)), or explicitly scope the CM-5 claim to base controls / to Vol VIII only.

All eight other volume counts (I:41, II:22, III:54, IV:54, V:2, VI:38, VIII:6, IX:10) and the series total (146 distinct) DO reproduce exactly — only Vol VII is wrong.

findings.claim: FedRAMP 20x KSI View: "Where a book maps a control to a FedRAMP 20x Key Security Indicator, those associations are aggregated here."
findings.problem: The aggregation is incomplete against the master table's own KSI column: KSI-IAM omits AC-20 (line 154), KSI-PIY omits CA-3 (line 175), and KSI-SCR (carried by SA-9, line 245) has no row at all. The follow-on prose (line 332) also says KSI-PIY "is introduced by the CM-8 join-key reconciliation" while the table maps CA-3 to KSI-PIY too.
findings.fix: Add AC-20 to the KSI-IAM row, CA-3 to the KSI-PIY row, and a KSI-SCR row (SA-9); soften the KSI-PIY prose claim.

findings.problem: The spine — the declared SSOT for machine-checked closures — binds the same controls to "KSI-CMT"; the id "KSI-CM" appears nowhere in the spine's KSI vocabulary (KSI-CMT, KSI-CNA, KSI-IAM, KSI-MLA, KSI-PIY, KSI-SCR, KSI-SVC). Lesser drift in the same column: spine gives AC-4 KSI-CNA + KSI-IAM (master: CNA only) and CM-8 KSI-PIY only (master: KSI-CM + KSI-PIY).
findings.fix: Rename KSI-CM to KSI-CMT throughout the master table and KSI view (and reconcile the AC-4/CM-8 KSI sets with the spine), or record why the master intentionally diverges.

findings.claim: AT-2, AT-3, AT-4, CP-3, and IR-2 map to FedRAMP 20x KSI "KSI-022" (rows at lines 155, 158, 161, 191, 214; aggregated at line 317).
findings.problem: "KSI-022" does not match the KSI id convention used by the spine SSOT (three-letter mnemonics like KSI-CMT/KSI-CNA) and appears in no spine closure. Whether a numeric "KSI-022" exists in the CR26 FedRAMP 20x indicator set cannot be judged from in-repo SSOTs — it needs verification against the FedRAMP 20x KSI list. It is, however, used consistently across ~10 other series files, so if it is wrong it is a corpus-wide issue, not unique to this book.
findings.fix: Verify "KSI-022" against the current FedRAMP 20x / CR26 indicator registry; if it maps to a mnemonic id (e.g. the training/education KSI), rename corpus-wide.

findings.problem: The official title in reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json (catalog v5.2.0) is singular: "Information Security Program Leadership Role". All other 145 titles in the master table verify against the catalog (allowing the documented "Base — Enhancement" composition pattern).

findings.claim: SA-9 row marks "Vol VII Bk 06 †" with a dagger.

findings.claim: Section '## AC-11: Session Lock', figure pam-fig-07 alt text ('AC-11 Session lock'), and closure-table row 'AC-11 | Session Lock' all title AC-11 as 'Session Lock'.
findings.problem: The in-repo SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, catalog v5.2.0) titles AC-11 'Device Lock' — the Rev 5 rename from the Rev 4 title 'Session Lock'. Citing the Rev 4 title while claiming 'NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-11' (lines 814 and 1021) is exactly the kind of stale-revision tell a 3PAO flags.
findings.fix: Rename to 'AC-11: Device Lock' in the section header (line 812), the prose at line 814, the closure table row (line 1021), and regenerate/annotate figure pam-fig-07 alt text (line 810). The described behavior (idle lock + re-auth) still maps to AC-11 correctly.

findings.claim: FedRAMP 20x callout cites 'KSI-IAM-02 (Privileged Account Management)', 'KSI-IAM-03 (Multi-Factor Authentication)', and 'KSI-EDR-01 (Endpoint Detection and Response)', and says KSI-IAM-02 'requires that agencies implement just-in-time access'.
findings.problem: The repo's own CR26 KSI evidence artifacts (output/artifacts/ksi-bundle/ksi-ar.json, the ScubaDrift KSI wiring) use mnemonic IDs — KSI-IAM-JIT, KSI-IAM-APM, KSI-IAM-ELP, KSI-IAM-AAM, KSI-IAM-SNU, KSI-IAM-SUS — not numeric KSI-IAM-02/03, and no KSI-EDR family exists anywhere in the repo (the only KSI-EDR-01 hits are this file, its Part7 predecessor, and a training book that inherited it). KSIs also bind cloud service providers, not 'agencies'. A reviewer cross-checking CR26 will find none of these three indicators.
findings.fix: Map to the repo's CR26 KSI IDs (JIT elevation -> KSI-IAM-JIT; phishing-resistant MFA -> KSI-IAM-APM/AAM as appropriate; endpoint coverage -> the correct monitoring-family KSI or drop the claim), fix 'agencies' to the CSP obligation framing, and propagate the fix to AAN-Training-Program/books/book-10.qmd line 71 which repeats KSI-EDR-01.

findings.claim: 'CISA AA23-278A (Scattered Spider) and Microsoft's September 2023 threat intelligence on Storm-0558 both document adversaries that specifically targeted standing Global Admin accounts.'
findings.problem: Two external attributions that a hostile reviewer will check: (a) the Scattered Spider advisory is widely cited as AA23-320A, while AA23-278A is the NSA/CISA top-misconfigurations advisory — the ID pairing looks wrong; (b) Storm-0558 was a forged-token intrusion into Exchange Online via a stolen MSA signing key — characterizing it as 'specifically targeted standing Global Admin accounts' needs a citation. Not judged true/false here — verify against CISA and Microsoft sources.
findings.fix: Verify the advisory number (likely AA23-320A for Scattered Spider) and either cite the specific Microsoft Storm-0558 report language or swap in an incident that actually turned on standing Global Admin (e.g., Midnight Blizzard/January 2024 is the usual citation for standing privileged access abuse).

findings.claim: 'RDP via Arc. The `az network bastion rdp` command ... establishes a proxied RDP session' (line 324), but the operator flow at line 451 shows RDP via `az ssh arc --resource-group ... --rdp`.
findings.problem: The document gives two different mechanisms for the same Arc RDP path. `az ssh arc --rdp` (line 451) is the Arc-native SSH-tunneled RDP; `az network bastion rdp` is the Azure Bastion path with different prerequisites (a Bastion host) that the architecture section never mentions deploying. A reviewer following section 'Arc JIT SSH and RDP Architecture' cannot reproduce the operator flow, and whether Bastion even supports Arc-enabled machines needs external verification.
findings.fix: Pick one mechanism — presumably `az ssh arc ... --rdp` since no Bastion is deployed anywhere in the book — and make line 324 describe it; or add the Bastion prerequisite explicitly if that path is intended.

findings.claim: Naming guidance (line 667) says a break-glass account name must carry 'no indicator of elevated privilege' and calls out `bg-acct-01@agency.gov` as discoverable — yet the creation script builds `bg-cloud-01@agency.gov` / `bg-cloud-02@agency.gov` with DisplayName 'Break Glass 01', and the Sentinel alert (line 752) hardcodes those same UPNs.
findings.problem: The runnable artifact directly violates the doctrine stated three paragraphs earlier. An assessor executing the provided script produces exactly the discoverable naming the document prohibits.
findings.fix: Parameterize the UPN/DisplayName in New-BreakGlassAccount with a comment that the value must follow the agency's normal naming convention, and drive the Sentinel KQL from the account object IDs (or a watchlist) instead of hardcoded bg-* UPNs.

findings.claim: The standing-assignment enumeration script pipes a `foreach` statement into Format-Table (`foreach ($roleId in $privilegedRoles) { ... } | Format-Table -AutoSize`, line 188) and the $privilegedRoles array has a trailing comma after the Intune Administrator GUID (line 161).
findings.problem: Both are PowerShell parse errors — a foreach statement cannot be piped, and a trailing comma inside @( ) is a syntax error — so the published discovery script cannot run at all. Additionally, Get-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleAssignment returns PIM-activated (time-bounded) assignments too, so even when fixed the output overstates 'standing' assignments unless activated-eligible entries are excluded.
findings.fix: Remove the trailing comma; wrap the loop output in $(foreach ...) or ForEach-Object before piping; note that results should be cross-checked against roleEligibilitySchedule/roleAssignmentSchedule to exclude currently-activated PIM sessions from the 'standing' list.

findings.claim: PAW compliance policy sets `deviceThreatProtectionRequiredSecurityLevel = "secured"` under the comment '# Credential Guard (requires Virtualization-Based Security)', and the comment '# Mark non-compliant after 1 day (no grace period...)' precedes password-length settings.
findings.problem: deviceThreatProtectionRequiredSecurityLevel is the Mobile Threat Defense risk-level property in the Graph windows10CompliancePolicy resource — it does not configure or verify Credential Guard — and no property in the block actually sets the 1-day non-compliance grace period the comment promises (that lives in scheduledActionsForRule). A reviewer validating the policy against its stated intent finds neither control present. (Exact Graph property semantics: needs-external-verification against Microsoft Graph docs.)
findings.fix: Enforce Credential Guard via the correct mechanism (deviceGuard settings in a configuration profile, verified by the Win32_DeviceGuard check already shown at line 573) and add scheduledActionsForRule with a 0-1 day grace period; fix or delete the misleading comments, including the '# Minimum OS version -- require Windows 11 22H2' comment over a Windows 10 22H2 value (line 513).

findings.claim: 'NIST SP 800-207 ... requires that privilege be granted per-request, not standing. PIM is the Microsoft implementation of these requirements. CMMC 2.0 Level 2 and FedRAMP Moderate both require AC-6 ... and AC-6(5) ... controls that PIM directly satisfies.'
findings.problem: 800-207's tenet is per-session resource access, not 'per-request privilege', and 800-207 is an architecture publication, not a requirements mandate on agencies. 'PIM directly satisfies' AC-6/AC-6(5) overstates — PIM is one mechanism contributing to satisfaction; assessment requires the full implementation (policy, inventory, review) this document elsewhere correctly describes. A 3PAO rejects 'directly satisfies' phrasing on a single product feature.
findings.fix: Rephrase to 'per-session' per 800-207 Tenet 2, and soften to 'PIM provides the enforcement mechanism agencies use to implement AC-6 and AC-6(5)' consistent with the closure-table framing.

findings.claim: 'Across a federal environment operating 8,760 hours per year, a standing Global Administrator has that scope for 8,752 hours more than is operationally necessary.'
findings.problem: 8,760 - 8,752 = 8 implies exactly eight hours of administrative need per YEAR, an assumption stated nowhere and obviously false for a real admin (the book's own policy allows 4-8 hours per activation, multiple activations). The arithmetic is reproducible only from an unstated and implausible premise, so the number reads as rhetorical rather than derived.
findings.fix: Either state the premise ('even an admin who needs only one 8-hour window per year...') as an explicit illustrative bound, or recast qualitatively ('active for thousands of hours in which no administrative work is occurring').

findings.claim: Vendor authorization statuses: 'SailPoint Identity Security Cloud (owned, FedRAMP Moderate)', 'Prisma Cloud / Wiz CIEM (High)', CyberArk as the vaulting layer, and 'Defender for Cloud CIEM (Moderate)'.
findings.problem: These are external FedRAMP Marketplace facts that change over time; the document itself instructs 'Verify each on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement' (line 998), which correctly scopes them, but a reviewer will still require the authorization type/impact level and package IDs to be checked at citation time. Not judged true/false here. (Note: the Prisma/Wiz '(High)' marks are the intentional PR #1112 correction but this file has no entry in aan-high-claim-baseline.yml, so they sit outside the gated baseline.)
findings.fix: Keep the at-procurement caveat; consider adding Marketplace package identifiers or a last-verified date alongside each status, matching the registry pattern used for deadlines.

findings.claim: Prose says 'The activation flow has five stages' while figure pam-fig-02's alt text (line 108) enumerates Step 1 through Step 6 (audit logging counted as its own step).
findings.problem: Five vs six for the same flow within four lines; trivially caught by a reviewer comparing figure to text.
findings.fix: Either fold audit into the prose as a sixth stage or note in the figure caption that logging spans all stages.

findings.claim: Closure table titles AC-6(2) 'Non-privileged Access for Non-security Functions'.
findings.problem: SSOT title is 'Non-privileged Access for Nonsecurity Functions' (no hyphen in 'Nonsecurity'). Exact-title pedantry, but the table column is explicitly 'Title' mapped to the Rev 5 catalog.
findings.fix: Match the catalog spelling.

findings.claim: 'queryable in Microsoft Sentinel (Defender for Cloud via the Entra connector) and in Log Analytics.'
findings.problem: The parenthetical is garbled — PIM audit events reach Sentinel via the Microsoft Entra ID data connector; Defender for Cloud is a different product and plays no role in this path. As written it names the wrong product for the stated mechanism.
findings.fix: Change to '(via the Microsoft Entra ID connector)'.

findings.claim: 'the recommended baseline for federal environments operating at FedRAMP Moderate or High.'
findings.problem: Not an inheritance claim, but it is a FedRAMP High mention in a file that has NO entry in aan-high-claim-baseline.yml (baseline 0) — the gate pattern evidently doesn't match 'Moderate or High', so this sits outside both the baseline and the ratchet. Authoring-spec section 2 says the series never cites High.
findings.fix: Drop 'or High' (the settings are identical at Moderate) or route the mention through whatever ruling the owner issues on the High-claim debt.

findings.claim: "A KEV entry that is internet-facing must be patched within two weeks of catalog publication. A KEV entry that is internal-only must be patched within four weeks" — attributed to BOD 22-01 (also SLA table lines 86-87, script logic lines 370-381, KSI section lines 1102/1105).
findings.problem: BOD 22-01 does not define an internet-facing/internal exposure split; it requires remediation by the per-entry due date CISA publishes in the KEV catalog (the doc itself acknowledges the dueDate field at line 252). The exposure-based remediation-timeline model is the BOD 26-04 construct per the series' own SSOTs: aan-authority-deadlines.yml entries bod-26-04-policies (2026-08-07) and bod-26-04-vdr-ver (timelines in force 2026-12-07), and the spine's SI-2(3) entry keyed to the 'BOD 26-04 four-variable model' with driver cisa-bod-26-04. This book never mentions BOD 26-04 at all, five months before its timelines bind and one month before agency policies are due. A hostile ISSO checks the 14/28-day tiers against the BOD 22-01 text and rejects the authority column.
findings.fix: Re-attribute the exposure-based 14/28-day tiers to BOD 26-04 (citing the registry dates), keep BOD 22-01 as the catalog-due-date authority, and add a transition note that BOD 26-04 remediation timelines are in force 2026-12-07.

findings.claim: Closure table row: "RA-5(5) | Privileged Access for Scanning" (repeated in fig-alt at line 1087).
findings.problem: The SSOT catalog (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, v5.2.0) gives RA-5(5) the title "Privileged Access". "Privileged Access for Scanning" is not the official title; a 3PAO checking control titles against the catalog flags it.
findings.fix: Change the title to "Privileged Access" in the table row and the vuln-fig-04 fig-alt (and regenerate the figure if it renders the wrong title).

findings.claim: "SQL Server 2019 mainstream support ends July 2024 (extended security updates available through 2029 via Arc enrollment). SQL Server 2022 mainstream support runs through January 2028." (repeated in the vuln-fig-06 fig-alt, line 695).
findings.problem: Contradicts the same document's own CU map 40 lines later, which records SQL 2019 EOS as 2030-01-08 (line 734). July 2024 is the SQL Server 2014 date in that same map (2024-07-09, line 737) — the sentence conflates 2014's lifecycle with 2019's, and "ESU through 2029" matches neither. An assessor reproducing either date from the script or from Microsoft's lifecycle page gets a different answer than the prose.
findings.fix: Correct the prose (and fig-alt/figure) to the actual SQL 2019 lifecycle consistent with the script's EOS map, and remove or re-source the "ESU through 2029 via Arc" claim.

findings.claim: "A machine that is more than 30 days behind the required patch level is marked non-compliant, which triggers the Conditional Access enforcement gate."
findings.problem: The compliance-policy script that immediately follows (lines 606-652) contains no setting that implements a 30-day patch-currency test: the comment '# Patch currency: mark non-compliant if updates available for more than 30 days' sits above an empty validOperatingSystemBuildRanges array, and no other property in the posted windows10CompliancePolicy body evaluates patch age. The claimed enforcement mechanism — the CA block on stale machines — is asserted but not implemented by the artifact offered as its implementation.
findings.fix: Either add the actual mechanism (e.g., populate build ranges from the current patch baseline, or use the update-compliance signal the platform actually exposes) or downgrade the prose to say the policy enforces the listed health criteria and patch currency requires an additional mechanism.

findings.claim: "PatchComplianceRate (FedRAMP 20x target is 95% or higher for High/Critical severity across a 30-day rolling window)" — repeated at line 1102 and in the vuln-fig-07 fig-alt (line 930) as "the FedRAMP 20x SI-2 target".
findings.problem: A specific numeric threshold is attributed to FedRAMP 20x with no source; no FedRAMP 20x KSI in the series' SSOTs defines a 95% patch-compliance-rate target. Presenting an invented threshold as the program's requirement is exactly what a hostile reviewer rejects — and it creates a false pass/fail line the agency could be held to.
findings.fix: Restate 95% as the agency's internal target chosen to demonstrate SI-2 KSI performance, or cite the actual FedRAMP 20x KSI definition if one exists; remove "FedRAMP 20x target is" phrasing everywhere including the figure.

findings.claim: "SLABreachedKEV ... must be zero for BOD 22-01 compliance" (line 955; fig-alt line 930 calls it "the BOD 22-01 pass/fail").
findings.problem: The script computes KEV SLA due dates as dateAdded + 14/28 days and never uses the catalog dueDate field it downloads and parses (line 304), even though the doc states at line 252 that dueDate is "the CISA-assigned remediation deadline, which may differ from the ... standard timelines". SLABreachedKEV therefore does not measure compliance with the deadline CISA actually assigned: it can read 0 while catalog dueDates are breached, or flag breaches that don't exist.
findings.fix: Use the catalog dueDate when present (falling back to the computed window otherwise) as the SLA due date for KEV findings, and align the pass/fail prose with what is computed.

findings.claim: PatchComplianceRate is the SI-2 KSI "across the active finding population for Critical and High severity (P0 through P3)".
findings.problem: The script computes PatchComplianceRate as 1 − SLABreached/TotalFindings over ALL findings including P4-Medium and P5-Low (lines 428-430), not over P0-P3. The published metric cannot be reproduced from the stated definition; also P0/P1 are KEV tiers of any severity, so "Critical and High severity (P0 through P3)" is doubly wrong as a description of the population.
findings.fix: Either filter the rate computation to the P0-P3 population or describe the metric as computed across all active findings; fix the P0-P3 severity characterization.

findings.claim: P2 Critical non-KEV = 15 days and P3 High non-KEV = 30 days with "Authority: NIST SP 800-40 R4" (also line 76: "CVSS 9.0 ... carries a 15-day SLA under the standard federal framework").
findings.problem: NIST SP 800-40 Rev 4 is deliberately non-prescriptive and defines no numeric remediation timelines; the 15-day-critical/30-day-high numbers resemble the CISA BOD 19-02 requirements for internet-accessible systems. Citing SP 800-40 R4 as the authority for specific day counts is a mis-citation an assessor will check.
findings.fix: Cite these tiers as agency policy informed by SP 800-40 R4's risk-based guidance (or cite BOD 19-02 where it actually applies), rather than presenting the day counts as SP 800-40 R4 requirements.

findings.claim: CU map EOS values: 2022 = '2028-01-11', 2019 = '2030-01-08', used uniformly for the WithinSupport/EOSBreached test (line 771).
findings.problem: The EOS field mixes lifecycle phases: 2028-01-11 is SQL 2022's mainstream-support end (extended support runs years later) while 2030-01-08 is SQL 2019's extended-support end. Under the script's single WithinSupport test, every SQL 2022 instance will be flagged "End-of-support breached — immediate upgrade planning" in January 2028 while still inside extended support, so the EOSBreached count in the evidence artifact is not a defensible number.
findings.fix: Pick one lifecycle semantic (extended-support end is the compliance-relevant one), populate all rows consistently, and rename the field/summary label to match.

findings.claim: Intune Windows Update for Business rings (and the windows10CompliancePolicy at line 611) are the patch-delivery and enforcement lane for the Arc-enrolled Windows Server estate, with "domain controllers, database servers" placed in the production ring (lines 490, 553).
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but this is the load-bearing remediation mechanism of the book and its applicability to Windows Server SKUs needs vendor verification: WUfB deferral policies and Intune windows10 compliance policies are documented by Microsoft as client-OS (Windows 10/11) capabilities, and the doc's own "Remediation Beyond Windows" section names Azure Update Manager as the tool that rides the Arc channel. If WUfB/Intune does not manage Server SKUs, the DC/SQL-server population described has no delivery mechanism as written, and RA-5/SI-2 closure claims for the server estate fail.
findings.fix: Verify against current Microsoft documentation; if confirmed client-only, route Arc-enrolled Windows Server patching through Azure Update Manager (as already done for Linux) and scope the WUfB ring section to the Intune-joined Windows 10/11 population.

findings.claim: MDVM "uses the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) channel that was installed during Arc enrollment" / "No additional agent installation" (also line 54), and Windows Server 2012 R2 coverage "via MMA fallback" (lines 120, 133).
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but two vendor-architecture claims need verification: (a) Defender for Endpoint's modern unified server solution is documented as using its own MDE sensor rather than transporting vulnerability data over AMA, which would undercut the repeated "no additional agent" claim; (b) the Microsoft Monitoring Agent (MMA/Log Analytics agent) was retired by Microsoft in August 2024, well before this document's 2026-07-08 date, so prescribing MMA as the 2012 R2 channel is likely stale.
findings.fix: Verify the current MDE-on-Arc onboarding architecture and the post-MMA path for legacy OS coverage against Microsoft documentation, and restate the agent-channel claims accordingly.

findings.claim: "Arc enrollment on 2012 R2 provides Extended Security Updates (ESU) at no additional cost."
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but Microsoft's published model bills Arc-delivered Windows Server 2012/R2 ESUs as a paid per-core monthly subscription (the no-cost ESU applies to workloads running in Azure). A cost claim in a roadmap document that procurement will rely on must be verified; if wrong, it misstates a budget line.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft's ESU licensing documentation and either correct to "ESU available through Arc (billed)" or cite the specific no-cost condition.

findings.claim: "No vulnerability scanner automatically flags KEV status ... not linked in standard scanner outputs."
findings.problem: Not judged true/false, but this absolute claim about the entire scanner market needs verification: current MDVM, Tenable, Qualys, and Rapid7 outputs all advertise CISA-KEV/exploited-in-the-wild flags. The claim motivates the custom cross-reference pipeline, so if overbroad it overstates the necessity argument (the pipeline is still justified by the SLA-assignment and evidence layers).
findings.fix: Soften to "KEV flags in scanner output vary by product and do not carry the BOD SLA assignment; this implementation performs the cross-reference explicitly so the SLA logic and evidence record are self-contained."

findings.claim: "The daily compliance summary JSON produced by the script above maps directly to the CDM Agency Dashboard vulnerability data schema."
findings.problem: "Maps directly" to a named federal schema is a verifiable-sounding claim with no schema citation, field mapping, or version reference anywhere in the document; the summary JSON is a custom structure defined in this book. An ISSO coordinating with the CDM team on the strength of this sentence would find no mapping to hand them.
findings.fix: Either include/refer to an actual field mapping to the CDM data-exchange requirement (the Multi-Cloud Evidence Fabric book per the spine owns telemetry-to-CDM), or soften to "is structured to support onward reporting into CDM; coordinate the field mapping with your CDM team."

findings.claim: Cloud-native posture feeds "KSI-CM (Configuration Management)" — stated in prose (line 174), in the fig-alt (line 181, "Card one, KSI-CM: Configuration Management"), and in the CM-6 row of the authorities table (line 165, "KSI-CM, KSI-SVC").
findings.problem: No KSI-CM theme exists. The spine SSOT (aan-compliance-spine.yml line 288) maps this book's CM-6 to ksi: [KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC], and the in-repo CR26 theme registry (AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md) enumerates the FedRAMP 20x themes — KSI-CMT is 'Change Management'; there is no 'KSI-CM' and no 'Configuration Management' theme. The table claims to be 'generated from aan-compliance-spine.yml' yet diverges from it, so a 3PAO tracing the KSI id to the FedRAMP 20x definitions would find a nonexistent indicator theme.
findings.fix: Regenerate the authorities table from the spine (KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC) and rewrite the prose/fig-alt to name the real theme id and its official name (KSI-CMT — Change Management), or, if Configuration-Management semantics are intended, change the spine mapping deliberately — but the doc and spine must agree and the id must exist in CR26.

findings.claim: Fig-alt for the KSI figure glosses KSI-MLA as "Monitoring, Logging and Alerting".
findings.problem: The in-repo CR26 registry (AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md lines 42-46, 74) gives the official theme name as "Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing". Misnaming an official FedRAMP 20x theme in a compliance book invites a credibility hit from a reviewer who checks it.
findings.fix: Change the fig-alt (and the source figure spec specs/Vol_III_Book_04.yaml line 574, which has the same error) to "Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing".

findings.claim: Defender for Cloud is 'a clean fit' as the Moderate default because it 'does multi-cloud CSPM/CWPP across AWS, GCP, and Azure' — while the estate is defined (lines 61-62) as 'AWS GovCloud, Azure, OCI, plus Kubernetes — AKS/EKS/OKE/OpenShift', and the CM-6 closure mechanism is 'misconfiguration detection across CSPs / every CSP'.
findings.problem: The recommended Moderate default's stated coverage (AWS, GCP, Azure) does not include OCI, which the same document names as part of the estate; GCP, which it does cover, is not in the estate. The doc never says how CM-6 'across every CSP' is closed for OCI/OKE if Defender for Cloud is chosen — a hostile ISSO will ask exactly this, since the CM-6 row claims closure across CSPs.
findings.fix: Either state the OCI posture path explicitly (native OCI Cloud Guard feed into the evidence fabric, or acknowledge OCI as a residual gap under the Defender option) or scope the Defender claim to the CSPs it actually covers and note the OCI decision in the flag list.

findings.claim: Cloud-control-plane and container-layer questions 'are where most real cloud incidents begin: misconfiguration, excessive entitlement, and exposure — not an unpatched kernel.'
findings.problem: An uncited majority claim ('most real cloud incidents') presented as fact. It is a widely repeated industry assertion, but with no source a reviewer can strike it, and the book's motivation leans on it.
findings.fix: Either cite an authoritative source (e.g., a Verizon DBIR / CISA advisory figure) in the References table, or soften to a defensible statement ('a dominant class of cloud incidents' / 'a persistent leading cause in incident reporting').

findings.claim: 'Prisma Cloud is the most complete CNAPP' (line 97-98) and Prisma Cloud/Wiz 'are the most complete CNAPPs' (line 189).
findings.problem: Competitive superlative asserted as fact with no analyst citation or evaluation criteria. In a procurement-adjacent document this reads as pre-judging the market and would be challenged in formal review; it also sits oddly beside the document's own recommendation of Defender for Cloud.
findings.fix: Attribute it ('per the agency's market evaluation' / cite an analyst source in the References table) or soften to 'among the most feature-complete CNAPPs'.

findings.claim: Microsoft Defender for Cloud 'does multi-cloud CSPM/CWPP across AWS, GCP, and Azure and is available within GCC at FedRAMP Moderate'.
findings.problem: Vendor capability + authorization-level claim that must be confirmed against the FedRAMP Marketplace and Microsoft's Government service-availability docs at procurement (the doc does add a 'Verify on the FedRAMP Marketplace' caveat at line 191). Note also 'within GCC' is M365-tenant terminology applied to an Azure service — a reviewer may flag the wording as conflating GCC with Azure Government/Azure Commercial scope.
findings.fix: Keep the marketplace-verification caveat; consider rewording 'within GCC' to the correct cloud environment (Azure commercial/Azure Government) once verified.

findings.claim: Prisma Cloud is 'FedRAMP High-only, as is Wiz for Government' (also lines 190, 205-206).
findings.problem: External authorization-status claims sourced only to vendor blog posts (References lines 205-206). Authorization levels change; the FedRAMP Marketplace, not vendor blogs, is the authoritative record. The doc's own 'Verify on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement' caveat (line 192) mitigates but the References table should point at the authoritative source too.
findings.fix: Add the FedRAMP Marketplace listing URLs alongside (or instead of) the vendor blog links in the References table.

findings.claim: CM-8 row of the 'Authorities Closed Here' table lists FedRAMP 20x KSI as 'KSI-CM'.
findings.problem: The spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml, book-patch-sysmgmt block) maps CM-8 to KSI-PIY, and 'KSI-CM' does not exist in the vendored FedRAMP CR26 catalog (valid themes are 3-letter: KSI-CMT, KSI-CNA, KSI-CED, KSI-IAM, KSI-INR, KSI-MLA, KSI-PIY, KSI-RPL, KSI-SVC, KSI-SCR). Running `render_authorities_table.py --book book-patch-sysmgmt` produces KSI-PIY. A 3PAO checking KSI ids against the CR26 catalog would reject an invented theme id.
findings.fix: Replace the inline table with the current renderer output (CM-8 -> KSI-PIY).

findings.claim: CM-2 and CM-6 rows list FedRAMP 20x KSI as 'KSI-CM'.
findings.problem: The spine maps both CM-2 and CM-6 to KSI-CMT (Change Management). 'KSI-CM' is not a CR26 KSI theme. The committed partial authorities/authorities-book-patch-sysmgmt.md is correct (KSI-CMT); only this inline copy in the .qmd is wrong.
findings.fix: Re-paste the renderer output: CM-2 and CM-6 -> KSI-CMT.

findings.claim: SI-2(3) is titled 'Time to Remediate / Benchmarks'.
findings.problem: The official title in reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json and in the spine is 'Time to Remediate Flaws and Benchmarks for Corrective Actions'. The table claims to be generated from the spine, so this truncated title contradicts both SSOTs.
findings.fix: Use the full official title as emitted by render_authorities_table.py.

findings.claim: Table header comment states 'generated from aan-compliance-spine.yml; do not hand-edit'.
findings.problem: The inline table diverges from the renderer output in 4 cells (three KSI ids, one control title) and omits the generated 'Closure-Necessity — alternate-path rebuttals' block for CM-8 and SI-2 that the renderer emits. The drift gate (`render_authorities_table.py --check authorities`) passes because it only validates the authorities/*.md partials, not this inline copy — so this drift is NOT covered by the existing gate.
findings.fix: Sync the inline block (table + rebuttal bullets) with `python render_authorities_table.py --book book-patch-sysmgmt`, and consider extending the --check gate to scan the qmd inline copies.

findings.claim: 'the CM family feeds KSI-CM (Configuration Management)' in the FedRAMP 20x KSI Alignment section.
findings.problem: No KSI-CM theme exists in the CR26 catalog and no CR26 theme is named 'Configuration Management'. Per the spine, CM-2/CM-6 feed KSI-CMT (Change Management) and CM-8 feeds KSI-PIY (Policy and Inventory). The section's central mapping statement is wrong on both the id and the name.
findings.fix: Rewrite: CM-2/CM-6 feed KSI-CMT (Change Management); CM-8 feeds KSI-PIY (Policy and Inventory).

findings.claim: 'KSI-MLA (Monitoring, Logging, Alerting)'.
findings.problem: The CR26 catalog title for KSI-MLA is 'Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing' — Auditing, not Alerting. The id is right; the gloss misnames the indicator.
findings.fix: Change the parenthetical to 'Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing'.

findings.claim: 'Every stack in the actuation matrix is a CSP service, so its gate is FedRAMP — verify each stack's authorization status on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement'.
findings.problem: The doc's own actuation matrix includes stacks that are not CSP services: vSphere Lifecycle Manager on on-premises VMware (the doc itself frames VMware as 'on-premises'), Red Hat Satellite/Ansible on customer infrastructure, and MECM/WSUS (legacy, on-prem). FedRAMP authorizes cloud services only; a Marketplace check is inapplicable to these rows. A hostile ISSO would reject the blanket Theme F gate statement as factually wrong for at least three rows of the matrix.
findings.fix: Scope the FedRAMP-Marketplace gate to cloud-delivered stacks (Azure Update Manager/Intune, AWS SSM, OCI OS Management Hub, SaaS-delivered Workspace ONE) and state that on-prem tooling (vLCM, Satellite, MECM/WSUS) is gated by the agency ATO boundary, not FedRAMP.

findings.claim: 'The native stacks mapped here are each FedRAMP-authorized CSP capabilities' (Stack Selection Status callout), and the overlay option is described as 'an additional FedRAMP-authorized product in the boundary' (Tanium / BigFix / Ivanti).
findings.problem: Authorization status of Oracle OS Management Hub in OCI Government regions, Omnissa Workspace ONE, and Tanium/BigFix/Ivanti cannot be verified from in-repo SSOTs and is asserted as present-tense fact here, while the same callout and the Theme F section say verification on the FedRAMP Marketplace is still required — the flat claim and the pending-verification posture conflict.
findings.fix: Soften to conditional ('subject to Marketplace verification at procurement') or verify each product's Marketplace status externally before asserting.

findings.claim: Vendor capability claims: Ksplice 'applies kernel and user-space patches without a reboot'; OCI Autonomous DB 'self-patching'; Workspace ONE patching Windows, Linux, and macOS.
findings.problem: These are external vendor capability claims that cannot be confirmed from in-repo SSOTs. Vendor source links are present in the References table (per the series' vendor-sources convention), but the specific breadth claims (user-space Ksplice coverage; Workspace ONE as the Linux patch mechanism for on-prem VMware estates) should be checked against current vendor docs — Workspace ONE is now an Omnissa product and its Linux server-patching role is the weakest cell in the matrix.
findings.fix: Verify against the linked Oracle/Omnissa docs; if Workspace ONE does not cover Linux server patching, point that cell at Satellite/Ansible or Aria instead.

findings.claim: Artifact 3 says US-CERT/CISA notification is 'per OMB M-20-04 (72-hour reporting requirement for major incidents)'.
findings.problem: The callout at line ~728 in the same file says OMB M-20-04 requires major-incident reporting to US-CERT 'within 1 hour of discovery'. Both cannot be true, and M-20-04's actual requirement is 1 hour to CISA for major incidents (7 days to Congress); there is no 72-hour requirement in M-20-04. A 3PAO would reject an IR plan built on a wrong notification clock.
findings.fix: Change Artifact 3 to the 1-hour CISA notification requirement so it matches the callout; delete the 72-hour figure or attribute it to the authority that actually imposes it.

findings.claim: The retention script sets TotalRetentionInDays 730 (2 years) for DeviceEvents, CommonSecurityLog, and AzureDiagnostics.
findings.problem: The file's own AU-11 doctrine says the floor is 3 years: the callout at line ~246 states 'not less than 3 years... under NARA GRS 3.2', Tier 2 at line ~739 says '90 days to 3 years total', and the closure-table AU-11 row (line ~811) claims 'per-table retention configured to meet NARA GRS 3.2 minimum'. CommonSecurityLog and AzureDiagnostics hold the InfoBlox DNS, SASE, and SQL audit records the series treats as audit evidence — configuring them at 730 days contradicts the stated 3-year floor and would surface as an AU-11 finding.
findings.fix: Either set TotalRetentionInDays 1095 for the high-volume tables or explicitly scope which tables are audit records subject to the 3-year floor (with the WORM tier covering the rest) and reconcile the Tier 2 and closure-table language.

findings.claim: The retention architecture presents 90-day interactive + archive + WORM as satisfying AU-11, citing only NARA GRS 3.2.
findings.problem: OMB M-21-31 (the governing federal log-retention memo, which FedRAMP Rev5 AU-11 parameters reference) requires 12 months of ACTIVE (readily accessible) storage plus 18 months cold at EL1. A 90-day interactive tier with everything beyond in the async-query archive tier does not meet the 12-month active-storage requirement, and the document never mentions M-21-31. A hostile ISSO would raise exactly this gap.
findings.fix: Address M-21-31 explicitly: either extend interactive retention to 12 months for in-scope tables or document how the archive tier's query-job latency is argued to satisfy 'active storage', with the risk acceptance noted.

findings.claim: The auto-isolate playbook references 'the KEV CVE Actively Exploited rule (Section 4, Rule 10)'.
findings.problem: By document order the KEV rule is the 9th rule in Section 4 (rules 1-10 in prose: DNS C2, Impossible Travel, PIM off-hours, New GA, MFA fatigue, SA re-enabled, SQL unexpected IP, NTLM post-block, KEV, SASE upload; the table then starts at Rule 11). Rule 10 is the SASE data-volume rule. The cross-reference points at the wrong rule.
findings.fix: Change 'Rule 10' to 'Rule 9', or add explicit rule numbers to the Section 4 prose headings so references are unambiguous.

findings.claim: InfoBlox contribution totals '10-15 EPS average'; Entra ID sign-ins '50,000-200,000 per day... averaging 2-7 EPS'.
findings.problem: Neither total reproduces from its own stated components. InfoBlox: ~6 EPS DNS + 0.5 EPS DHCP + <1 RPZ event/min sums to ~6.5-7 EPS, not 10-15. Entra: 50,000-200,000 events/day is 0.6-2.3 EPS, not 2-7 EPS (7 EPS would be ~600,000/day, line ~137). A reviewer checking the arithmetic gets different numbers than the document asserts.
findings.fix: Recompute and make the totals consistent with the per-source figures (or state what additional volume the higher totals include, e.g. DNS response logging doubling query EPS).

findings.claim: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 is cited as the incident-response lifecycle authority (Section 7 heading, mapping table, and the IR-8 closure-table Authority column).
findings.problem: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 (April 2025) superseded and withdrew Rev 2, replacing the four-phase lifecycle with a CSF 2.0-aligned model. A 2026-dated document mapping its IR plan structure to a withdrawn revision is a citation a 3PAO would flag on the IR-8 artifact review.
findings.fix: Cite SP 800-61 Rev 3 and either re-map the table to its model or note that the agency IR plan retains the Rev 2 phase names as an internal convention.

findings.claim: OMB M-20-04 is cited as the operative major-incident reporting authority, with 'US-CERT' as the reporting destination.
findings.problem: M-20-04 is the FY2019-2020 FISMA guidance memo and has been superseded by successive annual FISMA memos; the US-CERT brand was retired into CISA. An IR plan citing an expired memo and a retired organization as its reporting pathway would draw an assessor comment even though the 1-hour requirement itself carried forward.
findings.fix: Cite the current-year OMB FISMA guidance memo (verify the current M-number) and 'CISA' as the reporting destination.

findings.claim: 'The CISA advisory AA22-119A documents this technique [MFA fatigue/push bombing] as actively used against federal agencies by nation-state actors.'
findings.problem: The advisory ID cannot be verified against in-repo SSOTs. The CISA advisory commonly cited for nation-state MFA abuse against organizations is AA22-074A (Russian state actors exploiting default MFA protocols); AA22-119A does not obviously match this topic. If the ID is wrong, the rule's threat justification cites a nonexistent or unrelated source.
findings.fix: Verify the advisory number against cisa.gov and correct or add the source link per the series' 'Vendor sources:' convention.

findings.claim: 'The 2023 CISA/NSA advisory on Microsoft cloud security vulnerabilities documented cases where adversaries maintained persistent access to federal tenant environments for months before detection.'
findings.problem: No advisory ID or link is given, and the claim carries the document's core motivation. Unverifiable as written; a reviewer cannot locate 'the 2023 CISA/NSA advisory' from this description (the Storm-0558 incident was covered by a CSRB report and CISA guidance, not obviously a joint CISA/NSA advisory).
findings.fix: Name the specific advisory/report with its identifier and link, or soften to a sourced example.

findings.claim: SA account must be disabled 'per CIS SQL Server benchmark and STIG V-79075'.
findings.problem: The specific STIG vulnerability ID cannot be verified in-repo; SQL Server 2016 STIG IDs in the V-791xx range cover the sa account, so V-79075 may be the wrong rule. A wrong STIG ID in a detection-rule justification is the kind of detail a 3PAO spot-checks.
findings.fix: Verify the STIG rule ID against the current DISA SQL Server STIG and cite the SRG/STIG version alongside it.

findings.claim: The Microsoft 365 Defender connector streams 'DeviceAlertEvents' and 'DeviceVulnerabilityAssessmentEvents' tables into Sentinel; the KEV rule queries 'DeviceVulnerabilityAssessmentEvent' with EventType == "Exploit".
findings.problem: Two issues. Internal: the table name is spelled 'DeviceVulnerabilityAssessmentEvents' at line ~163 and 'DeviceVulnerabilityAssessmentEvent' at line ~167 — at most one can be a real table. External: the current M365 Defender streaming API exposes AlertInfo/AlertEvidence (not DeviceAlertEvents) and does not stream TVM vulnerability-assessment data as an event table, so the KEV detection logic in Section 4 may reference tables and an EventType field that do not exist in Sentinel.
findings.fix: Verify the streaming API event-type list against Microsoft Learn; likely rewrite to AlertInfo/AlertEvidence and base the KEV rule on Defender alerts or a DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities export rather than a nonexistent streaming table.

findings.claim: UEBA is enabled via a 'Set-AzSentinelUeba' PowerShell cmdlet with a -DataSources parameter.
findings.problem: No such cmdlet is known in Az.SecurityInsights; Sentinel UEBA is enabled through the portal Entity Behavior settings or the settings REST API. If the cmdlet does not exist, the only enablement procedure the document provides fails as written.
findings.fix: Verify against the Az.SecurityInsights module reference; replace with the documented portal steps or the REST/az rest call.

findings.claim: Sentinel analytics rules 'support a "test rule" function that fires a simulated alert through the full automation chain', offered as a way to satisfy the IR-3 annual test.
findings.problem: This is load-bearing for the IR-3/Artifact-7 evidence claim, and Sentinel's rule simulation feature previews historical match results — it is not known to fire a live alert through automation rules and playbooks. If the capability does not exist as described, the proposed annual-test method cannot produce the claimed artifact.
findings.fix: Verify the capability on Microsoft Learn; if absent, substitute a documented method (e.g., a benign trigger event or manually created incident driving the automation chain).

findings.claim: Built-in TI map analytics rules cross-reference all log sources against the indicator table 'every 15 minutes' (repeated in the SI-4(2) closure row as 'TI indicator correlation runs every 15 min').
findings.problem: The built-in TI map rule templates default to an hourly schedule; the 15-minute figure is a specific product-behavior claim with no source, and it is reused as SI-4(2) closure evidence.
findings.fix: Verify the default query frequency of the TI map rule templates and either correct the number or state it as a configured (not default) frequency.

findings.claim: The compound impossible-travel + high-risk condition 'has an extremely low false positive rate (legitimate impossible travel that also triggers Identity Protection high risk is essentially non-existent)', justifying automated account disable without SOC approval.
findings.problem: An absolute FP-rate claim with no data or citation is used to justify the document's most aggressive automated action (disabling a user account with no human gate). A hostile reviewer will ask for the evidence behind 'essentially non-existent' — none is provided, and the document elsewhere (line ~674) requires an approval gate for the analogous device-isolation action.
findings.fix: Either present measured/base-rate support, or align with the isolation playbook by adding a tuning-period approval gate before fully automated disable.

findings.claim: The cost model is 'illustrative at the EPS volumes estimated in Section 2'.
findings.problem: The per-connector EPS estimates are in Section 3 (Microsoft Sentinel Connector Architecture); Section 2 is the log-warehouse/detection-engine distinction and contains no EPS estimates. Wrong internal cross-reference.
findings.fix: Change 'Section 2' to 'Section 3'.

findings.claim: Vendor pricing/limits claims carry no sources: archive retention 'Up to 7 years' at '~1/12 the hot cost', and commitment tiers reducing ingestion cost 'by 15-65%'.
findings.problem: These are external Microsoft product claims (Log Analytics total retention was extended beyond 7 years, to 12 years) presented without the 'Vendor sources:' links the series' authoring spec requires for vendor claims; the 7-year figure is likely outdated.
findings.fix: Verify current Log Analytics retention maximums and Sentinel commitment-tier discounts on Microsoft Learn/pricing pages and add 'Vendor sources:' links.

findings.claim: AU-10 closure row cites 'FedRAMP Moderate AU-10' as authority, and the document argues AU-10 satisfaction (via Purview Audit Premium) is required for 'a complete FedRAMP Moderate authorization' (lines 53, 744, 859).
findings.problem: AU-10 (Non-repudiation) is not in the NIST SP 800-53B Moderate baseline or the FedRAMP Rev 5 Moderate baseline — it is a High-baseline control. The spine's stated baseline is '800-53B Moderate'. Citing 'FedRAMP Moderate AU-10' is a false authority citation a 3PAO would immediately correct, and it makes the Audit-Premium purchase argument look mandatory when it is not at Moderate scope.
findings.fix: Change the authority to 'NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-10 (above-baseline / defense-in-depth)' and reframe AU-10 as a deliberate above-Moderate-baseline enhancement rather than a Moderate requirement; remove AU-10 from any 'required for FedRAMP Moderate authorization' framing.

findings.claim: Standard M365 unified audit logs are 'mutable by a Global Administrator'; Purview Audit Premium provides 'immutable log storage in a location not accessible to tenant administrators, and cryptographic signatures on high-value audit events' bound to 'a timestamp issued by a trusted timestamping authority' (lines 654-657, 70, 859); MailItemsAccessed 'Proves' specific access (lines 702-711).
findings.problem: This is the load-bearing mechanism for the AU-10 closure, and neither half matches documented Microsoft behavior: Microsoft describes the unified audit log as immutable even at the standard tier (admins can disable ingestion going forward but cannot alter or delete existing records), and no Microsoft documentation describes cryptographic signatures or trusted-timestamping of Audit Premium records — Premium adds retention, events, and API bandwidth. No vendor source link is provided as the series authoring spec requires. A 3PAO asked to verify 'signed audit records' would find no such feature.
findings.fix: Rewrite the AU-10 mechanism to claims Microsoft actually documents (out-of-tenant storage, admin inability to modify records, long retention, MailItemsAccessed coverage), drop 'cryptographic signatures'/'timestamping authority'/'signed' language and the 'Proves' phrasing unless a Microsoft source is cited, and add 'Vendor sources:' links.

findings.claim: SC-12(1) is titled 'Cryptographic Key Availability' in the closure table (line 865) and 'Availability of Key Management' in the fig-alt (line 854).
findings.problem: The official Rev 5 title in the in-repo catalog (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json) is 'Availability'. The document gives two different invented titles for the same enhancement, contradicting the SSOT and itself.
findings.fix: Use 'SC-12(1) Availability' in both the table and the figure/fig-alt.

findings.claim: AU-10 'states: "Provide irrefutable evidence that an individual (or process acting on behalf of an individual) performed [Assignment: ...] on the information system."'
findings.problem: The Rev 5 AU-10 control statement ends at the assignment; 'on the information system' is not in the Rev 5 text (Rev 5 deliberately dropped 'information system' phrasing). Presenting altered text as a verbatim quote of a control is exactly what a hostile reviewer spot-checks.
findings.fix: Quote the Rev 5 statement exactly, ending at the assignment bracket.

findings.claim: SC-17 'states: "Issue public key certificates under an appropriate certificate policy or obtain public key certificates from an approved service provider."' and the CPS chapter then claims SC-17 closure.
findings.problem: Rev 5 SC-17 is two parts: (a) issue under an [Assignment: organization-defined certificate policy] or obtain from an approved provider, AND (b) include only approved trust anchors in trust stores. The quote substitutes 'an appropriate certificate policy' for the assignment and omits part (b) entirely; the chapter never addresses trust-anchor management, so the claimed SC-17 closure covers only half the control.
findings.fix: Quote both parts accurately and add a trust-anchor management paragraph (e.g., GPO/Intune-managed trust stores containing only the agency Root CA and approved public roots) to the CPS section and closure-table 'With' cell.

findings.claim: MP-2 (Media Access) and MP-3 (Media Marking) are closed by sensitivity labels on SharePoint documents; MP-4/MP-5 by CMK encryption and DLP (closure table lines 860-863).
findings.problem: The MP family governs system media (removable media, paper, output). Mapping label-based access and marking of SaaS files to MP-2/MP-3 is a mapping a 3PAO would challenge; the natural Rev 5 control for sensitivity labels is AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes), which the document never cites. Only the endpoint-DLP USB/print controls have a defensible MP nexus (MP-5/MP-7 territory).
findings.fix: Re-anchor labels/DLP to AC-16 and AC-4, keep MP claims only where physical/removable media is actually controlled (endpoint USB/print), and mark the remaining MP rows as 'supports' rather than 'closes'.

findings.claim: FIPS 140-2 Level 2 is 'required to satisfy SC-12 and SC-13 at the Moderate impact level' (line 477); CPS Section 6 mandates 'FIPS 140-2 Level 2 minimum' (line 771); SC-13 authority cell cites 'FIPS 140-2 Level 2' (line 866).
findings.problem: The document's own multi-cloud section (line 841) instructs verifying FIPS 140-3 CMVP certificates and warns against 'new procurement reliance on 140-2-only modules', and the deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml, fips-140-2-historical) records FIPS 140-2 validations moving to the CMVP Historical List on 2026-09-21 — about ten weeks after this document's Date Code. Prescribing FIPS 140-2 as the forward-looking requirement contradicts both.
findings.fix: State the requirement as FIPS 140-3 validated (or '140-3, or 140-2 only where the module remains on the Active list pending the 2026-09-21 Historical transition') in all three locations.

findings.claim: The listed events (MailItemsAccessed, SearchQueryInitiated*, Send, FileDownloaded, SensitivityLabelApplied/Updated) are 'captured exclusively by Purview Audit Premium (not available in standard Audit)'.
findings.problem: FileDownloaded and the sensitivity-label events are available in standard (Audit Standard) logging; only the MailItemsAccessed/SearchQueryInitiated/Send family is Premium-gated. The 'exclusively' claim overstates the Premium dependency and would fail a documentation check.
findings.fix: Split the table into Premium-only events vs. standard events, or drop 'exclusively', and cite the Microsoft audit-solutions comparison page.

findings.claim: 'Standard audit log retention is 90 days' (AU-10 'Without' cell).
findings.problem: Microsoft raised default Audit Standard retention from 90 to 180 days (effective for records generated on or after October 2023). As written the pre-implementation state is factually stale, weakening the document's credibility on its own vendor facts.
findings.fix: Update to 180 days and add a vendor source link.

findings.claim: 10-year audit retention 'Requires Purview Audit Premium license assigned to users' (lines 672-677, and '10-year retention' in the AU-10 closure row).
findings.problem: Ten-year retention requires the separate '10-Year Audit Log Retention' add-on license on top of Audit Premium/E5; Audit Premium alone caps at 1-year (configurable retention policies up to 1 year, 10 years only with the add-on). A budgeting reader would under-license.
findings.fix: Name the 10-Year Audit Log Retention add-on explicitly as the licensing prerequisite.

findings.claim: The FedRAMP 20x callout names KSIs 'Data Protection', 'Cryptographic Key Management', 'Non-repudiation and Audit Integrity', and 'Boundary Protection' as categories the controls contribute to.
findings.problem: These are not FedRAMP 20x KSI categories. The spine (the series KSI SSOT) uses the official theme ids (KSI-CNA, KSI-IAM, KSI-MLA, KSI-SVC, ...); there is no 'Non-repudiation and Audit Integrity' KSI. Free-invented KSI names in a 20x-alignment section are exactly what a 20x-literate reviewer would flag, especially given the series' own CR26 indicator-count discipline.
findings.fix: Map to the real KSI ids — encryption/key management under KSI-SVC, logging/audit under KSI-MLA, boundary under KSI-CNA — matching the spine's ksi vocabulary.

findings.claim: 'The minimum federal standard for symmetric encryption keys is annual rotation.'
findings.problem: No federal instrument sets annual rotation as a minimum standard for symmetric keys; NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 (which the SC-12 row itself cites) gives recommended cryptoperiods (e.g., up to 2 years originator-usage for symmetric data-encryption keys) and leaves the period organization-defined under SC-12. Stating a nonexistent 'minimum federal standard' invites an easy challenge.
findings.fix: Rephrase as an organization-defined policy choice ('this architecture adopts a 12-month cryptoperiod, within SP 800-57 Part 1 recommendations').

findings.claim: The key-management section frames a 'GCC (Government Community Cloud) environment' (line 463) while the code deploys Key Vault to 'USGov Virginia' with the comment '# GCC-High: use USGov regions' (line 487).
findings.problem: The comment attributes Azure Government regions to GCC-High, while the series scope (spine meta) is GCC/FedRAMP Moderate and Vol I Book 01 describes the SSA Azure estate as 'Microsoft Azure Government (GCC Moderate)'. As written the snippet tells a Moderate-scoped reader that the region choice belongs to a High enclave — a scope confusion an ISSO would query, in a series that must never lean on High.
findings.fix: Fix the comment to match the series posture (e.g., '# SSA Azure Government estate per Vol I Book 01; commercial regions if the tenant is commercial Azure') and remove the GCC-High reference.

findings.claim: 'Vol III Book 06 addresses Security Operations, Monitoring, and Incident Response.'
findings.problem: The spine registry (book-13) and the target file's own frontmatter title Vol III Book 06 as 'SIEM, XDR, and Detection Engineering' ('SIEM / XDR Detection' in the spine). The stale descriptive title breaks the cross-reference against the SSOT.
findings.fix: Reference it as 'SIEM, XDR, and Detection Engineering' (also at line 744 where it is called 'the Microsoft Sentinel SIEM deployed in Vol III Book 06' — that clause is fine, only the line-39 title needs the fix).

findings.claim: 'Azure Key Vault Premium tier uses HSM-protected keys (FIPS 140-2 Level 2)'; multi-cloud table asserts AWS KMS/CloudHSM are 'FIPS 140-3 validated HSM'; 'the Purview Data Map reaches multi-cloud sources'; portal at 'compliance.microsoft.com' (line 117).
findings.problem: Vendor facts with no 'Vendor sources:' links as the series authoring spec requires. Microsoft has since migrated Key Vault Premium HSMs toward FIPS 140-3 validation, and the compliance portal has been consolidated into purview.microsoft.com — both statements may be stale. Not judged true/false here; they need verification against current vendor documentation.
findings.fix: Verify each against current Microsoft/AWS documentation and add source links per the Federal_AAN_Series_Authoring_Spec vendor-claims rule.

findings.claim: 'An employee pasting a Social Security Number into a Teams message sends it to the Teams service in plaintext.'
findings.problem: Teams traffic is TLS-encrypted in transit and encrypted at rest; 'in plaintext' is literally false. The intended point is that the SSN is undetected/unclassified, not unencrypted.
findings.fix: Rephrase: 'sends it to the Teams service uninspected and unclassified' (the encryption is transport-level, not a content control).

findings.claim: The closure figure and fig-alt are titled 'Part 12 — NIST SP 800-53 Control Closure' / 'NIST control closure for Part 12 Data Protection'.
findings.problem: The document is Vol III Book 05 (spine book-12 is only the internal registry id); 'Part 12' is legacy series numbering that no longer appears anywhere else in the document — the table caption on line 870 correctly says 'Vol III Book 05'. Inconsistent numbering inside one section will read as a versioning error.
findings.fix: Regenerate the figure and fig-alt with 'Vol III Book 05' naming.

findings.claim: The volume is "a proof that the substrate holds under real production load."
findings.problem: The document's own banner declares it a draft proposal that has not been reviewed or approved, and no production migration has been executed. Nothing in Vol II Books 01-03 (runbooks and architecture guidance) constitutes evidence of behavior under real production load. A hostile ISSO/3PAO would reject 'proof' as an assurance claim with no supporting artifact.
findings.fix: Soften to intent, e.g. 'and the first end-to-end test of whether the substrate holds under real production load' or 'is designed to demonstrate that the substrate holds...'.

findings.claim: "eliminates stored SQL credentials through Arc Managed Identity and token-based authentication" and (line 61) "Entra Conditional Access as the SQL perimeter" — Microsoft product-capability claims (Arc-enabled SQL Server Entra managed-identity auth; Conditional Access applying to SQL connections).
findings.problem: These are vendor-capability claims that require verification against Microsoft documentation, and the series' own authoring spec (Federal_AAN_Series_Authoring_Spec.md) requires 'Vendor sources:' links wherever vendor claims are made; this overview carries none. Not judged true/false here — flagged as needing external verification or an explicit deferral to the sourced claims in Vol II Book 01.
findings.fix: Either add the 'Vendor sources:' links per the series spec, or rephrase to attribute the mechanism to the downstream book (e.g. 'as documented and sourced in Vol II Book 01') so this intro makes no free-standing vendor claim.

findings.claim: "its geo-replicated DR replicas are the Section-5 recovery content the Business Continuity book (Vol IV Book 01) assembles into a CP-2 plan"
findings.problem: Vol IV Book 01 states the DR RUNBOOKS from Vol II Books 02-03 are the Section-5 (Recovery Procedures) content; the geo-replicated replicas themselves are mapped to CP-6 (Alternate Storage Site) content. Saying the replicas are the Section-5 content slightly misstates the downstream book's own mapping.
findings.fix: Rephrase to 'its DR runbooks and geo-replicated replica architecture are the Section-5 recovery procedures and CP-6 alternate-storage content the Business Continuity book assembles into a CP-2 plan' (or simply cite the runbooks as the Section-5 content).

findings.claim: "the primary KSI-MLA (Monitoring, Logging, Alerting) evidence source"
findings.problem: FedRAMP 20x names the KSI-MLA family "Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing" — the A is Auditing, not Alerting. No in-repo SSOT carries KSI family names, so nothing gates this; a 3PAO working from the FedRAMP 20x KSI list would flag the mis-expansion of the exact KSI family this book claims as its primary alignment. (Corpus-wide: the same "Alerting" expansion appears 4 times across .qmd files, so fixing only this file leaves an internal inconsistency.)
findings.fix: Change the expansion to "Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing" after confirming against fedramp.gov/20x KSI list; sweep the other 3 corpus occurrences in the same pass, and consider adding KSI family names to an in-repo reference SSOT.

findings.claim: Table row: "AU-12(1) † | System-Wide / Time-Correlated Audit Trail"
