findings.problem: Both the NIST catalog SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json) and the spine give the title as "System-wide and Time-correlated Audit Trail"; regenerating with render_authorities_table.py --book book-evidence-fabric confirms the generator emits the spine title. The inline .qmd copy was hand-altered ("and" → "/", changed capitalization), contradicting the file's own claim at line 174 that the table is "generated ... not hand-maintained". The drift gate only checks the authorities/ partials (which are correct), not this inline copy, so this divergence is ungated.
findings.fix: Replace the inline table with the exact generator output (title "System-wide and Time-correlated Audit Trail"), and consider extending the drift gate to cover inline .qmd copies of the generated block.

findings.claim: "closes the AU/CA/SI controls that only a cross-surface fabric can close"
findings.problem: The spine marks only 2 of this book's 6 controls (AU-3, AU-12(1)) as Closure-Necessity anchors (necessity: true / no alternate closure path); AU-12, AU-6(1), CA-7, and SI-4(16) are necessity: false — CA-7 is even closed a second time by book-sn-attestation in the spine. Read naturally, the sentence claims all the book's controls are fabric-only closures, which contradicts the spine and the file's own table legend († on only two rows). A hostile ISSO would counter that CA-7 is closed by ordinary ConMon programs without any cross-surface fabric.
findings.fix: Rephrase to match the spine, e.g. "closes the AU/CA/SI controls of the telemetry slot — two of which (AU-3, AU-12(1)) only a cross-surface fabric can close".

findings.claim: BMC Helix listed under the "Moderate alternative" column of the realizations table
findings.problem: Placement in the "Moderate alternative" column implicitly asserts BMC Helix holds a FedRAMP Moderate authorization, but unlike Sentinel, Splunk, and ServiceNow, BMC Helix has no entry in the References table and no FedRAMP Marketplace link — violating the series' own vendor-sources convention. Cannot be judged true or false from in-repo SSOTs.
findings.fix: Verify BMC Helix's authorization on the FedRAMP Marketplace and add a sourced reference row, or remove/requalify the alternative.

findings.claim: "Microsoft Sentinel — ingests AWS (Security Hub / GuardDuty / CloudTrail), OCI, GCP, and NEM syslog/CEF; FedRAMP-authorized" and "Splunk Cloud Platform (FedRAMP Moderate)" (Marketplace id F1607197917 at line 227)
findings.problem: Vendor capability and authorization claims requiring external verification: Sentinel's specific connector coverage in the Government cloud, its authorization level, and Splunk Cloud Platform's Moderate listing/marketplace id cannot be confirmed from in-repo SSOTs. The file does hedge correctly ("Verify all authorizations on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement") and both claims carry source links, so this is a verification note, not an error.
findings.fix: At procurement review, verify Sentinel and Splunk entries on the FedRAMP Marketplace and Sentinel's Gov-cloud connector availability on Microsoft Learn; no text change required now.

findings.claim: "ServiceNow (FedRAMP-authorized; ITOM/CMDB/SecOps)" cited to a ServiceNow press release whose URL announces FedRAMP High authorization
findings.problem: The prose claims only "FedRAMP-authorized" (no scope violation — the hyphenated URL slug also does not trip the High-claim gate, and the file has a zero baseline), but a Moderate-scoped series citing a vendor High press release invites reviewer questions, and a press release is a weaker citation than the FedRAMP Marketplace listing used for the Splunk row. Which ServiceNow offering/level applies needs external verification.
findings.fix: Swap the citation to the ServiceNow FedRAMP Marketplace listing (parallel to the Splunk row) and verify the offering's authorization level at procurement.

findings.claim: fig-02 caption cites briefing-deck "Date Code 2026-07-09 08:15 ET" while figs 03/04/05 alt-text cite "Date Code 2026-07-09 17:00 ET" for the same deck
findings.problem: One source deck is cited with two different Date Codes within the same file, and the 08:15 ET code predates the document's own 08:41 ET Date Code — under the series' Date-Code-to-the-minute convention this reads as a stale figure caption. The derivative-freshness gate passed, so this pairing is evidently outside its 24 tracked pairs.
findings.fix: Align all four figure captions/alt-texts to the deck's actual current Date Code (presumably 2026-07-09 17:00 ET).

findings.claim: "BOD 25-01 and OMB M-22-09. Both directives require elimination of NTLM in federal environments" (and line 172: NTLMv1 "is prohibited under BOD 25-01").
findings.problem: The spine's own authority registry describes CISA BOD 25-01 as "Secure cloud baselines (SCuBA)" — a Microsoft-cloud (M365) baseline directive that does not address NTLM, an on-prem AD protocol. OMB M-22-09 (Federal Zero Trust Strategy) also does not name NTLM. A hostile ISSO checking either instrument will find no NTLM-elimination requirement, undermining the book's core mandate framing.
findings.fix: Rewrite the mandate anchor honestly: NTLM elimination is driven by zero-trust doctrine (M-22-09's move to phishing-resistant, centrally-verified auth) and Microsoft's own NTLM deprecation, not by a named prohibition in BOD 25-01. Remove both BOD 25-01 attributions.

findings.claim: Control table row: "AU-2 | Audit Events".
findings.problem: The in-repo SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, catalog v5.2.0) titles AU-2 "Event Logging". "Audit Events" is the Rev 4 title — an instant tell to a 3PAO that the mapping was written against the wrong revision. (Also referenced at lines 180 and 380.)
findings.fix: Change the AU-2 title to "Event Logging" everywhere it is spelled out.

findings.claim: Hand-authored table claims 14 controls (IA-2 … SI-4) are "Closed By" this book's mechanisms.
findings.problem: aan-compliance-spine.yml — the declared SSOT for closure claims — registers ZERO closures for book-07 (this file). The spine says closures are back-filled per book, but until they are, the book asserts closure of 14 controls that the series SSOT does not back, and this hand table is not covered by the render_authorities_table.py drift gate.
findings.fix: Back-fill book-07 closure rows in aan-compliance-spine.yml (or soften the table heading from "Control Closure" / "Closed By" to "controls addressed" until the spine rows exist).

findings.claim: "SQL Server 2019 is supported through Extended Security Updates (ESU) via Azure Arc at no additional cost."
findings.problem: External Microsoft licensing claim requiring vendor verification. Two elements look wrong on their face: SQL Server 2019 is still inside its normal extended-support window in 2026 (ESU is a post-end-of-support program), and Arc-delivered ESUs are generally a paid monthly subscription, not free. Do not judge here — verify against Microsoft lifecycle/ESU documentation.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft's SQL Server lifecycle and Arc ESU pricing pages; correct the support-window and cost characterization, and add a Vendor sources: link per the series authoring spec.

findings.claim: Layer 1 requirements: "SQL Server 2022 (or SQL Server 2019 with the Entra extension)".
findings.problem: External product claim needing verification: Microsoft documents Entra ID authentication for Arc-enabled SQL Server as a SQL Server 2022 feature; support on SQL Server 2019 is doubtful. It also contradicts the file's own line 104, which says only "SQL Server 2022 with the Entra authentication extension" can use the identity.
findings.fix: Verify minimum SQL Server version for Entra authentication against Microsoft docs; if 2022-only, delete the 2019 parenthetical so lines 104 and 110 agree.

findings.claim: "Windows Server 2025 (the first version with stable Entra ID OS login)" plus "Entra ID Joined enrollment (Entra Join, not Hybrid Join)" for servers.
findings.problem: External product claim needing verification: Microsoft's published guidance has historically stated Windows Server does not support Entra join for OS login (Entra join is a client-OS capability); Windows Server 2025's exact posture must be confirmed. If wrong, the entire Layer 2 architecture rests on an unsupported configuration — a rejection-grade finding.
findings.fix: Verify Windows Server 2025 Entra join / Entra OS-login support against Microsoft documentation before shipping; cite the source, or reframe Layer 2 around a supported mechanism (e.g., Arc-based access controls).

findings.claim: "schema migration from SQL Server to PostgreSQL requires the SQL Server Migration Assistant (SSMA) for PostgreSQL".
findings.problem: External product claim needing verification: the SSMA family (Oracle, MySQL, DB2, Access, SAP ASE) migrates INTO SQL Server; a Microsoft "SSMA for PostgreSQL" that converts SQL Server schemas to PostgreSQL does not appear to exist. Naming a nonexistent tool as "required" is an easy credibility hit.
findings.fix: Verify the tooling; likely replace with an actual SQL Server→PostgreSQL path (e.g., Azure DMS, pgloader, or third-party converters) with a source link.

findings.claim: "For cross-site NTLM, Phase B deploys Cloud Kerberos Trust — an Azure AD Kerberos server that issues partial Kerberos tickets satisfied by Entra ID. This allows Kerberos authentication across network boundaries without requiring a reachable on-premises KDC."
findings.problem: External product claim needing verification: Cloud Kerberos Trust (Microsoft Entra Kerberos) is documented for Windows Hello for Business sign-in and Azure Files scenarios, and the partial TGT still requires the client to exchange it with an on-prem DC for service tickets to on-prem SQL. Presenting it as a general no-KDC-needed fix for cross-site SQL Kerberos overstates the documented scope.
findings.fix: Verify the exact Cloud Kerberos Trust ticket flow against Microsoft docs and restate what it does and does not remove (on-prem DC reachability for service tickets), or route this pattern to Entra-native auth only.

findings.claim: Connection-string "Before/After" example: before is Server=sql01.agency.gov (on-prem), after is Server=sql01.database.usgovcloudapi.net (Azure SQL Government endpoint).
findings.problem: The section is about changing the authentication directive on existing (Arc-enabled, on-prem) SQL Servers, but the example silently swaps the server to an Azure SQL Database Gov endpoint — conflating an auth-mode change with a platform migration. A reviewer will ask which transformation is actually being prescribed; for the book's Layer 1 story the hostname should not change.
findings.fix: Keep Server=sql01.agency.gov in the After string (only Integrated Security=SSPI → Authentication=Active Directory Default changes), or explicitly label the endpoint change as the separate Managed Instance path.

findings.claim: "These artifacts satisfy the IA-2, IA-5, AU-2, AU-12, CA-7, and CM-8 KSI requirements under FedRAMP 20x."
findings.problem: FedRAMP 20x KSIs are not keyed by NIST control ID — they are themed indicators (KSI-IAM, KSI-MLA, etc.). There is no such thing as "the IA-2 KSI requirement," and "satisfy" asserts closure with no mapping shown. The spine itself models KSIs as themes.
findings.fix: Map the five evidence artifacts to actual KSI themes (e.g., KSI-IAM, KSI-MLA) per the spine's ksi field, and soften "satisfy" to "provide evidence toward."

findings.claim: The Arc Managed Identity certificate "is not accessible to any user or process outside the agent context" (and line 102: "No human ever sees the certificate or its private key").
findings.problem: Absolute claim with no mechanism: the credential material lives on the host, and a local administrator or SYSTEM-level process can reach the agent's key store. A hostile reviewer will demand the threat-model caveat; as written it reads as a security guarantee the vendor does not make.
findings.fix: Qualify: certificate is managed and rotated by the Arc agent and not exposed through any configuration surface; local-admin compromise of the host still compromises the identity (which is why host hardening and PAM controls in Vol III apply).

findings.claim: Fig-alt texts use retired flat numbering: line 317 "the certificate authority decisions were made in Part 1 … Book 07 consumes that PKI foundation"; line 239 "the Part 4 SSOT" and "Book 04's HR-driven identity SSOT".
findings.problem: This document is Vol II Book 01; "Book 07" is its own pre-reorg slot number. The spine explicitly directs: "Cross-reference books by id/title, never by a hardcoded number." The body text uses Vol/Book form, so the alt text contradicts the document it sits in and will break again at the Phase G renumber.
findings.fix: Regenerate/edit the fig-alt prose in san-fig-08 and san-fig-09 to Vol/Book-title references (Vol I Book 01 Landing Zone IPAM/DDI/PKI; Vol I Book 04 HRIT Identity & Org SSOT; this book).

findings.claim: "Kerberos tickets expire at five minutes of clock skew."
findings.problem: Misstates the mechanism: tickets have their own lifetime (typically 10 hours); the 5-minute figure is the default maximum tolerable clock skew, beyond which authentication requests are rejected (KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW) — the ticket doesn't "expire."
findings.fix: Rephrase: "Kerberos rejects authentication when client/server clocks differ by more than the default five-minute skew tolerance."

findings.claim: "NTLM logon events have LogonType = 3 and AuthenticationPackage = NTLM."
findings.problem: Over-specific as a discovery filter: LogonType 3 is simply "network logon" (Kerberos network logons are also type 3), and NTLM can appear under other logon types (2 interactive, 10 RemoteInteractive). Filtering on LogonType=3 AND Package=NTLM misses NTLM RDP/interactive events during Phase A discovery.
findings.fix: Filter on the Authentication Package field (NTLM / NtLmSsp) across all logon types; note that Kerberos vs NTLM is distinguished by the package field, not the logon type.

findings.claim: "a credential architecture designed in 1999. Kerberos was built for..."
findings.problem: Kerberos was designed at MIT in the late 1980s (Kerberos v5 standardized in RFC 1510, 1993); 1999 is roughly when Microsoft implemented it for Windows 2000. Minor, but a pedantic reviewer will note it.
findings.fix: Say "adopted by Windows in 1999/2000" or "designed in the late 1980s for campus LANs."

findings.claim: "No action in Books 01–07 is irreversible. The first irreversible action is `DROP LOGIN` in Book 05"
findings.problem: The two sentences contradict each other in the same paragraph: Book 05 is inside the Books 01–07 range, and Book 05 Phase 4 (line ~410) does execute DROP LOGIN. A reviewer reading the safety model cannot tell which books are actually reversible.
findings.fix: Change to "No action in Books 01–04 is irreversible" (or restate: the first irreversible action is the Phase-4 DROP LOGIN in Book 05, gated behind the 30-day observation).

findings.claim: NTLM source-identification script filters `$_.Properties[8].Value -eq 'NTLM'` with comment "AuthenticationPackageName", then in the same pipeline labels `Properties[8]` as "LogonType"
findings.problem: Internally contradictory and produces a false negative: Properties[8] cannot be both AuthenticationPackageName and LogonType. In event 4624, index 8 is LogonType (a number) and AuthenticationPackageName is index 10, so the filter matches nothing and the NTLM export is always empty — which then satisfies Book 03 closure condition 3 ("NTLM sources classified") with fabricated-clean evidence. A 3PAO testing the runbook would reject it.
findings.fix: Use the correct property index per event id (4624: LogonType=Properties[8], AuthenticationPackageName=Properties[10]) or filter on the event XML field name instead of positional index, and correct the Select-Object labels.

findings.claim: Phase 2 validation: "Expected output: `Authentication scheme: KERBEROS` (for Entra ID token-based connections on the server side)"
findings.problem: Contradicts the document's own Book 09 doctrine, which argues token-based authentication is precisely NOT Kerberos ("Kerberos is session- and location-bound... the token-based authentication these runbooks deploy"). If Entra token connections reported KERBEROS, the Book 09 monitoring logic and the series' Kerberos-replacement argument would be incoherent; the actual auth_scheme value for Entra connections also needs external verification against Microsoft docs before an operator uses it as a pass/fail gate.
findings.fix: Verify the actual sys.dm_exec_connections auth_scheme value returned by Entra-authenticated connections on Arc-enabled SQL Server 2022 and state that value; do not tell operators to expect KERBEROS for a token-based connection.

findings.claim: Zombie-instance utilization query: `CAST(ring_buffer_address AS XML)` and `sys.dm_os_ring_buffers.timestamp - cpu_tick_count`
findings.problem: The query cannot run as written: the XML payload of sys.dm_os_ring_buffers is the `record` column (ring_buffer_address is a varbinary memory address that fails CAST to XML), and `cpu_tick_count` is not a column in scope (the standard pattern joins sys.dm_os_sys_info ms_ticks). The RETIRE/CONSOLIDATE disposition evidence this feeds is therefore not reproducible from the runbook.
findings.fix: Rewrite using the documented pattern: CAST(record AS XML) and DATEADD(ms, rb.timestamp - si.ms_ticks, GETDATE()) joined to sys.dm_os_sys_info si.

findings.claim: "Testing against SQL Server 2019 with the Entra extension is acceptable for Books 03 and 04"
findings.problem: Book 04's own completion criteria include enabling Entra authentication via `ALTER SERVER CONFIGURATION SET EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATION PROVIDER ENABLED`, which the file itself labels "For SQL Server 2022:" (line ~341) — Entra authentication for Arc-enabled SQL Server requires 2022. Book 04 cannot be meaningfully validated on 2019, contradicting the test-environment guidance.
findings.fix: Restrict the 2019 allowance to Book 03 (audit only), or state which Book 04 steps (Arc agent + extension install only, not Entra enablement) are testable on 2019.

findings.claim: "the token-based authentication these runbooks deploy is the only mechanism that closes IA-2 for SQL Server on modern transport"
findings.problem: An exclusivity ("only mechanism that closes") closure-necessity claim with no spine backing: aan-compliance-spine.yml registers zero closures for book-08 (or its companion book-07), and the only IA-2 closure row in the spine belongs to book-sn-saas with necessity: false. Until an IA-2 closure row with a necessity flag and alternative_rebuttal exists for this book, a hostile ISSO reads this as an unregistered, unrebutted necessity assertion.
findings.fix: Either back-fill the IA-2 closure (with necessity + alternative_rebuttal) for this book in aan-compliance-spine.yml, or soften to "the mechanism this series uses to close IA-2 for SQL Server on multipath transport" until the spine row exists.

findings.claim: "SQL Server 2019 instances have ESU coverage confirmed via Arc enrollment (free via Arc)"
findings.problem: Two Microsoft-lifecycle claims that need verification against Microsoft before an assessor relies on them: (a) whether SQL Server 2019 needs ESUs at all in 2026 (its extended support window is generally understood to run to 2030, making ESU inapplicable), and (b) whether ESUs delivered through Arc are free (Arc-delivered ESUs are generally a paid monthly subscription; the free-ESU benefit applies to Azure-hosted workloads). As written the checklist item may direct agencies to confirm a benefit that does not exist.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft lifecycle/Arc ESU documentation and either delete the ESU item for 2019 or restate which versions need ESU and the actual Arc ESU cost model.

findings.claim: Linked-server remediation: `sp_addlinkedsrvlogin ... @rmtuser = 'svc-linkedserver@agency.gov', @rmtpassword = NULL; -- Token authentication — no password`
findings.problem: The claim that passing an Entra UPN as @rmtuser with a NULL password yields token authentication needs verification against Microsoft documentation — sp_addlinkedsrvlogin's rmtuser/rmtpassword pair is the SQL-authentication mapping, and Entra-based linked-server authentication is normally configured through the OLE DB provider/connection options, not a NULL password. As written the runbook step may simply create a mapping that fails to authenticate.
findings.fix: Verify the supported Entra authentication path for linked servers on SQL Server 2022 and replace the snippet with the documented mechanism; remove the "Token authentication — no password" annotation if unsupported.

findings.claim: Conditional Access target: "Cloud app = Azure SQL (App ID 022907d3-0f1b-48f7-badc-1ba6abab6d66)"
findings.problem: A hard-coded first-party application GUID that an assessor will check; it also needs confirmation that Conditional Access policies scoped to the Azure SQL cloud app actually govern Entra token issuance for Arc-enabled SQL Server (not just Azure SQL Database/MI), and whether the same App ID applies in Azure Government (usgovvirginia is the region used elsewhere in this guide).
findings.fix: Verify the App ID and its applicability to Arc-enabled SQL Server in Azure Government against Microsoft documentation and cite the source.

findings.claim: Caption: "The five closure conditions gate progression from authentication audit to Arc deployment" on image figs/san-fig-03-ntlm-elimination.png
findings.problem: The caption claims the figure shows the five closure conditions, but the image file and its fig-alt ("Diagram showing NTLM elimination phases and source patterns") describe a different, reused diagram — the figure does not depict what the caption asserts.
findings.fix: Either author a five-closure-conditions figure or rewrite the caption/fig-alt to describe the NTLM-elimination diagram actually shown.

findings.claim: "It closes the control families that are satisfied by artifacts rather than configuration: contingency planning (CP), supply-chain risk (SR), program management (PM), privacy/PII processing (PT), awareness and training (AT), and assessment/authorization/continuous monitoring (CA)."
findings.problem: The closure registry SSOT (aan-compliance-spine.yml) contains zero closure rows for any Vol IV book (book-14 through book-19), and no CP-, SR-, PM-, PT-, or AT-family closures anywhere in the file (the only CA closures belong to Vol III/VII books). The spine's own status note says closures are still being back-filled per book, so the volume-level 'closes' assertion cannot currently be reproduced from the SSOT — a 3PAO asking for the control-to-book closure mapping behind this sentence would find nothing registered.
findings.fix: Either soften to forward-looking language ('the volume's books carry the closures for CP/SR/PM/PT/AT/CA — registered per book in the compliance spine as each book is finalized'), or back-fill the spine closure rows for book-14..book-19 before shipping this overview.

findings.claim: Book 02 row: "SBOM / VDR / VEX pipeline under BOD 26-04" (repeated in the fig-alt on line 54: "SBOM/VDR/VEX under BOD 26-04").
findings.problem: The deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml, id bod-26-04-vdr-ver) names the BOD 26-04 / FedRAMP mandated artifacts as VDR/VER, and Vol IV Book 02's own subtitle is 'SBOM, VDR, and VER Framework for FedRAMP 20x and BOD 26-04' — VEX is an input format Book 02 uses to produce the VER evidence contract, not the artifact the directive mandates. Attributing 'VEX' directly to BOD 26-04 in the overview misstates the binding requirement a hostile reviewer would check against the directive.
findings.fix: Change both the table row and the fig-alt to 'SBOM / VDR / VER pipeline under BOD 26-04' (optionally '(VEX-fed VER)') to match the deadline SSOT and Book 02's subtitle.

findings.claim: "A request from San Francisco to a database in Virginia travels roughly 2,500 miles. At the speed of light in fiber (approximately 200,000 km/s), that is a minimum round-trip time of approximately 25 milliseconds."
findings.problem: Unit slip: 2,500 miles is about 4,023 km, so the RTT floor is 2 x 4,023 / 200,000 km/s = ~40 ms, not 25 ms. The 25 ms figure results from treating 2,500 MILES as if it were 2,500 KM. This is the book's flagship physics example and the number is wrong by ~40%.
findings.fix: Either restate distance in km (SF-to-DC great circle ~3,900-4,000 km) and give ~40 ms RTT floor, or keep 2,500 miles and correct the RTT to ~40 ms.

findings.claim: "A strongly consistent read from LA requires at minimum one round trip to DC: 54ms physics floor, observed 130-180ms" — repeated at line 114 ("costs 54ms round trip") and in both fig-alt texts (lines 122 and, by derivation, the fig-05 PNG).
findings.problem: The document's own route table (line 86) gives the DC-to-LA physics floor as 27 ms RTT with 65-90 ms typical observed. One round trip = one RTT = 27 ms by the table's own methodology (2 x 2,700 km / 200,000 km/s). The 54 ms / 130-180 ms figures are exactly double — the RTT was counted twice. The doc contradicts itself three times on its self-declared 'most important number.'
findings.fix: Reconcile to one set of numbers (and note the table's underlying 2,700 km distance is itself wrong — see next finding). Fix lines 98-99, 114, and the fig-alt at 122; figs/db-fig-05-physics-not-procurement.png must be regenerated since the 54 ms claim is baked into the rendered figure.

findings.claim: Route table row: "DC to LA (2,700 km) | 2,700 km | 27 ms | 65-90 ms | 38-63 ms"
findings.problem: Washington DC to Los Angeles is ~3,700 km great circle (~2,300 miles); fiber-route distance is longer still. 2,700 appears to be a mileage figure mislabeled as km (same miles/km confusion as line 68). With the correct distance the physics floor is >=37 ms RTT, which changes the addressable-gap column (65-90 observed gives ~28-53 ms gap) and every downstream use of '27 ms floor' (lines 92, 98, 114) and the fig-02 chart.
findings.fix: Correct the distance to ~3,700 km (or an explicit fiber-route km figure with a stated basis), recompute the floor and addressable-gap columns, and propagate to lines 92/98/114 and figs/db-fig-02-speed-of-light.png.

findings.claim: The 'NIST Control Closure' table claims this book closes 9 controls (SC-28, SC-8, SC-5, SI-12, CA-3, SA-8, AU-9, CP-9, CP-10).
findings.problem: aan-compliance-spine.yml — the declared SSOT for series control closures — registers zero closures for book-09 (this book); its only appearance is the book-registry entry at spine line 130. The table is hand-authored (not the spine-generated 'Authorities Closed Here' partial), so no drift gate covers it, and it lacks the spine's required fields (gate, plane, KSI, necessity). All nine control TITLES match the NIST r5 catalog, so the ids/titles are fine — the claim set is simply unregistered against the SSOT. Also note the two in-text 'Closure Necessity' callouts (SC-5 line 171, SC-8 line 281) assert necessity-class closures that would need alternative_rebuttal entries in the spine.
findings.fix: Back-fill book-09 closure rows into aan-compliance-spine.yml (including necessity + alternative_rebuttal for SC-5 and SC-8), then replace or reconcile the hand table with the spine-generated partial. Until then the table should be flagged as pending spine registration.

findings.claim: "this architectural framework closes the FedRAMP 20x gap in the database and data management layer."
findings.problem: 'Closes the FedRAMP 20x gap' has no mechanism anywhere in the document: no KSI is named, no evidence artifact is identified, and the spine records no KSI-bearing closures for this book. A 3PAO would ask which KSI(s) this satisfies and with what machine-readable evidence.
findings.fix: Either name the specific KSIs and the evidence path (as sibling books do via the spine's ksi: field), or soften to 'contributes to' / 'establishes the architecture for'.

findings.claim: "Entra access tokens for SQL Server are scoped to the specific SQL Server resource. A token issued for sql01.agency.gov is not valid against sql02.agency.gov" — also load-bearing in fig-06 alt (line 200: "sql01's token opens nothing else") and the lateral-movement argument at line 190.
findings.problem: For Azure SQL the documented token audience is the shared resource https://database.windows.net/ (one audience for all servers), and Arc-enabled SQL Server token audiences need checking per Microsoft docs — so per-SERVER token scoping is at minimum configuration-dependent, not automatic. This claim underpins the book's core 'stolen token cannot move laterally' security argument, so it must be verified against current Microsoft documentation before the argument stands. Not judging true/false — flagging that it rests on unverified product behavior.
findings.fix: Verify token audience/scoping behavior for the actual deployment shapes covered (Azure SQL vs Arc-enabled SQL Server vs on-prem with Entra auth) against Microsoft Learn; add the citation per the series' vendor-sources convention, or narrow the claim to the shapes where per-resource scoping is real. fig-06 PNG regeneration required if the claim changes.

findings.claim: "The firewall rule becomes simpler (allow port 1433 from any Entra-authenticated client)"
findings.problem: A network firewall cannot evaluate Entra authentication state — L3/L4 rules match source/port, so the rule as written is 'allow 1433 from any', which contradicts Principle 5 (line 331: firewalls "still block unauthenticated connection attempts" as defense-in-depth). As phrased, the defense-in-depth layer described later is impossible under the rule described here.
findings.fix: Rephrase: the firewall constrains reachability to known network scopes while authentication moves to the token layer — e.g. 'allow 1433 from approved segments; authentication no longer depends on the rule' — so it no longer implies the firewall can see token state.

findings.claim: "For intra-agency database traffic ... this can reduce observed latency by 30-50% versus traditional MPLS."
findings.problem: The 30-50% range has no source and cannot be reproduced from the document's own route table (whose addressable gaps imply route-dependent reductions from ~20% to ~58%). The series authoring spec requires sources for vendor/performance claims.
findings.fix: Either derive the range explicitly from the route table ('the addressable gap is 25-60% of observed latency on the routes above') or cite an SD-WAN vendor/analyst source under the Vendor sources convention.

findings.claim: fig-06 alt text: "versus the NTLM hash from Book 07 which was reusable indefinitely"
findings.problem: Hardcoded book number. In the spine, temp_slot 07 is the SQL Server Authentication Modernization book (Vol II Book 01) with target_slot 08 — the spine (lines 106-110) explicitly says to cross-reference by id/title, never hardcoded number, until the Phase G renumber. After renumber, 'Book 07' points at a different book and the comparison silently breaks; it is also ambiguous inside a doc that self-identifies as Vol II Book 03.
findings.fix: Reference by title/volume-local id ('the SQL Server Authentication Modernization book, Vol II Book 01'). The text is baked into figs/db-fig-06-token-scope.png alt/source line, so update alt text and regenerate if the deck citation changes.

findings.claim: "SQL Server TDE encrypts data files at rest with AES-256"
findings.problem: TDE's cipher is configuration-dependent (AES-128/192/256 historically); AES-256 is the default only on newer SQL Server versions. Stated as an unconditional property in the SC-28 closure row.
findings.fix: State 'TDE configured with AES-256' (a settable requirement) rather than implying it is inherent, or cite the SQL Server version baseline where AES-256 is default.

findings.claim: "access tokens expire, typically in one hour" (repeated in fig-06 alt, line 200)
findings.problem: Entra access-token default lifetime is a variable 60-90 minutes, not a fixed hour. 'Typically in one hour' is close but is a product-behavior claim used in the 'stolen token buys one resource for one hour' security argument, so it should carry a citation.
findings.fix: Say 'typically 60-90 minutes (Entra default)' with a Microsoft Learn citation, or keep 'about an hour' with the citation.

findings.claim: "NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 defines seven sections for a federal Contingency Plan" (also line 42 'aligned to NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1' and line 699 'authored per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure').
findings.problem: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1's ISCP format is not a seven-section structure. Its Appendix A sample plan is Introduction/Supporting Information + Concept of Operations + the three phases (Activation and Notification, Recovery, Reconstitution) + appendices; Roles/Responsibilities and Plan Maintenance are folded into ConOps and appendices, not standalone 'defined' sections. The seven-section layout is this document's own synthesis. A 3PAO who opens 800-34 will find the attribution wrong, and the closure table's CP-2 row rests on it ('authored per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure'). Note: 800-34 is not among the in-repo SSOTs, so this was verified from the publication's well-known structure, not a repo file.
findings.fix: Change 'defines seven sections' to language that owns the synthesis, e.g. 'This document organizes the 800-34 Rev 1 plan elements into seven sections' and drop 'per NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 seven-section structure' from the CP-2 closure row (say 'consistent with NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1' instead).

findings.claim: The FedRAMP 20x callout names two KSIs: 'KSI: Backup and Recovery (maps to CP-6, CP-7, CP-9)' and 'KSI: Incident Response and Continuity (maps to CP-2, CP-4, IR-4)'.
findings.problem: Neither KSI name exists. The series' own KSI vocabulary (aan-compliance-spine.yml `ksi:` fields and Vol_IV_Book_06_FedAAN_Authorization_Package_ConMon.qmd lines 190-191, 737-743) uses the official 20x theme identifiers: continuity/recovery is KSI-RPL (Recovery Planning, rules KSI-026–029) and incident is KSI-INR (Incident Reporting, KSI-023–025). Inventing 'Backup and Recovery' and 'Incident Response and Continuity' contradicts the corpus SSOT and would fail a check against the published KSI list.
findings.fix: Rename the two callout headings to the official identifiers used by Vol IV Book 06 and the spine: 'KSI-RPL — Recovery Planning (KSI-026–029; maps to CP-6, CP-7, CP-9, CP-10)' and 'KSI-INR — Incident Reporting (KSI-023–025; maps to CP-2, CP-4, IR-4)'.

findings.claim: "This document closes that gap ... and closes the full CP control family through CP-10."
findings.problem: Two problems. (1) 'Full CP control family' is wrong even on the document's own terms: CP-1 (Policy and Procedures — confirmed in reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json) is in the family and is addressed nowhere; the closure table starts at CP-2. (2) The document is a template — Section 1.6 approval, BIA sign-off, and test records are all placeholders ('[Authorizing Official Name and Title]'). A template cannot 'close' CP-2/CP-4; closure occurs when an agency authors, signs, and tests its plan. The spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers zero closures for book-14, so the claim is also unbacked by the closure SSOT.
findings.fix: Reword to 'provides the template and evidence framework to close CP-2 through CP-10' and either add a CP-1 row (or an explicit statement that CP-1 policy is out of scope / addressed elsewhere) or drop 'full CP control family'.

findings.claim: Closure Necessity — CP-8: 'Traditional dual-homing fails over on routing-protocol reconvergence — tens of seconds to minutes ... against a 15-minute RTO and a 30-minute MTD for the network layer. The mechanism that makes the alternate service resume operations inside that budget is SD-WAN active-active multipath.'
findings.problem: The quantitative core does not hold: 'tens of seconds to minutes' is comfortably inside a 15-minute RTO, so the paragraph's own numbers do not prove the overlay is necessary to meet the stated budget. It also sits in tension with the document's Section 5.2 table, which lists 'SD-WAN automatic circuit failover' at '3–5 minutes (automatic)' while this section claims sub-second per-class steering — a hostile reviewer will ask which number is the CP-8 evidence. The real differentiators (per-class policy, brownout detection, recorded path-health evidence) survive; the 'inside that budget' framing does not.
findings.fix: Rebase the necessity argument on what reconvergence-based failover actually lacks (brownout detection, per-class policy, recorded evidence, all-or-nothing cutover) rather than on the RTO arithmetic, and reconcile the sub-second steering claim with the 3–5 minute figure in Section 5.2 (e.g. label 5.2 as blackout circuit failover including validation, and this as brownout per-class steering).

findings.claim: "At Moderate baseline, FedRAMP accepts tabletop exercises as the minimum, with functional testing required for critical systems."
findings.problem: This is a specific FedRAMP acceptance rule stated with no citation, and it is load-bearing: the entire Year-1 'tabletop only' test cycle rests on it. It is not verifiable against any in-repo SSOT (the deadlines registry and spine carry no CP-4 parameter), and FedRAMP's Rev5 CP-4 parameter language is what an assessor would quote back. As written, a 3PAO could reject the Year-1 plan.
findings.fix: Cite the FedRAMP Rev5 Moderate CP-4 parameter/test-plan requirement explicitly (and verify the current parameter text before citing), or soften to 'agencies should confirm the FedRAMP-defined CP-4 test type for their baseline before relying on a tabletop-only year'.

findings.claim: Closure table CP-3 row: 'Tabletop exercise constitutes annual training for all participants; attendance record satisfies CP-3'.
findings.problem: CP-3 (Contingency Training — title confirmed in the controls catalog) requires training within an organization-defined period of personnel assuming a contingency role and when required by system changes, not only annually. An attendance record from one tabletop does not 'satisfy CP-3' for personnel who joined mid-cycle, and an assessor would test exactly that. The word 'satisfies' overclaims.
findings.fix: Reword to 'tabletop participation provides the annual training component of CP-3; onboarding training within [defined period] of role assignment must be added to fully satisfy the control', and add the onboarding requirement to Section 7 or Section 3.

findings.claim: "The CSP's FedRAMP ATO covers both regions, satisfying the requirement for a formally authorized alternate processing environment."
findings.problem: Load-bearing inheritance claim: whether a given secondary region is inside the CSP's FedRAMP authorization boundary is a per-CSP, per-region Marketplace fact that must be verified, not asserted generically. 'Satisfying the requirement' also overstates — CP-7 requires agreements, capacity, and tested failover beyond authorization (which the document itself then lists). Not judged true/false here; it needs external verification and a hedge.
findings.fix: Reword to 'verify in the CSP's FedRAMP Marketplace package that both the primary and secondary regions are inside the authorization boundary; if so, the alternate processing environment inherits the CSP authorization' and keep the additional CP-7 requirements as conditions, not extras.

findings.claim: "For Microsoft 365 Government Cloud tenants, multi-geo data residency configuration replicates content to a secondary geo location" (with 'Microsoft's SLA defines the replication commitment', line 344).
findings.problem: Microsoft 365 Multi-Geo is a data-residency feature (placing different users' data in different geos), which is commonly confused with DR replication of the same content to a secondary geo; its availability and behavior in Government Cloud tenants, and the existence of an SLA-defined 'replication commitment', are vendor facts that must be verified before this stands as the CP-6 mechanism for unstructured data. No 'Vendor sources:' link is provided as the AAN authoring spec requires for vendor claims.
findings.fix: Verify against Microsoft documentation whether Multi-Geo (a) is available for the target Government Cloud tenant type and (b) actually provides secondary-geo replication of content vs per-user residency; cite the source with a 'Vendor sources:' link, or replace the mechanism with Microsoft 365's native service-resilience/backup documentation.

findings.claim: CP-7(3) priority of service: 'For commercial CSPs, this is typically addressed through the FedRAMP authorization and the CSP's service continuity commitments.'
findings.problem: A FedRAMP authorization does not confer priority-of-service provisions; CP-7(3) needs a contractual/SLA mechanism guaranteeing capacity access during widespread disaster. Whether a given CSP support tier or continuity commitment actually provides that is an external, per-contract fact. As written, an assessor could reject FedRAMP authorization offered as CP-7(3) evidence.
findings.fix: Drop 'the FedRAMP authorization' from the sentence and require documenting the specific contractual commitment (support tier, capacity reservation, or SLA clause) that guarantees alternate-region capacity, verified against the CSP agreement.

findings.claim: "per-class steering completes in under a second" (and 'sub-second steering on brownout', line 511).
findings.problem: Vendor performance claim stated as fact with no 'Vendor sources:' link, in a document that itself insists failover time 'must be documented from observation, not from the datasheet'. Sub-second brownout steering is platform- and configuration-dependent.
findings.fix: Hedge to 'typically sub-second per vendor datasheets — document the observed value from the annual test' and add a Vendor sources: link, or drop the specific number and rely on the observed-value requirement already in the paragraph.

findings.claim: Series integration table, Vol I Book 01 row: 'CP-8: DNS continuity supports all other failover dependencies.'
findings.problem: CP-8 (Telecommunications Services — title confirmed in the controls catalog) covers alternate telecommunications services and provider agreements. DNS/DDI continuity is a CP-6/CP-7 dependency, not a telecommunications service; mapping DDI Grid replication to CP-8 dilutes the CP-8 story the same document builds carefully around the SD-WAN dual underlay.
findings.fix: Change the row's CP-8 entry to a dependency note (e.g. 'recovery-sequencing dependency: DNS must be restored before CP-7 alternate processing cutover') or move the contribution under CP-7.

findings.claim: "CISA Binding Operational Directive 26-04 activates the SBOM/VDR/VER requirement for all federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) agencies effective December 7, 2026. The directive defines three tiers" (Tier 1 SBOM / Tier 2 VDR / Tier 3 VEX, all due Dec 7, 2026).
findings.problem: The deadline SSOT (aan-authority-deadlines.yml, id bod-26-04-vdr-ver) defines Dec 7, 2026 as 'BOD 26-04 remediation timelines in force; FedRAMP VDR/VER mandatory adoption' — sourced to a FedRAMP notice. It does not support (a) a BOD-defined three-tier SBOM/VDR/VEX structure, (b) an SBOM-for-all-production-systems mandate on that date, or (c) attributing the VDR/VER adoption (a FedRAMP program obligation) to the BOD as an FCEB agency requirement. The tier table is presented as directive text but cannot be reproduced from any SSOT — a 3PAO checking the directive would find no such tiers. The date itself (Dec 7, 2026) matches the SSOT; the attributed content does not.
findings.fix: Restate Dec 7, 2026 per the SSOT event text: BOD 26-04 remediation timelines in force plus FedRAMP VDR/VER mandatory adoption. Remove or clearly label the 'three tiers' table as the book's own implementation phasing, not directive text. Also consider citing the SSOT's other BOD 26-04 date (agency policies due 2026-08-07, id bod-26-04-policies), which this implementation plan currently ignores.

findings.claim: Vendor Disclosure Matrix (SR-6 evidence): Microsoft (Defender VM, Sentinel, Purview, Key Vault) — FedRAMP Authorization: "Yes — GCC High".
findings.problem: This is a load-bearing High authorization claim in an SR-6 evidence table, and this .qmd has NO entry in aan-high-claim-baseline.yml (only the spec file Vol_IV_Book_02.yaml is baselined at 1), so it is not pre-existing baselined debt. It also contradicts the corpus scope doctrine (spine: 'FedRAMP Moderate only', GCC Moderate boundary): SSA's Microsoft services run in GCC, not GCC High — citing GCC High as the supplier authorization for the very services the series deploys misstates the environment the agency actually inherits from.
findings.fix: State Microsoft's authorization in the terms the series scope uses (GCC / FedRAMP Moderate boundary posture) or cite the actual Marketplace authorization for the specific service offerings in the SSA tenancy; do not anchor SR-6 evidence to GCC High.

findings.claim: Vendor Disclosure Matrix: Cisco SD-WAN (IOS XE, vManage) — FedRAMP Authorization: "Yes — GCC Moderate".
findings.problem: 'GCC' is Microsoft-specific terminology (Government Community Cloud); a Cisco product cannot hold a 'GCC Moderate' authorization. The category error would be caught instantly by a 3PAO reading the SR-6 evidence table. Whether Cisco's SD-WAN cloud management plane holds a FedRAMP Moderate authorization is a separate claim needing external verification against the FedRAMP Marketplace.
findings.fix: Replace with the correct FedRAMP Marketplace status for the specific Cisco offering (verified against the Marketplace), e.g. 'FedRAMP Moderate — <package>' if true; also note on-prem IOS XE gear is not FedRAMP-authorizable (it is the NIAP/STIG gate per the spine's gates model).

findings.claim: A "CISA VEX Portal" exists and is the submission target: pipeline stage 7, 'Signed URLs for CISA VEX Portal submission', 'CycloneDX 1.6 XML natively, the format required by the CISA VEX Portal', VEX 'submitted to CISA VEX Portal', checklist Phase 1 'Submit SBOM + VDR to CISA VEX Portal (test submission)'.
findings.problem: No in-repo SSOT establishes a CISA VEX Portal, its existence, or a CycloneDX 1.6 XML format requirement. The entire pipeline terminus and two checklist milestones depend on this unverified external service — if the portal or its format mandate does not exist as described, the architecture's submission stage and the Aug 2026 test-submission milestone are unexecutable. (Not judged true/false; must be verified against CISA before this book is released.)
findings.fix: Verify the actual BOD 26-04 submission mechanism against CISA guidance and cite it (the SSOT source is the CISA BOD 26-04 implementation-guidance page); if no portal exists, replace the submission stage with the actual reporting channel.

findings.claim: SR-1 titled "Supply Chain Risk Management Policy and Procedures".
findings.problem: The NIST catalog SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, v5.2.0) gives SR-1's official title as "Policy and Procedures". All seven other SR titles in the table match the catalog exactly, making the one deviation stand out.
findings.fix: Change the SR-1 title cell to "Policy and Procedures" (family context is already carried by the SR prefix).

findings.claim: VEX status table: under_investigation has a "max 7-day window"; fig-02 alt text: "under_investigation (30-day triage SLA)".
findings.problem: The prose table and the figure state different SLAs for the same VEX status (7 days vs 30 days). A reviewer cannot tell which SLA the agency is committing to; neither number is traceable to an SSOT.
findings.fix: Pick one triage SLA, state its source (internal policy), and align table, figure, and figure alt text.

findings.claim: Fig-01 alt text describes stage 6 as "Signed Artifact Store (S3 + KMS, SHA-256 integrity, immutable)".
findings.problem: The body architecture (ASCII diagram, workflow YAML, evidence manifest storage_uri, technology stack table) is GitHub Releases + Azure Blob immutable tier. The rendered figure apparently shows AWS S3 + KMS — a different cloud than the design it illustrates. In a GCC-Moderate Azure-centric corpus this reads as an unreviewed figure contradicting the authored architecture.
findings.fix: Regenerate figs/scrm-fig-01-sbom-pipeline.png (and its alt text) with Azure Blob immutable tier as stage 6, matching the body.

findings.claim: "Syft (Anchore) is the CISA-recommended SBOM generator for federal systems" and produces "the format required by the CISA VEX Portal".
findings.problem: No SSOT supports a CISA recommendation of a specific vendor tool; CISA guidance is normally tool-neutral. This is a vendor claim, and per the series authoring spec vendor claims require a 'Vendor sources:' link — none is given. (Not judged true/false; flagged for verification.)
findings.fix: Either cite the CISA document that names Syft, or soften to 'a widely used open-source SBOM generator that meets the minimum-elements requirements' with a vendor source link.

findings.claim: "SLSA ... is the NIST-endorsed framework for measuring build integrity"; Level 2 = "Hosted build, signed provenance"; Level 3 = "Hardened build, two-party review".
findings.problem: 'NIST-endorsed' is unsupported by any SSOT (NIST SP 800-218 references SLSA; endorsement overstates it). Additionally, 'two-party review' is not a SLSA v1.0 Build-track requirement (that was SLSA v0.1 source-track language), yet the References table cites 'SLSA v1.0 Framework' — the level descriptions contradict the cited version. Repeated in fig-03 alt text.
findings.fix: Say 'referenced by NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF)' instead of 'NIST-endorsed', and align the Level 2/3 requirement descriptions with SLSA v1.0 Build L2/L3 (build platform isolation/hardening), moving reviewer requirements to a separate branch-protection control statement.

findings.claim: Vendor Disclosure Matrix row: supplier "Anchore/CISA" for the "NVD data feed".
findings.problem: The National Vulnerability Database is operated by NIST, not by Anchore or CISA. In an SR-6 supplier-assessment evidence table, misattributing the data supplier is exactly the kind of error a supplier-review control assessment exists to catch. (CISA supplies the KEV feed, which is a different row's concern.)
findings.fix: Change the supplier to NIST for the NVD feed; if the KEV feed belongs in the matrix, add CISA as its own row.

findings.claim: References table: "CISA Minimum SBOM Elements (July 2021)".
findings.problem: The body (SBOM Content Requirements section) correctly attributes the minimum SBOM elements to NTIA; the July 2021 minimum-elements document is NTIA's (published under EO 14028). CISA's own SBOM minimum-elements guidance is a later, separate document. The reference row contradicts the body's attribution and misdates/misattributes the source.
findings.fix: Either cite 'NTIA — The Minimum Elements For a Software Bill of Materials (July 2021)' or cite CISA's later SBOM guidance with its correct date; keep body and references consistent.

findings.claim: Subtitle promises an "SBOM, VDR, and VER Framework" and the pipeline "provides the VER (Vulnerability Exploitability Report) evidence contract", but the body's third artifact is VEX and the compliance tiers are SBOM/VDR/VEX.
findings.problem: VER is never reconciled with VEX: the deadline SSOT names 'VDR/VER' (FedRAMP terms), the book expands VER as 'Vulnerability Exploitability Report' with no source, and then delivers VEX documents. A 3PAO will ask whether the VEX artifacts produced actually satisfy the FedRAMP VER requirement — the book asserts it (line ~397) without defining the mapping.
findings.fix: Add one paragraph defining VDR/VER per the FedRAMP notice cited in the deadline SSOT (fedramp.gov/notices/0014) and explicitly state how the CycloneDX VDR + VEX artifacts satisfy each; use one term consistently thereafter.

findings.claim: "Any CVE ... in the KEV catalog is automatically escalated to P0 — 14-day remediation SLA per BOD 22-01", and the KQL rule computes overdue as days_since_disclosure - 14.
findings.problem: BOD 22-01 does not set a blanket 14-day SLA: each KEV entry carries its own dueDate (the ~2-week window applied to CVEs assigned in 2021 or later at catalog-addition time; older CVEs got 6 months), and the clock runs from KEV catalog addition, not from disclosure. The KQL as written would mark items overdue that BOD 22-01 does not, and miss the actual dueDate field the KEV feed provides.
findings.fix: Drive the SLA from the KEV feed's dueDate field (kev_due_date_t) in both the triage script and the KQL rule; describe the BOD 22-01 timeline as per-entry due dates rather than a flat 14 days.

findings.claim: "Controls closed: 8" (SR-1, SR-2, SR-3, SR-5, SR-6, SR-8, SR-10, SR-11), presented as this book's NIST control closure.
findings.problem: aan-compliance-spine.yml — the declared SSOT for every (control x book) closure — contains zero closure rows for book-15 (this book). The spine header says closures are back-filled sequentially, so this is a known-process gap rather than a contradiction, but as long as the registry is empty the book's closure count is an unregistered claim: the generated 'Authorities Closed Here' machinery and its drift gate cannot vouch for it.
findings.fix: Back-fill the eight SR closure rows for book-15 into the spine (with gate: artifact per the book's own Closure Necessity note) before this book is cited as closing them.

findings.claim: Infoblox — Products: "NIOS Grid, BloxOne DDI" — FedRAMP Authorization: "Yes — FR2017257053".
findings.problem: The specific FedRAMP package identifier and the implication that on-prem NIOS Grid software is covered by a FedRAMP authorization (FedRAMP authorizes cloud service offerings, not on-prem appliances) both require verification against the FedRAMP Marketplace. (Not judged true/false.)
findings.fix: Verify the package ID and scope on the FedRAMP Marketplace; scope the 'Yes' to the cloud offering only and handle on-prem NIOS under the NIAP/STIG/FIPS gate the spine defines for network gear.

findings.claim: The GitHub Actions workflow scans with output-format: cyclonedx-xml, then uploads "${{ steps.scan.outputs.sarif }}" as the VDR release asset.
findings.problem: The scan step is configured to emit CycloneDX XML, but the upload references the action's SARIF output — which will be empty/undefined in this configuration — so the workflow as published would not attach the VDR to the release. Since this YAML is presented as the evidence-producing pipeline for Tier 2, an assessor replaying it would find the VDR artifact missing.
findings.fix: Give the scan step an explicit output file and upload that file (the CycloneDX VDR), not steps.scan.outputs.sarif.

findings.claim: "Retention: 7 years (NARA standard)" for SBOM/VDR/VEX artifacts.
findings.problem: No SSOT establishes a 7-year NARA retention period for these artifact types; NARA General Records Schedules are item-specific. (Not judged true/false.)
findings.fix: Cite the specific GRS item (or SSA records schedule) that sets the retention period, or state it as a proposed internal policy.

findings.claim: Example evidence manifest points slsa_provenance_url at "https://github.com/WhalerMike/uiao/attestations/...".
findings.problem: An SSA compliance document's sample production manifest references the author's personal GitHub repository. Harmless as an example, but a hostile reviewer will ask why agency provenance evidence points at a personal account.
findings.fix: Use a neutral placeholder org (e.g. github.com/ssa-example/repo/attestations/...) in the sample manifest.

findings.claim: BOD 26-04 posture table lists SSA Status = 'Implemented' for all three tiers (SBOM, VDR, VER).
findings.problem: Unreproducible status claim. The cited evidence source, Vol IV Book 02, presents a phased implementation checklist whose Phase 4 ('Final BOD 26-04 VDR/VER submission') is dated Dec 7, 2026 — i.e., future work — and both books carry the 'draft proposal, not reviewed or approved' banner. A 3PAO/ISSO would reject 'Implemented' with no completed-submission evidence.
findings.fix: Change SSA Status to 'Pipeline designed (Vol IV Book 02)' / 'On track for Dec 7, 2026' or a phase-accurate status consistent with Book 02's implementation checklist.

findings.claim: 'The Vol I Book 05 evidence artifacts satisfy CM-8(1) automated inventory updates for the identity plane.'
findings.problem: Wrong control enhancement. Per the catalog SSOT, CM-8(1) is 'Updates During Installation and Removal'; automated inventory maintenance is CM-8(2) 'Automated Maintenance'. Mapping 'automated inventory updates' evidence to CM-8(1) is a factually wrong control citation an assessor would flag.
findings.fix: Cite CM-8(2) for the automated-maintenance claim (or rephrase the CM-8(1) claim to install/removal-driven updates).

findings.claim: PM-15 title rendered as 'Security/Privacy Contact with Groups' (§1 table) and 'Security Contact with Groups' (Appendix A, line 617).
findings.problem: Contradicts the catalog SSOT: the official PM-15 title is 'Security and Privacy Groups and Associations'. The value sits in a 'Title' column, so it reads as the official title, and the two tables also disagree with each other.
findings.fix: Use the official title 'Security and Privacy Groups and Associations' in both tables.

findings.claim: 'Tier 3: VER | Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange | ... OpenVEX JSON'.
findings.problem: Conflates VER with VEX. 'Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange' is the expansion of VEX; Vol IV Book 02 defines VER as 'Vulnerability Exploitability Report' and its own BOD 26-04 tier table defines Tier 3 as 'VEX present'. The row label, requirement text, and sibling book disagree.
findings.fix: Align with Book 02: label Tier 3 'VEX' (expansion 'Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange'), and reserve 'VER' for the FedRAMP Vulnerability Exploitability Report usage.

findings.claim: Cross-book pointers: 'Vendor disclosure matrix (Vol IV Book 02 §7)', 'PSIRT/MSRC subscriptions (Vol IV Book 02 §6.3)', 'VEX assertions ... (OpenVEX format, Vol IV Book 02 §5)'.
findings.problem: All three section numbers are wrong against Book 02's actual numbered structure: VEX is §4, the Vendor Disclosure Matrix is §5 (§7 is SLSA), and §6 has only two subsections so §6.3 does not exist. A reviewer following the pointers lands in the wrong sections.
findings.fix: Correct to Vol IV Book 02 §5 (vendor matrix), §4 (VEX), and the actual location of the PSIRT/MSRC subscription content — or cite by section name instead of number.

findings.claim: 'Together these artifacts close nine NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PM family controls.'
findings.problem: 'Close' is unsupported: every artifact in the book is an unfilled [FILLABLE] template requiring named individuals and signatures (Appendix A itself says only 'Template provided'), and the closure SSOT (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers zero closure entries for book-16. The claim is at minimum ahead of the spine.
findings.fix: Say the artifacts 'provide the templates/framework to close' the nine PM controls, or back-fill the book-16 closures in the spine before claiming closure.

findings.claim: CISA contact methods given as 'ir@cisa.dhs.gov' (incident reporting) and 'kev@cisa.dhs.gov' (KEV team).
findings.problem: Specific mailbox addresses attributed to a real agency cannot be verified in-repo; CISA's published incident-reporting channels are report@cisa.gov / central@cisa.dhs.gov, and a dedicated 'kev@' intake mailbox is not a known published channel. If wrong, the PM-15 registry fails on first use.
findings.fix: Verify against cisa.gov before publication or replace with '[verify current CISA reporting channel]' placeholders like the other rows.

findings.claim: 'MS-ISAC | Active member' as an SSA industry contact.
findings.problem: MS-ISAC membership is scoped to state, local, tribal, and territorial (SLTT) governments; SSA is a federal agency, so an 'active member' assertion needs verification and is likely not the correct ISAC relationship for a federal CSO contact registry.
findings.fix: Verify the actual relationship (e.g., CISA/US-CERT federal channels, or mark as liaison) or replace with a federal-appropriate body.

findings.claim: PM-7 mapped to '§2.4 EA Integration' and PM-11 to '§2.5 Mission Mapping' (repeated in Appendix A lines 613/615); SCRM output 'referenced in PM-9 §5.2 above' (line 536).
findings.problem: With number-sections enabled, EA Integration is §2.2 and Mission/Business Process Definition is §2.3 — §2.4/§2.5 do not exist; likewise the risk register format is §5.3, not §5.2 (§5.2 is the Risk Appetite Statement).
findings.fix: Correct the section numbers to §2.2, §2.3, and §5.3.

findings.claim: PM-2 title rendered 'Info Security Program Leadership Roles' (also Appendix A line 611).
findings.problem: Official catalog title is singular: 'Information Security Program Leadership Role'. Minor, but it sits in a 'Title' column and PM-2 is about designating one senior official.
findings.fix: Use the singular official title.

findings.claim: Suppliers must 'Submit VEX assertions for CVEs ... within 30 days of CISA CVE publication'.
findings.problem: CVEs are published by the CVE Program (MITRE/CNAs) and enriched in the NIST NVD; CISA publishes the KEV catalog, not CVEs. As contract-clause language, the trigger event is misattributed and therefore ambiguous.
findings.fix: Rephrase to 'within 30 days of CVE publication (NVD)' or 'of KEV catalog addition' depending on the intended trigger.

findings.claim: 'CISA PSIRT feeds | Subscription | VEX/VDR-relevant vendor advisories'.
findings.problem: PSIRTs are vendor product-security teams; CISA publishes cybersecurity advisories and the KEV catalog, not 'PSIRT feeds'. The row conflates vendor PSIRT subscriptions with CISA advisory feeds.
findings.fix: Split into 'Vendor PSIRT subscriptions' and 'CISA cybersecurity advisories / KEV feed' rows.

findings.claim: PT Control Closure Summary table titles: PT-1 "Privacy Policy and Procedures", PT-3 "Purpose Specification", PT-4 "Consent Requirements"
findings.problem: Contradicts reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json (catalog v5.2.0): PT-1 = "Policy and Procedures", PT-3 = "Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes", PT-4 = "Consent". "Purpose Specification" is the retired Rev 4 Appendix J (AP-2) name and is also used as the section heading (line 255) and throughout. A 3PAO checking the traceability table against the catalog rejects the title column.
findings.fix: Use the official Rev 5 titles in the closure table (abbreviating PII is fine); rename the PT-3 section heading to "PII Processing Purposes (PT-3)" or keep "Purpose Specification" only as an explicitly-labeled shorthand, and align the PT-4 heading to "Consent (PT-4)".

findings.claim: "PT controls underpin the KSI-PIY (Privacy Inventory) theme, which assesses whether the agency has a current, accurate understanding of its PII holdings"
findings.problem: Factually wrong per the series' own CR26 SSOT (AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md): KSI-PIY = "Policy and Inventory" (asset inventory, policies, SDLC, vulnerability disclosure — 5 indicators, none about PII holdings). The expansion "Privacy Inventory" and the described purpose are invented; the claimed PT underpinning of PIY evaporates once the theme is named correctly.
findings.fix: Correct KSI-PIY to "Policy and Inventory" and rewrite the indirect-coverage rationale honestly (e.g., PT artifacts feed the policy/inventory evidence corpus) or drop the PIY linkage.

findings.claim: KSI Indirect Coverage table rows: "KSI-DAT (Data Protection)", "KSI-IDM (Identity Management)", "KSI-CMT (Continuous Monitoring)"
findings.problem: KSI-DAT and KSI-IDM do not exist in FedRAMP 20x CR26. The 10 themes per AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md are IAM, CNA, SVC, MLA, CMT, PIY, SCR, CED, INR, RPL. Identity is KSI-IAM, and KSI-CMT = "Change Management", not Continuous Monitoring (monitoring is KSI-MLA). Three of the four rows in this table cite indicators a reviewer cannot find in the CR26 schema. These invented themes appear ONLY in this book, its derived training book-17.qmd, and specs/Vol_IV_Book_04.yaml — nowhere in the spine, which uses only real themes.
findings.fix: Replace KSI-DAT with KSI-SVC (or drop), KSI-IDM with KSI-IAM, and re-expand KSI-CMT as Change Management (or move the ConMon-cadence point to KSI-MLA). Propagate the same fix to specs/Vol_IV_Book_04.yaml (closing slide + notes) and AAN-Training-Program/books/book-17.qmd.

findings.claim: "SAOP submits to OMB and Congress for 40-day comment period (5 U.S.C. §552a(e)(4) and (11))" and "Published in the Federal Register at least 30 days before live PII collection begins"
findings.problem: The cited statute does not say this: §552a(e)(4) requires Federal Register publication of the SORN; (e)(11) prescribes a 30-day public comment period for new/revised routine uses. The 40-day OMB/Congress advance-review figure comes from OMB circular guidance (A-108/legacy A-130), not the statute cited. Likewise "30 days before live PII collection" (repeated at lines 242 and 695 and in fig-02 alt) is a derived rule — the statutory 30 days attaches to routine-use effectiveness, not a collection start date. A privacy attorney reviewing the package flags both.
findings.fix: Cite OMB Circular A-108 for the OMB/Congress advance review and §552a(e)(11) for the 30-day routine-use comment period; restate the go-live milestone as agency policy ("SSA practice: SORN published and effective before collection begins") rather than a statutory deadline.

findings.claim: Lifecycle figure alt text: stage 2 lists "PT-6 Dissemination"; stage 4 lists "PT-6, PT-8 SORN Records"
findings.problem: Per the catalog SSOT, PT-6 = "System of Records Notice" and PT-8 = "Computer Matching Requirements". Labeling PT-6 as "Dissemination" and grouping PT-8 under "SORN Records" misattributes both controls; since fig-alt doubles as the diagram source, the rendered figure carries the wrong control labels. The companion deck spec compounds it ("PT-6 (dissemination accounting)").
findings.fix: Correct the figure: PT-6 belongs with the SORN artifact at collection/share stages; PT-8 only applies if computer matching programs exist (drop it or label it Computer Matching). Regenerate figs/pii-fig-01 and fix the PT-6 description in specs/Vol_IV_Book_04.yaml slide 3 notes.

findings.claim: "This document closes the Privacy Transparency (PT) control family gap" while claiming only PT-1..PT-5 and PT-7
findings.problem: The PT family has 8 base controls; PT-6 (System of Records Notice) and PT-8 (Computer Matching Requirements) are never mentioned in the body, yet the doc contains a full SORN registry — PT-6's closing artifact — attributed instead to PT-2. A hostile reviewer asks: (a) why is the family-gap claim 6-of-8, and (b) why is the SORN requirement hung on PT-2 when PT-6 is the control that requires the SORN? The deck spec explicitly acknowledges the PT-6/PT-8 exclusion; the book itself does not.
findings.fix: Either claim PT-6 (the SORN registry already closes it) or add one sentence scoping the claim to six controls and stating why PT-6/PT-8 are out of scope, mirroring the deck notes. Also fix the family name — the official Rev 5 family is "Personally Identifiable Information Processing and Transparency", not "Privacy Transparency" (line 80) or "Privacy (PT)" (line 41).

findings.claim: "The templates in this document, when completed, close the following NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 Privacy controls" (six PT closures)
findings.problem: aan-compliance-spine.yml — the declared closure SSOT ("Every book's Authorities Closed Here table is GENERATED from this file") — contains zero PT-* closure rows for book-17; this book's closure table is hand-authored, not spine-generated. The spine header says closures are back-filled per book, so this is a known gap, but as reviewed today the book asserts six closures the registry does not record, and the drift gate cannot protect a table that was never wired to the spine.
findings.fix: Back-fill six PT closure rows (book: book-17) into the spine and replace the manual closure table with the generated partial, so the claim and the registry cannot diverge.

findings.claim: Special-categories authority column: "OMB M-07-16" (SSN), "Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act" (financial accounts), "GINA (29 U.S.C. §1182)" (genetic), "INA §274B" (citizenship status)
findings.problem: OMB M-07-16 was rescinded and replaced by M-17-12 (2017) — citing it as live authority is stale. GLBA governs financial institutions, not a federal benefits agency's handling of direct-deposit data (the Privacy Act/M-17-12 are the operative authorities). GINA is Pub. L. 110-233, principally 42 U.S.C. §2000ff; 29 U.S.C. §1182 is the ERISA/HIPAA nondiscrimination section GINA merely amended. INA §274B is employment antidiscrimination, not a data-protection authority. The column is exactly what Legal Counsel is told to rely on.
findings.fix: Drop M-07-16 (M-17-12 superseded it), replace GLBA with Privacy Act + M-17-12, cite GINA as 42 U.S.C. §2000ff et seq., and swap INA §274B for a sensitivity-based rationale or agency policy citation.

findings.claim: "OMB M-14-06" cited as authority for precise geolocation; "OMB M-22-10" cited as authority for biometric data
findings.problem: Neither memo number matches those subjects in any in-repo source, and neither matches the memos' commonly known subjects (M-14-06 concerns administrative data for statistical purposes). These two OMB citations need verification against whitehouse.gov before the table goes in front of a reviewer; a wrong memo number in an authority column is an instant credibility hit.
findings.fix: Verify both memo numbers against the OMB memoranda index; if no on-point memo exists, cite the Fair Information Practice Principles via A-130 or agency policy instead.

findings.claim: "FedRAMP 20x requires machine-accessible privacy notices for the CSOs it authorizes"
findings.problem: No in-repo SSOT supports a specific 20x machine-accessible privacy-notice requirement: the CR26 reconciliation's 46 indicators across 10 themes contain no privacy-notice indicator, and the deadline registry has no related entry. The sentence properly hedges the agency side ("this series adopts the same standard") but states the CSO-side requirement as fact.
findings.fix: Verify against the CR26/20x requirement text (FRR/MAS documents); if it is an inference from the 20x machine-readable-evidence philosophy, say so ("consistent with 20x machine-readable evidence expectations") instead of "requires".

findings.claim: "confirm encryption and authentication standards meet GCC Moderate requirements (TLS 1.3 minimum; mutual TLS preferred...)"
findings.problem: Presents TLS 1.3 as the GCC/FedRAMP Moderate minimum. FedRAMP Moderate requires FIPS-validated TLS 1.2 or higher (NIST SP 800-52r2); TLS 1.3-minimum is the series' own stricter standard, not the baseline requirement. An assessor reading this as a baseline citation would mark it wrong; an engineer might fail compliant TLS 1.2 endpoints against a nonexistent requirement.
findings.fix: Rephrase: "meet GCC Moderate requirements (FIPS-validated TLS 1.2+; this series standardizes on TLS 1.3 with mutual TLS preferred for cross-agency APIs)."

findings.claim: "SSA systems that process health information in connection with Medicare Part B coordination..., disability determination..., or employee health programs are subject to HIPAA where SSA acts as a covered entity or business associate"
findings.problem: SSA is generally not a HIPAA covered entity (not a health plan, provider, or clearinghouse), and disability-determination medical records held by SSA are ordinarily Privacy Act records, not HIPAA-covered PHI. The template's determination step is good, but the framing presupposes HIPAA applicability scenarios (including a required Azure BAA) that need verification with SSA privacy counsel before appearing in an ATO artifact.
findings.fix: Reframe: "Complete a HIPAA applicability determination; note that SSA is generally not a covered entity — HIPAA obligations typically attach via CMS data-use agreements rather than direct covered-entity status" and make the BAA requirement conditional on that determination.

findings.claim: "E-Government Act of 2002, 44 U.S.C. §3501, Title III (FISMA)" (also "(44 U.S.C. §3501)" at line 143)
findings.problem: Muddled citation in the legal-authority list Legal Counsel is meant to reuse: the E-Gov Act is Pub. L. 107-347 (codified as a note to 44 U.S.C. §3501); its privacy provision is §208; Title III (FISMA 2002) was codified at 44 U.S.C. §3541 et seq. and superseded by FISMA 2014 (§3551 et seq.). As written, one line conflates the E-Gov Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act's code section, and FISMA.
findings.fix: Cite "E-Government Act of 2002, Pub. L. 107-347, §208 (44 U.S.C. §3501 note)" and list FISMA separately as "44 U.S.C. §3551 et seq." if needed.

findings.claim: "The following four scenarios must be documented in the registry above before the system can achieve FedRAMP 20x authorization"
findings.problem: The four-scenario set is this document's own template rule, but the sentence attributes it to FedRAMP 20x authorization ('must ... before the system can achieve'). No 20x source in the repo imposes scenario-level data-flow documentation.
findings.fix: Attribute the rule to the series/agency: "must be documented before the AO's authorization decision under this program's privacy documentation standard."

findings.claim: Financial account data (direct deposit) authority cited as "Social Security Act §205(j), 42 U.S.C. §405(j)"
findings.problem: §205(j) is the representative-payment provision; the usual authority for collecting bank account data for benefit payment is the EFT mandate (31 U.S.C. §3332). The table is fillable and tells users to consult Legal Counsel, but a wrong example citation tends to get copied verbatim.
findings.fix: Change the example citation to 31 U.S.C. §3332 (or leave [CITATION — confirm with Legal]) so the sample row does not propagate a dubious citation.

findings.claim: Section heading "Special Categories of PII (PT-7)" and repeated "special categories" phrasing
findings.problem: Rev 5 PT-7 is "Specific Categories of Personally Identifiable Information" — the closure table (line 652) gets it right, so the doc is internally inconsistent, and "special categories" reads as imported GDPR Art. 9 terminology a federal privacy reviewer will notice.
findings.fix: Use "Specific Categories" in the heading and first use, optionally noting the informal 'special categories' shorthand once.

findings.claim: Purview auto-labeling table: built-in classifiers "U.S. SSN", "Credit Card Number", "U.S. Passport", and "Trainable classifier: PHI"
findings.problem: Names of Microsoft Purview built-in sensitive information types and the existence of a PHI trainable classifier in the GCC Moderate service description are vendor-product claims not verifiable from in-repo SSOTs; per series doctrine these need a 'Vendor sources:' style verification against Microsoft Learn (including GCC feature parity for trainable classifiers).
findings.fix: Verify exact SIT/classifier names and GCC availability against Microsoft Learn and cite the page, consistent with the series' vendor-sources convention.

findings.claim: "KSI-CED-RAT Activation — evidence contract wiring for KSI-022, completing all 29 CR26 KSIs to evaluable status"
findings.problem: Calls the 29 internal rules 'CR26 KSIs'. AAN_CR26_Reconciliation.md (SSOT, line 14) states explicitly that 29/29 is the internal rule set, NOT the CR26 Moderate catalog, which has 46 indicators with only 19 mapped 1:1. The file's own KSI-022 Status section (lines 651-666) makes the same correction — so line 69 contradicts both the SSOT and the rest of the file. A hostile reviewer reading the summary would catch the overstated CR26 coverage immediately.
findings.fix: Rephrase to 'completing all 29 internal KSI rules to evaluable status (CR26 indicator coverage remains 19/46 — see §KSI-022 Status)'.

findings.claim: Dimension 3 'Secure delivery' is anchored to 'AT-3(3), SA-16' (also §'Tier 3 — Developer / Engineer Secure Delivery Training (AT-3(3), SA-16)' at line 294 and schema key 'secure_delivery_at3_sa16' at line 503)
findings.problem: SA-16's official title in the catalog SSOT is 'Developer-provided Training' — it requires the DEVELOPER OF THE SYSTEM to provide training to organizational personnel on the delivered system's security functions. This book uses it as the authority for training the agency's own developers in secure coding (OWASP, SBOM/Grype labs), which is the opposite direction. A 3PAO would reject the SA-16 mapping; the correct anchors for developer secure-coding training are AT-3/AT-3(3) (content drivers: SA-11, NIST SP 800-218 SSDF).
findings.fix: Drop SA-16 from the dimension-3 mapping (lines 101, 294, 327-344, 503) or replace with AT-3(3) alone / SA-11-family drivers; also fix the companion deck spec specs/Vol_IV_Book_05.yaml (slides 3, 4, 8) which repeats the mapping.

findings.claim: "Together these artifacts close five NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 controls" (line 71) vs 'Net New Controls Closed' table 'Total: 9 controls' (line 604)
findings.problem: The same document claims 5 controls closed (counting base controls only) and 9 controls closed (counting enhancements as controls) with no reconciliation of the counting convention. The deck spec says 'nine net-new controls'. A reviewer asked 'how many controls does this book close?' gets two answers from one file.
findings.fix: State one convention once, e.g. '5 base controls plus 4 enhancements (9 closure rows)' in both places.

findings.claim: "the seventeen-book series"
findings.problem: Count is not reproducible against any SSOT and contradicts sibling artifacts: the file's own Series Completion Summary lists 14 books; line 664 says 'ten-volume ... series'; the companion deck spec (specs/Vol_IV_Book_05.yaml, slides 13/15/16) says 'eighteen-book series'; the spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers ~60 books across 10 volumes. Three different counts across the book and its deck.
findings.fix: Anchor to the spine: either drop the count ('the series') or use the volume framing ('the ten-volume series') consistently in the qmd and the deck spec.

findings.claim: Table 'Federal AAN Series — Complete Control and KSI Coverage' (lines 670-687) lists 14 books with per-book 'Controls Closed' counts (16, 7, 12, 7, ...)
findings.problem: Captioned 'Complete ... Coverage' but omits many spine-registered books (Vol I Books 02/03/04/07, Vol III Books 03/04/07, Vol IV Book 06, Vols V-IX). The per-book counts cannot be reproduced from the spine — aan-compliance-spine.yml has no closure rows for book-01 through book-18 yet (closures are back-filled sequentially), and this is a hand-authored table, not a generated one. A hostile reviewer would ask for the derivation of '16' for Vol I Book 01 and get none.
findings.fix: Retitle to scope it ('Volumes I-IV control-closure summary as of this book') or generate it from the spine once closures are back-filled; remove the word 'Complete'.

findings.claim: "The four dimensions KSI-CED-RAT evaluates:" (line 95), and 'the four-dimension model required by KSI-CED-RAT' (line 53)
findings.problem: The CR26 reconciliation SSOT records KSI-CED-RAT as a single indicator ('Reviewing All Training', theme CED = 1 indicator).
