M-22-09 is the federal Zero Trust strategy; attributing a QoS/DSCP steering requirement to a specific section of it, and a sub-second-failover requirement to the ZTMM Networks pillar, are exactly the citations a hostile ISSO will pull the source documents to check. Not judged true/false — flagged for verification against the issuing documents.
findings.fix: Verify each Federal Mandate cell against the cited memo/model text; where the source does not state the requirement, relabel as "agency engineering requirement" rather than federal mandate.

findings.claim: "AWS has exactly two FedRAMP boundaries — there is no middle tier"; "Amazon Connect ... holds FedRAMP High authorization" in GovCloud and "FedRAMP Moderate authorization in the commercial regions"; GovCloud capability-gap claims (Contact Lens / Amazon Q lag, Marketplace integration certification, support cadence).
findings.problem: Load-bearing external-product claims underpinning the entire .com-exception narrative; none is verifiable against in-repo SSOTs. The doc partially hedges ("at time of evaluation", re-evaluation warning at line 120), but the authorization-status assertions are stated as present-tense fact. Not judged true/false — must be verified against the FedRAMP Marketplace and AWS documentation before external review.
findings.fix: Verify Amazon Connect's current authorization status per region against the FedRAMP Marketplace and add "as listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace as of <date>" qualifiers; keep the existing time-of-evaluation hedges on capability gaps.

findings.claim: Timeline row: "June 11, 2027 | No new Rev5 certifications".
findings.problem: The SSOT event (aan-authority-deadlines.yml, fedramp-rev5-last-applications) is "FedRAMP stops accepting applications for new Rev5 Certifications" on that date. Applications cease; certifications already in the pipeline can still issue afterward. The date matches, but the event wording overstates it.
findings.fix: Reword to "No new Rev5 certification applications accepted".

findings.claim: Federal Framework table cites "TIC 3.0 Use Case E" as an external Standard/Reference.
findings.problem: Line 308 of the same file concedes the letter labels are series shorthand ("elsewhere in this series shorthand-labeled Use Case E"); CISA's TIC 3.0 use cases are named (Branch Office, Remote User), not lettered. Presenting the shorthand as the official reference in a standards column invites a reviewer to check CISA's catalog and find no "Use Case E".
findings.fix: Cite "TIC 3.0 Branch Office Use Case" in the table and keep the letter shorthand only where it is flagged as series-internal.

findings.claim: Kari's Law reference given as "47 CFR §9.4".
findings.problem: The FCC's MLTS direct-911-dialing and notification rules implementing Kari's Law are generally codified at 47 CFR §9.16, not §9.4 (§9.4 addresses interconnected-VoIP 911 obligations). Not verifiable against in-repo SSOTs — flag for verification against the eCFR before external distribution.
findings.fix: Verify and correct the CFR section (likely 47 CFR §9.16).

findings.claim: "NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 CA-7" appears twice (lines 439 and 449) as the standard reference for ConMon.
findings.problem: CA-7 is an SP 800-53 control; SP 800-37 Rev 2 defines the RMF Monitor step but contains no control named CA-7. The compound citation misattributes the control to the wrong publication.
findings.fix: Cite "NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-7; NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 (Monitor step)".

findings.claim: Fig-13 alt text: "August 31 Class B plus C opens Amazon Connect pathway"; body table (line 338) instead says at August 3 "Evaluate whether Connect .com falls under Class A".
findings.problem: The figure asserts Connect's 20x class (B/C pathway) while the body says the class is still to be evaluated (possibly Class A). Internally inconsistent about which pipeline applies; both dates individually match the deadline SSOT.
findings.fix: Make the figure match the body's undetermined-class framing (e.g., "Class B + C open — candidate Connect pathway pending class evaluation").

findings.claim: SC-20 titled "Secure Name/Address Resolution (Authoritative)" and SC-22 titled "Architecture / Provisioning for Name/Address Resolution" (lines 98-99).
findings.problem: Both titles contradict the official NIST 800-53r5 catalog SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json): SC-20 is "Secure Name/Address Resolution Service (Authoritative Source)" and SC-22 is "Architecture and Provisioning for Name/Address Resolution Service". The compliance spine and the gated generated partial (authorities/authorities-book-ddi-xplat.md) both carry the full official titles — only this embedded copy is shortened. A 3PAO checking control titles against the catalog would flag both rows.
findings.fix: Replace the two embedded table rows with the exact rows from authorities/authorities-book-ddi-xplat.md (full official titles).

findings.claim: "Both tables below are generated from the series compliance spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) by render_authorities_table.py; they are not hand-edited here." (plus the in-table comments "do not hand-edit").
findings.problem: The embedded tables diverge from what render_authorities_table.py actually produces: the SC-20/SC-22 titles are shortened, and both table captions carry appended source-path suffixes ("(infoblox-ddi-book/06-cross-platform-operations.md)", "(infoblox-ddi-book/07-servicenow-orchestration.md)") that the generator does not emit (compare authorities/authorities-book-ddi-xplat.md and authorities-book-ddi-servicenow.md). So the provenance claim is false as stated. This is NOT covered by the existing drift gate — render_authorities_table.py --check only diffs the authorities/*.md partials, not the .qmd-embedded copies.
findings.fix: Re-embed the generator output verbatim (or state that the embedded copy is a hand-adapted rendering of the generated partial and move the path annotation outside the generated block).

findings.claim: "the ServiceNow Government Cloud platform holds FedRAMP High authorization and coordinates a Moderate boundary" (Governance Boundary, line 86; repeated in the fig-alt footer, line 47).
findings.problem: This is a load-bearing inheritance premise: the volume's federal control closure (CM-3/CM-5/AU-2 at the front door) rests on the High-on-Moderate treatment, which in turn rests on ServiceNow Government Cloud actually holding a current FedRAMP High authorization — an external-marketplace fact this repo cannot attest. Both "FedRAMP High" mentions are within the file's 2-mention baseline in aan-high-claim-baseline.yml, and the treatment is properly anchored once in Vol VII Book 00 §"Authorization Boundary Treatment — ServiceNow High-on-Moderate" (verified present), so this is not a scope violation — but the authorization status itself needs periodic external verification, not judged true/false here.
findings.fix: Verify ServiceNow Government Cloud's current FedRAMP High authorization against the FedRAMP Marketplace and record the verification (date + marketplace listing) where the series tracks externally verified claims, e.g. alongside Vol VII Book 00's boundary-treatment section.

findings.claim: The 'Books in This Volume' table lists Books 00-05 (6 books), and the volume-map figure caption/alt (line 88) says 'six ServiceNow-automation books'.
findings.problem: aan-compliance-spine.yml registers SEVEN books for vol-7 (VII-00 through VII-06), including book-sn-saas 'SaaS Integration Governance (the Entra app gallery as a governed SA-9 event)' at slot VII-06 — and Vol_VII_Book_06_FedAAN_SaaS_Integration_Governance.qmd exists on disk. The volume overview omits one of its own registered books, so the overview contradicts the book-registry SSOT and the shipped corpus.
findings.fix: Add a Vol VII Book 06 row (SaaS Integration Governance) to the table, and update the figure caption/alt (and the underlying SVG/PNG) from 'six' to seven books.

findings.claim: 'Moderate-authorized alternatives already named in the Product Inventory Questionnaire include ... Ivanti Neurons for ITSM (Moderate)'.
findings.problem: Vol_0_Book_01_FedAAN_Product_Inventory_Questionnaire.qmd never names 'Neurons' anywhere, and mentions Ivanti only once — in the patch/systems-management candidate row (line 165) with no authorization level and no workflow/CMDB role. The claim that the questionnaire names Ivanti Neurons for ITSM as a Moderate workflow/CMDB alternative is false against the cited in-repo source; the '(Moderate)' status itself is also asserted nowhere else in the repo (needs external verification if kept).
findings.fix: Either add Ivanti Neurons for ITSM (with a source link and authorization class) to the questionnaire's Volume VII section and source table, or drop Ivanti from this sentence and cite only the Atlassian Government Cloud entry the questionnaire actually carries.

findings.claim: 'Single source of truth: the platform's authorization status is pinned in the Product Inventory Questionnaire (Vol 0 Book 01 §product-status).'
findings.problem: The questionnaire has no 'product-status' section or anchor. Its anchors are #scope-rule, #known-ssa, #discovery, and #flags. A pointer that declares itself the single-source-of-truth reference and does not resolve is exactly what a hostile reviewer pulls on.
findings.fix: Point at the real section — the ServiceNow row lives in 'Known SSA Inventory' (#known-ssa, table line ~105) and the flags summary (#flags) — or add an explicit product-status anchor to the questionnaire and reference that.

findings.claim: ServiceNow is described as 'FedRAMP-authorized for the Moderate boundary this series targets'.
findings.problem: The same file states three times that ServiceNow Government Cloud holds a FedRAMP High authorization and explicitly that this 'is a High-on-Moderate treatment (not a Moderate authorization)' (line 50). Line 62 reads as an implicit Moderate-authorization claim, contradicting the file's own boundary-treatment section — the one it insists must be 'explicit, not a footnote'.
findings.fix: Rephrase line 62 to match the treatment, e.g. 'FedRAMP-authorized (High — see the Authorization Boundary Treatment subsection) operating against the Moderate boundary this series targets'.

findings.claim: 'A High-authorized service over-satisfies every Moderate control requirement' (line 109), and line 48: 'High fully encompasses the Moderate control baseline this series targets, so the platform over-satisfies the boundary'.
findings.problem: This is a load-bearing use of the platform's High authorization to justify boundary fit, and as stated it is wrong in the shared-responsibility sense: a CSO's authorization (at any level) covers only controls inside the CSO's boundary per its customer-responsibility matrix. Customer-responsible controls — instance configuration, workflow/approval design, access grants, the MID Server deployment — are not satisfied at all by the platform's High authorization, so 'every Moderate control requirement' does not follow from baseline-superset logic. (These High mentions are within the file's 8-mention baseline; the issue is the inference, not the mention.)
findings.fix: Narrow the claim to what is true: FedRAMP High's baseline is a superset of Moderate's, so the platform-side (inheritable) controls are assessed at or above the Moderate bar; customer-responsibility controls remain the agency's per the CRM and are the subject of this volume's workflows.

findings.claim: MID Server callouts mean 'credentials and execution never leave' the ATO boundary, and 'Cloud-to-cloud integrations use the platform's in-boundary integration surface, not a commercial multi-tenant relay'.
findings.problem: Vendor-architecture claims about ServiceNow MID Server credential containment and the integration surface's boundary placement cannot be verified from repo SSOTs; the 'Vendor sources:' convention (authoring spec) expects a citation for vendor-specific claims, and none is given here.
findings.fix: Add a ServiceNow product-documentation citation for the MID Server credential/execution model, or soften to a design requirement ('callouts MUST run through an in-boundary MID Server') rather than a vendor-behavior assertion.

findings.claim: ServiceNow Government Cloud holds FedRAMP High authorization (lines 47, 94, 103); Atlassian Government Cloud (Jira/Confluence) is FedRAMP Moderate (line 122).
findings.problem: External marketplace/authorization statuses that no repo SSOT can prove. Both are consistent with the Product Inventory Questionnaire (ServiceNow Class D High with a vendor press-release source; Atlassian Gov Cloud Moderate, line 108/260) and the file already hedges with 'verify on the FedRAMP Marketplace at procurement' — flagged for the external-verification ledger only, not judged true or false.
findings.fix: No text change required; ensure these entries stay pinned to the questionnaire's source-link table and get re-verified at procurement as the file already states.

findings.claim: "neither of which re-closes the naming-plane necessity (that stays in Vol I Book 01)" — repeated at line 76 ("The naming plane is the necessity anchor (Vol I Book 01)") and line 99 ("Vol I Book 01 ... the CM-8 SSOT").
findings.problem: The spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers the CM-8 necessity:true closure under book-patch-sysmgmt = Vol III Book 03 (spine line 272), NOT under book-01. book-01 carries no CM-8 closure entry at all; its necessity anchors are SC-20/SC-21. A 3PAO tracing 'where is the CM-8 Closure-Necessity anchor' via the registry lands in Vol III Book 03, contradicting this book's claim that the naming-plane necessity 'stays in Vol I Book 01'. (The spine's own comment at line 297 attributes the identity SSOT to Vol I Book 01, so the SSOT-of-identity phrasing is defensible — the necessity-anchor location claim is what contradicts the registry.)
findings.fix: Point the necessity-anchor references at Vol III Book 03 (book-patch-sysmgmt, where CM-8 necessity is registered), or split the phrasing: identity SSOT lives in Vol I Book 01, the CM-8 Closure-Necessity anchor is registered at Vol III Book 03. Alternatively, if the author intends the necessity anchor to live in Vol I Book 01, move the necessity:true CM-8 entry in the spine — but then Vol III Book 03 text must change too.

findings.claim: Provenance states "Vendor claims cite vendor documentation."
findings.problem: The file contains multiple vendor-product capability claims — ServiceNow Discovery / Service Graph Connectors, 'Service Graph Connector for Azure (subscriptions, resource groups, VMs, storage, key vaults, policy assignments)' (line 54), Conditional Access policy objects ingested via Microsoft Graph as configuration CIs (line 53), MID Server Discovery and Arc-projected servers as CIs (line 55), Defender for Cloud / MDVM inventory as attributes on existing CIs (line 56) — but carries zero vendor-source links. The series authoring spec requires 'Vendor sources:' links for vendor claims, so the Provenance sentence is contradicted by the document body.
findings.fix: Add vendor-documentation links for the Service Graph Connector for Azure coverage, the Graph-based ingest of CA policy objects, MID Server Discovery, and Defender/MDVM inventory integration — or soften the Provenance line to say vendor sourcing is pending.

findings.claim: Specific connector-capability assertions: Service Graph Connector for Azure ingests subscriptions, resource groups, VMs, storage, key vaults, and policy assignments as CI classes; Microsoft Graph integration models Conditional Access policy objects as configuration CIs; Defender for Cloud / MDVM findings land as attributes/relationships on existing CIs rather than a parallel CI tree.
findings.problem: These are externally verifiable product-capability claims (exact resource-type coverage of ServiceNow's Azure connector, whether CA policies are natively modeled as CIs, whether the Defender integration writes attributes vs. new CI classes) that cannot be confirmed from any in-repo SSOT. Not judged true or false here — flagged for external verification before an assessor-facing release.
findings.fix: Verify each capability against current ServiceNow and Microsoft documentation and attach the citations (see the companion Provenance finding); where a capability is actually custom integration work rather than out-of-box connector behavior, say so explicitly.

findings.claim: "the running measure of how completely the estate is enumerated, which is exactly what CM-8 and CISA BOD 23-01 require."
findings.problem: BOD 23-01 requires asset discovery on a 7-day cadence and vulnerability enumeration on a 14-day cadence with CDM reporting; CM-8 requires an accurate, current component inventory. An exception-queue completeness measure supports both but is not 'exactly' what either requires — a hostile reviewer would flag the overreach.
findings.fix: Soften to 'which directly supports the enumeration-completeness expectations of CM-8 and CISA BOD 23-01' or similar.

findings.claim: "The architecture and Vol VI baseline-as-code prove the mechanism is sufficient." (Closure Necessity callout)
findings.problem: "Prove ... sufficient" is asserted with no mechanism or test cited. Architecture documents and a baseline-as-code repo demonstrate a mechanism exists; sufficiency of the mechanism is exactly what a 3PAO tests, not something documentation proves. The first "proves" in the same callout (conformance tooling proves where M365 deviates) is defensible because a test result substantiates it; this second one is not.
findings.fix: Soften to "establish" or "document" the mechanism, or cite the Vol VI Book 08 validation harness (the spine's test field for CM-6 already points there) as the thing that demonstrates sufficiency.

findings.claim: Control Family 2 Actuate step: "on approval, the change is applied to Entra via Graph (the account provisioned, the exclusion group membership set) — logged, scoped, and reversible."
findings.problem: The loop table (line 44) states unqualified that "ServiceNow does not flip the setting" and the callout (line 48) says the coordination role needs only read + task-creation, "not admin over the estate it governs." The CF2 actuate step uses passive voice ("the change is applied") that reads as automated provisioning triggered by ServiceNow approval — the standard real-world JML pattern is a ServiceNow-to-Graph integration holding standing User.ReadWrite/Group write scopes. A hostile ISSO will ask which principal holds the Graph write permission; if it is the ServiceNow integration identity, the "no standing write authority" posture claim needs the callout's scoped-action qualification applied here explicitly.
findings.fix: Name the actor in the CF2 Actuate bullet: either "the identity team applies the change via Graph" (human-actuated, consistent with the table) or explicitly invoke the callout's scoped/individually-approved automation carve-out and state the integration identity's permission scope.

findings.claim: "account lifecycle and least privilege (AC-2, AC-5/6)"; repeated at line 71 as "the AC-2 / AC-5/6 lifecycle"
findings.problem: Per the catalog SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, v5.2.0), AC-5 is "Separation of Duties" — only AC-6 is "Least Privilege." Lumping AC-5 under the least-privilege label mislabels the control; a picky reviewer will flag it.
findings.fix: Reword to "least privilege and separation of duties (AC-2, AC-5, AC-6)" or drop AC-5 if separation of duties is not actually operated by this loop.

findings.claim: Vendor capability claims: ScubaGear "runs on a schedule and produces a per-policy pass/fail result" (line 55); Graph-applied changes are "logged, scoped, and reversible" (line 68); Purview posture reads of "label coverage, DLP policy version, audit-retention configuration" via ingestion (line 80).
findings.problem: These are external-product behavior claims. They are cited to vendor documentation in the References table (cisa.gov/scuba, github.com/cisagov/ScubaGear, Microsoft Learn Graph/Purview), which satisfies the series' vendor-sources doctrine, but their truth rests on external documentation and must be verified there — not judged from this corpus.
findings.fix: No change required; flagged for the external-verification pass only.

findings.claim: CM-2 is presented as an obligation this book coordinates: prose says Azure 'carries ... baseline configuration and settings (CM-2, CM-6) ... the coordination role is to make each one owned, clocked, approved ... and evidenced'; the engine table and the Control Engine 1 section header both map Azure Policy to 'CM-2 / CM-6'.
findings.problem: The spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers NO CM-2 closure for book-sn-azure — only CM-6, SI-2, RA-5 — and the book's own Authorities Closed Here table accordingly omits CM-2. CM-2 closure lives in book-patch-sysmgmt (Vol III Book 03, 'Desired-state config baseline per platform') and book-day2-landingzone. A hostile ISSO reading 'the coordination role is to make each one owned...' over a list that includes CM-2 will ask where the CM-2 coordination closure is registered and find it absent from this book.
findings.fix: Either add a CM-2 closure row for book-sn-azure to the spine and regenerate the table, or add one sentence noting CM-2 closure is registered in Vol III Book 03 and this book touches CM-2 only through Azure Policy actuation of the baseline — mirroring the disclaimer already used for the posture/patch mechanisms.

findings.claim: The CM-6 closure row lists 'CISA SCuBA' as an authority driver for 'Azure Policy / Defender-for-Cloud recommendations raised as ServiceNow remediation tasks'.
findings.problem: CISA SCuBA (Secure Cloud Business Applications) publishes secure-configuration baselines for M365 and Google Workspace SaaS — it does not cover Azure IaaS/PaaS resource configuration, which is this book's surface. The driver is inherited from the spine row (aan-compliance-spine.yml line ~307, book-sn-azure CM-6, drivers [nist-800-53r5, cisa-scuba]), so the table is drift-gate-consistent, but the mapping itself is the kind an assessor challenges: BOD 25-01/SCuBA belongs on the M365 book's CM-6 row (where it already appears), not the Azure one.
findings.fix: Fix at the spine: change the book-sn-azure CM-6 drivers to [nist-800-53r5] (optionally omb-a-130 or cisa-bod-23-01 if defensible) and regenerate the book table via render_authorities_table.py.

findings.claim: The loop depends on named vendor capabilities inside the government boundary: Azure Policy deployIfNotExists/modify remediation, Defender for Cloud CSPM + MDVM workload/image findings via 'the security-posture API', Azure Update Manager + Arc guest-OS patching, and the ServiceNow 'Vulnerability Response' module as the task type.
findings.problem: Vendor claims are cited to vendor documentation per series spec (References table), but availability/feature parity of these specific services within the FedRAMP Moderate government boundary is not evidenced in-repo — e.g., whether MDVM premium features, Defender security-posture APIs, and Update Manager/Arc have parity in the agency's government cloud, and whether ServiceNow's Vulnerability Response plugin is within the scope of the ServiceNow government-offering authorization the Expansion Plan §16 relies on. Not judging these true or false — they require verification against Azure Government service-availability and the ServiceNow authorization package.
findings.fix: Verify each named capability against the government-cloud availability matrices and the ServiceNow Gov authorization scope; add a one-line boundary-availability note (or an Honest Limits bullet) recording the verification date, consistent with the series' verified-source convention.

findings.claim: "POA&M items are ServiceNow IRM issues, so they inherit the same SLA, approval, and audit-trail machinery as remediation tasks" and "A POA&M whose linked remediation task closes with passing re-test evidence closes automatically; one whose milestone slips escalates."
findings.problem: These are ServiceNow IRM/GRC product-behavior claims (issue-model inheritance, automatic POA&M closure on linked-task re-test, milestone-slip escalation) stated as existing mechanism with no vendor citation. A 3PAO would ask for the vendor documentation or a configured demonstration; auto-closure of POA&M items in particular is a behavior that typically requires custom Flow/rule configuration, not out-of-box IRM. Not judged true/false — flagged as requiring external verification.
findings.fix: Add a vendor-documentation citation for the IRM issue/POA&M capabilities relied on, or reframe the auto-close/escalate behavior as designed configuration ("configured to close automatically") rather than inherent product behavior.

findings.claim: "assessed control state and POA&M are exported as OSCAL assessment-results / POA&M models into the authorization package"
findings.problem: Presented as an existing emit mechanism, but ServiceNow IRM/GRC OSCAL export is a product/integration capability that cannot be verified from anything in-repo — no vendor source is cited and no in-series build artifact (Vol VI kit) is referenced as the thing that performs the OSCAL transformation. A hostile ISSO would ask who produces the OSCAL: ServiceNow natively, or a custom exporter that does not yet exist. Not judged true/false — flagged as requiring external verification.
findings.fix: Either cite ServiceNow documentation for OSCAL export, or attribute the OSCAL transformation to a named in-series component (e.g., the Vol VI Book 07 evidence pipeline or the Vol VII Book 05 scoped app) so the mechanism is traceable.

findings.claim: Provenance states "Vendor claims cite vendor documentation."
findings.problem: The file contains zero vendor-documentation citations while making ServiceNow IRM/GRC capability claims (lines ~52, 56, 62). The provenance assertion is not true of this document as written.
findings.fix: Add the vendor source links the provenance promises, or soften the provenance line to match the document's actual sourcing.

findings.claim: The code block labeled "// control-map.json — one entry per (finding class → task). Projection of the spine." presents entries m365.scuba.fail, azure.updatemgr.missing_critical, azure.defender.finding with fields control/task_type/severity/sla_class/ksi/slot.
findings.problem: The shipped artifact x_ssa_fed_compliance/data/control-map.json contains none of these keys (actual keys: m365.baseline.drift, azure.patch.remediation, azure.vuln.finding, etc.) and uses a different schema (title/approval/actuation; no severity or sla_class fields exist anywhere in it). Values also conflict: doc shows RA-5 task_type "vulnerability_response" vs shipped "change"; doc CM-6 ksi [KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC] vs shipped [KSI-CMT]; doc SI-2 ksi [KSI-SVC, KSI-MLA] vs shipped [KSI-SVC]. Worse, the doc's sample entries would FAIL the CI gate the doc itself cites — validate_day2_control_maps.py REQUIRED = {title, control, task_type, approval, actuation, ksi, slot}, so every sample entry errors on missing title/approval/actuation. Line 45's table description of the binding as "(control, task type, severity, SLA, KSI slot)" repeats the phantom severity/SLA fields. A 3PAO diffing the doc against the deployable artifact rejects the section.
findings.fix: Replace the sample block with a verbatim excerpt of the shipped data/control-map.json (e.g. the m365.baseline.drift and azure.patch.remediation entries), and correct the line-45 table cell to the actual binding fields (control, task type, approval, actuation, KSI, slot).

findings.claim: "A CI check ... fails when the app's control map diverges from the spine — so the deployable app and the series SSOT cannot silently drift." (also line 77: "Each entry mirrors a closure row in aan-compliance-spine.yml")
findings.problem: The actual gate (validate_day2_control_maps.py) compares only the SET of control IDs against the union of book-sn-m365/azure/attestation closures, plus vocabulary validity (slot exists, KSI theme exists in CR26). Per-entry KSI lists, slots, and task types are NOT checked against the specific spine rows, and such drift already exists and passes green today: shipped m365.baseline.drift carries ksi [KSI-CMT] while the spine's CM-6/book-sn-m365 row carries [KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC]; shipped azure.patch.remediation carries [KSI-SVC] while the spine SI-2 row carries [KSI-SVC, KSI-MLA]. "Cannot silently drift" and "mirrors a closure row" overstate the mechanism.
findings.fix: Scope the claim to what the gate enforces: the map's control set cannot drift from the spine's closures and its slots/KSI themes must be valid vocabulary; per-entry attribute bindings are review items (or extend the validator to row-level checks and keep the strong claim).

findings.claim: The record-model table column "Path (in the app)" lists rest/sys_rest_message_graph.xml, ..._arm.xml, atf/*.xml, and update-set/x_ssa_fed_compliance-update-set.xml ("The whole app assembled into one importable XML"); the subtitle and Closure Necessity callout (line ~103) assert "one importable update set" / "This book is the importable artifact."
findings.problem: None of those XML files exist in the shipped kit — rest/, atf/, and update-set/ contain only README specs, and update-set/README.md states the XML "is deliberately not committed" (assemble in sub-prod, export, ship). The starter-skeleton callout (line 32) honestly says "ATF spec, and update-set spec," but the table presents the XMLs as present paths and the Closure Necessity callout claims importability the shipped artifact does not provide — the exact slideware-vs-artifact gap the callout argues against. Import step 7 ("run the ATF suites") likewise presupposes suites that must first be built per atf/README.md.
findings.fix: Mark the XML rows as build outputs/specs (e.g. "exported per tenant — see rest/README.md", "assembled in sub-prod — update-set/README.md") and soften Closure Necessity to "the buildable/assemblable artifact" consistent with the deliberate not-committed disposition.

findings.claim: "Under GCC Moderate the Graph and ARM callouts resolve to the commercial endpoints that serve the GCC Moderate boundary (graph.microsoft.com / management.azure.com...)"
findings.problem: Microsoft-product endpoint-resolution fact (GCC rides the commercial Graph/ARM endpoints; GCC High/DoD use graph.microsoft.us etc.). Consistent with rest/README.md and the series convention, but it is a vendor claim a 3PAO would verify against Microsoft national-cloud endpoint documentation, and the doc carries no vendor source link (the series authoring spec requires 'Vendor sources:' for vendor claims).
findings.fix: Add a Microsoft Learn national-cloud/Graph-endpoints source link where the series cloud-resolution convention is invoked. Not judged true/false here.

findings.claim: "a FedRAMP-authorized ServiceNow instance" (Boundary & Governance) and connector capability claims (Graph app registration/managed identity scopes, Azure Resource Manager/Defender/Update Manager read via scoped SP).
findings.problem: External product/authorization claims. The spine's Vol VII doctrine says to refer to ServiceNow as authorized (Moderate boundary), so the wording is consistent with the series SSOT, but the authorization status and the specific Microsoft connector capabilities are externally verifiable facts (FedRAMP Marketplace / vendor docs) with no source link in this book.
findings.fix: Carry a 'Vendor sources:' link (FedRAMP Marketplace listing for ServiceNow; Microsoft permissions reference) per the series authoring spec. Not judged true/false here.

findings.claim: Fig-03 fig-alt: 'the VI-08 validation harnesses ... sit across all books and close CA-2 and CA-7(3)'
findings.problem: Uses the closure verb 'close' while the file's own Closure Necessity callout (line ~97) states 'Volume VI does not claim to close controls', and the spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml) registers ZERO closure rows for any vol-6 book — CA-2 is closed by book-sn-attestation (spine line 312) and CA-7 by book-evidence-fabric/book-sn-* (spine lines 284/304/314/347). The body table correctly says 'Representative controls operationalized'; the figure alt-text (and presumably the rendered figure) makes a closure claim the SSOT does not support and the file itself disclaims.
findings.fix: In the fig-alt (and the rendered figure banner), change 'close CA-2 and CA-7(3)' to 'operationalize CA-2 and CA-7(3)' (or 'validate', matching the spine's test-field wording 'Vol VI Book 08 — telemetry-completeness workbook (CA-7(3))').

findings.claim: VI-05 row lists 'AC-4, SC-12/28, AU-10' as representative controls operationalized
findings.problem: AU-10 (Non-repudiation) appears nowhere in aan-compliance-spine.yml — the declared SSOT for the control x book map — and AU-10 is selected only in the 800-53B High baseline, while the spine's hard scope parameter is 'FedRAMP Moderate only. Never map to High.' A hostile ISSO would ask why a Moderate-scoped series presents an above-Moderate-baseline control with no 'above baseline' qualifier. (CA-7(3) at line 90 is also not baseline-selected, but the spine itself cites CA-7(3) in its test fields, so it is series-sanctioned; AU-10 has no spine sanction at all. The same unqualified AU-10 usage recurs in Vol_VI_Book_05 lines 60/71/96.)
findings.fix: Either drop AU-10 from the VI-05 row, or qualify it (e.g. 'AU-10 — above Moderate baseline, agency-elected'), and reconcile Vol_VI_Book_05's AU-10 rows with the spine when its closures are back-filled.

findings.claim: 'The architecture volumes prove the mechanism is sufficient'
findings.problem: 'Prove ... sufficient' is an assessor/AO determination, not something a design document can establish; the architecture volumes argue sufficiency from control text and protocol behavior. A 3PAO would push back on 'prove'.
findings.fix: Soften to 'argue the mechanism is sufficient' or 'demonstrate why the mechanism suffices', keeping the operationalize/demonstrable contrast intact.

findings.claim: "the existing gate picked it up and reported `5 day-2 control maps, 47 catalog items, all consistent with the spine`"
findings.problem: The quoted validator output cannot be reproduced. Running validate_day2_control_maps.py today prints "OK — 6 day-2 control maps, 55 catalog items, all consistent with the spine" (the validator also globs x_ssa_fed_compliance/data/control-map.json, which the book itself says now exists). Even restricted to servicenow-day2/, the five maps sum to 48 items (5+10+3+24+6), not 47 — so the quote is wrong under either framing. A reviewer re-running the gate gets numbers that match nothing in the book.
findings.fix: Re-run the validator and update the quote to the current output (6 maps, 55 items), or rephrase to avoid quoting a point-in-time count (e.g., "the existing gate picked the lane up with zero wiring and validates it on every run").

findings.claim: Authorities table rows for AC-2(1), AC-2(3), IA-5(2), SA-9(2), AC-2(4) carry titles like "Account Management | Automated System Account Management"
findings.problem: The unescaped "|" inside the Title cell of these five rows (lines ~271, 272, 281, 284, 285) splits the cell in the pipe table: the 8-column header gets 9 cells, so every downstream column shifts — e.g., the AC-2(1) row renders with the closing mechanism in the "Accreditation gate" column and "KSI-IAM" under "Tool-attestable?". The rendered table shows factually wrong values in named columns. The drift gate checks content-vs-spine, not markdown column integrity, so this is not covered by the existing gate. (The base+enhancement titles themselves are correct per reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json.)
findings.fix: In the generator that emits the authorities block, escape the separator as "\|" or replace it with an em dash (e.g., "Account Management — Automated System Account Management") before writing table cells. The same spine titles feed other books' tables, so fix at the generator, not by hand-editing the generated block.

findings.claim: Figure caption and alt text: "The provisioning spine — six phases, twenty-four governed catalog items" / footer "Six phases, 24 governed catalog items, 24 controls"
findings.problem: The catalog the figure claims to depict is organized into SEVEN phases (Phase 1 Intake … Phase 7 Attest and exit, per the generated catalog sections and the control map's phase fields). The figure's six boxes (Request/Verify/Classify/Agree/Configure/Attest) are a different, simplified decomposition, but the caption asserts "six phases" over the same 24 items the seven-phase catalog governs. A reviewer counting phases will find the book disagreeing with its own diagram.
findings.fix: Either regenerate the figure with seven phases matching the catalog, or reword the caption/alt to present the six boxes as a simplified request-lifecycle view ("six lifecycle stages") explicitly distinct from the seven catalog phases.

findings.claim: Subtitle: "onboarding a third-party SaaS as the moment 24 controls are closed"; phase table captions: "Phase N — closes AC-20, SA-9 …"
findings.problem: The book's own convention callout (line ~259) states that per the Vol 0 Book 02 convention, Volume VII/IX rows record where a control is "coordinated, evidenced and operated — not a second independent closure claim," with SA-9 the sole primary closure in this book. The subtitle and the seven "Phase N — closes …" captions assert closure of all 24, directly contradicting that convention two pages later. A hostile reviewer will quote the two statements against each other.
findings.fix: Soften the subtitle and caption verb to match the stated convention (e.g., "the moment 24 controls are operationalized/evidenced" and "Phase N — operates AC-20, …"), keeping "closes" only for SA-9; caption wording lives in the catalog generator/map, so change it there.

findings.claim: "The marketplace has no API. The export is taken by hand from fedramp.gov/marketplace"
findings.problem: This is a load-bearing external claim — it justifies the manual-export process, the freshness caveat, and the name-matching heuristic. FedRAMP has published machine-readable marketplace data feeds, and FedRAMP 20x/CR26 emphasizes machine-readable program data, so "no API" may be false or stale as of the Date Code. Not judged true/false here; it is outside the in-repo SSOTs and must be verified against fedramp.gov.
findings.fix: Verify against fedramp.gov whether a machine-readable marketplace feed/API exists as of the Date Code; if one exists, replace the manual-export process description or narrow the claim (e.g., "no supported query API for authorization verdicts") with a source link.

findings.claim: "FedRAMP Moderate for M365 means GCC Moderate, which is paired with Commercial Entra ID on Azure Commercial infrastructure (only GCC High and DoD sit on Azure Government)" and "the full commercial gallery is available: thousands of apps … nothing blocked and nothing marked"
findings.problem: Microsoft cloud-pairing and gallery-availability facts underpin the whole motivating argument. The Provenance section says they were verified against Microsoft Learn, but Microsoft Learn is outside the in-repo SSOTs this review can check, and Microsoft changes cloud pairings and gallery behavior over time. Flagged for external verification, not judged.
findings.fix: Keep the existing Provenance note but add the specific Microsoft Learn URL(s) and a verified-on date so the claim is re-checkable, consistent with the series' vendor-sources convention.

findings.claim: Graph API surface: endpoints such as POST /applicationTemplates/{id}/instantiate, POST /servicePrincipals/{id}/addTokenSigningCertificate, PUT …/synchronization/secrets; permission names Application.ReadWrite.OwnedBy and Synchronization.ReadWrite.All; gallery detection constant applicationTemplateId ≠ 8adf8e6e-67b2-4cf2-a259-e3dc5476c621
findings.problem: The entire actuation design (and the standing_admin_is_refused test) depends on these Microsoft Graph endpoint paths, permission names, and the custom-app template GUID being current. Provenance claims verbatim verification against the Graph reference, but that source is outside the in-repo SSOTs. Flagged for external verification, not judged.
findings.fix: Add the Graph reference URLs and verified-on date next to the surface table (or in Provenance), and note that Application.ReadWrite.OwnedBy's sufficiency for servicePrincipal synchronization writes should be confirmed in a sub-prod tenant before the Script Include ships.

findings.claim: "Gallery risk scores name SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA and PCI — not FedRAMP — and sit behind additional licensing"
findings.problem: This describes Microsoft's app risk-scoring product behavior (Defender for Cloud Apps app catalog) and its licensing, both of which change; Defender for Cloud Apps' compliance attributes have historically included FedRAMP fields, so "not FedRAMP" is contestable. Outside the in-repo SSOTs; flagged for external verification, not judged.
findings.fix: Verify the current risk-score attribute set and licensing against Microsoft documentation as of the Date Code and cite it under the vendor-sources convention, or drop the parenthetical licensing/attribute detail since the argument stands without it.

findings.claim: DNSSEC signed responses are attributed to SC-20(1) in three places: the Controls Operationalized table row "SC-20/20(1) — Secure Name/Address Resolution (Authoritative) — DNSSEC-signing authoritative resolver as code" (line 107), the HCL comment `dnssec = "on"  # SC-20(1): signed responses` (line 70), and the fig-alt "tagged SC-20(1)" (line 64).
findings.problem: Per the catalog SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json, v5.2.0), SC-20(1) is "Child Subspaces" — it concerns child zones/subspaces of parent domains, not DNSSEC signing. Data-origin authentication and integrity artifacts (signed responses) are the SC-20 BASE control requirement. A 3PAO would reject the enhancement citation outright.
findings.fix: Replace every SC-20(1) tag with SC-20 (base). If an enhancement is genuinely intended for signing artifacts, none fits better than the base control; drop "/20(1)" from the table row, fix the code comment and fig-alt card 1.

findings.claim: The Controls Operationalized table's Title column gives: SC-20 "Secure Name/Address Resolution (Authoritative)", SC-21 "Secure Name/Address Resolution (Recursive)", SC-22 "Architecture & Provisioning for Name/Address" (lines 107-109).
findings.problem: Official titles per the catalog SSOT are "Secure Name/Address Resolution Service (Authoritative Source)", "Secure Name/Address Resolution Service (Recursive or Caching Resolver)", and "Architecture and Provisioning for Name/Address Resolution Service". The spine itself (aan-compliance-spine.yml lines 276-277, 354-355) uses the full official titles, so this book is inconsistent with both the catalog and the series SSOT in a column explicitly labeled "Title".
findings.fix: Use the official catalog titles verbatim in the Title column (SC-7, CM-8, AC-4 rows are already correct).

findings.claim: "A hand-built landing zone cannot satisfy CM-8's \"authoritative inventory\" claim because there is no authority to point at" (Closure Necessity callout, line 99).
findings.problem: Two issues: (1) the scare quotes attribute the phrase "authoritative inventory" to CM-8, but the CM-8 control text contains no such phrase — it requires an inventory that accurately reflects the system and includes all components; (2) the absolute "cannot satisfy" overstates — agencies routinely pass CM-8 assessments with documented, hand-maintained inventories. The spine's CM-8 necessity rebuttal (aan-compliance-spine.yml line 272) argues IPAM vs CMDB enumeration, not that hand-built inventories are categorically non-compliant.
findings.fix: Remove the quotation marks so the phrase is not attributed to control text, and soften to the defensible form: a hand-built zone's inventory cannot be re-derived or diffed against intent, weakening the evidence of accuracy/completeness CM-8 assessment demands.

findings.claim: The HCL tags the RPZ block action as SC-21 (`action = "nxdomain"  # SC-21: block known-bad resolution`, line 77) and fig-alt card 3 says RPZ "blocks known-bad resolution under SC-21" (line 64).
findings.problem: SC-21's requirement is DNSSEC validation by the recursive/caching resolver. The spine's book-01 SC-21 mechanism is "Recursive DNSSEC validation + protective-DNS RPZ" — validation is the load-bearing half, and the book's own table row (line 108) correctly says "Validating recursive resolver + RPZ". But the illustrative code shows only zone signing plus an RPZ; no validating-recursive-resolver declaration appears anywhere, so the only code-level SC-21 evidence is the RPZ, which alone does not meet SC-21. A hostile reviewer asks: where is validation configured?
findings.fix: Add a `dnssec_validation = "on"` (or equivalent) recursive-resolver stanza to the illustrative module tagged SC-21, and re-tag the RPZ action as the protective-DNS complement rather than the SC-21 closure itself.

findings.claim: SC-22 row: "Redundant resolver topology in the `ddi` module" (line 109).
findings.problem: Nothing else in the book supports redundancy: the module topology table (line 43) scopes `ddi` to "Authoritative DNS, DNSSEC signing, RPZ, DHCP scopes" with no redundancy/HA mention, and the illustrative code declares a single zone. The SC-22 closure claim cannot be traced to any described mechanism in this book.
findings.fix: Either add a sentence (or code fragment) showing the redundant/separated resolver topology the ddi module deploys, or add redundancy to the module's "Owns" description.

findings.claim: Deployable Artifacts table and code reference external products/services: "Zscaler/Netskope GovCloud config-as-code" as edge substitutions (line 56), "InfoBlox / cloud DNS as code" and "BlueCat; Route 53 + IPAM" as DDI options (line 55), and "CISA Protective DNS / commercial TI" as an RPZ feed (line 76).
findings.problem: These are capability/availability claims about third-party offerings (GovCloud editions, config-as-code support, whether CISA Protective DNS can be consumed as an RPZ feed by the chosen resolver) that cannot be verified against in-repo SSOTs. Not judged true or false. The Provenance section (line 129) does say vendor-specific IaC claims cite vendor documentation, which partially covers this, but no vendor sources are actually cited in this book.
findings.fix: Add the "Vendor sources:" links the series authoring spec requires for vendor claims, or annotate the substitution column as illustrative-unverified.

findings.claim: "Book VI-01 supplies the cert authority they trust" (Deployment step 3, line 86) and "Book VI-01 — the certificate authority the port-auth profiles trust" (Cross-References, line 115).
findings.problem: Vol_VI_Book_01_FedAAN_Landing_Zone_Network_as_Code.qmd contains zero occurrences of certificate, CA, PKI, trust, 802.1X, EAP, or issuance — its modules are platform/ipam/ddi/network/edge only. The VI-00 overview map likewise assigns VI-01 'Terraform/Bicep landing zone, IPAM/DDI, SASE/TIC PEP' and assigns 'cert/token automation' to VI-02 itself. The dependency the 802.1X EAP-TLS profiles rely on is unfulfilled anywhere in Volume VI; a reviewer following the pointer finds nothing.
findings.fix: Either add the certificate-authority artifact to Book VI-01 (and its VI-00 map row), or repoint both references to where the CA actually lives (e.g., this book's own certificate-lifecycle section, or Vol I Book 03 Certificates & Tokens as the architecture source) and state explicitly which deployable book stands up the issuing CA.

findings.claim: Controls Operationalized row: "IA-5(2)/SC-17 | PKI-based Authentication".
findings.problem: Against reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json: IA-5(2) is "Public Key-based Authentication" (the r5 title; "PKI-Based Authentication" is the retired r4 title) and SC-17 is "Public Key Infrastructure Certificates" — a certificate-management control, not an authentication control. Labeling SC-17 as 'PKI-based Authentication' contradicts the catalog SSOT and is the kind of r4-era title a 3PAO flags in an r5 package.
findings.fix: Use the official r5 titles: "IA-5(2) Public Key-based Authentication" and "SC-17 Public Key Infrastructure Certificates" (split the row or list both titles).

findings.claim: Controls Operationalized row AC-2/5/6: "PIM/JIT role config; access reviews as code".
findings.problem: "Access reviews as code" appears only in this table. No deployable artifact, deployment step, figure, or illustrative code anywhere in the book covers access reviews — the artifacts table lists only CA policy, PIM/JIT config, port-auth profiles, and certificate lifecycle. The book claims to deploy a mechanism it never shows, which is exactly the assertion-without-evidence pattern the book itself argues against.
findings.fix: Either add an access-review artifact (e.g., Entra access-review configuration as code) to the Deployable Artifacts table and deployment steps, or drop "access reviews as code" from the AC-2/5/6 row.

findings.claim: Provenance: "Vendor claims cite vendor documentation."
findings.problem: The file names ten external products (Okta, Ping, CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, Keyfactor, Sectigo, Venafi, AppViewX) with capability claims (policy-as-code, JIT config, ACME support) but contains zero vendor-source links. The provenance statement is contradicted by the document body, and the series authoring spec requires 'Vendor sources:' links for vendor claims.
findings.fix: Add a 'Vendor sources:' block with vendor-documentation links for each substitution-column product, or soften the provenance line to say vendor claims are unverified substitution candidates.

findings.claim: Substitution-column capability claims: "Okta/Ping policy-as-code", "CyberArk/BeyondTrust JIT config", "Cisco ISE / Aruba ClearPass profiles", "Keyfactor/Sectigo + ACME as code", "Venafi / AppViewX" (lines 50-53).
findings.problem: These assert that each product supports the named as-code/JIT/ACME capability as a drop-in substitution path. Not judged true or false here — they are external-product capability claims that require verification against current vendor documentation (and FedRAMP marketplace status for the SaaS ones) before an assessor-facing release.
findings.fix: Verify each capability against vendor documentation and link it (ties into the missing 'Vendor sources:' block); note FedRAMP authorization status where the substitute is a SaaS offering.

findings.claim: "AC-5/6 least privilege" (artifacts table, line 51) and "AC-2/5/6 | Account Mgmt / Least Privilege" (line 101).
findings.problem: Per the catalog SSOT, AC-5 is "Separation of Duties", not least privilege (AC-6 is "Least Privilege"). Grouping AC-5 under a least-privilege label misstates its title, and nothing in the book describes a separation-of-duties mechanism distinct from PIM approval flow.
findings.fix: Rename to "AC-2 Account Management / AC-5 Separation of Duties / AC-6 Least Privilege" and, in the 'How this book deploys it' cell, tie AC-5 explicitly to the approver-cannot-self-activate property of the PIM policy.

findings.claim: "the library carries a translation column for Splunk (SPL) and Elastic (EQL/ES|QL) so a different SIEM realizes the same detections"
findings.problem: The shipped library at impl/detection-rules/ contains no Splunk/Elastic translation column in any of the 7 rule YAMLs or the README. The README claims only that the mechanism 'is portable to Splunk (SPL) / Elastic (EQL)' — a portability assertion, not shipped translations. An assessor asking to see the translation column finds it does not exist.
findings.fix: Either add the SPL/EQL translation column to the rule files, or soften the book to match the README: the mechanism is portable and translations are future work, not something the library 'carries'.

findings.claim: "The prerequisite is the Volume III connector fabric: the sign-in (interactive and non-interactive), unified-audit, and device-event tables the rules query must already be landing."
findings.problem: The kit README's minimum-tables list additionally requires IdentityInfo (XDR connector) for rule 02's atypical-IP baseline join. A team deploying from the book's prerequisite list leaves rule 02 without its baseline source. The fig-01 alt text repeats the same three-table list.
findings.fix: Add IdentityInfo (or 'an identity-baseline table') to the prerequisite sentence and the fig-01 alt text so the book matches the kit's stated minimum tables.

findings.claim: "Vendor-specific claims (table schemas, KQL functions, Sentinel rule format) cite Microsoft Learn as the vendor source"
findings.problem: The document contains zero Microsoft Learn links or citations, so the Provenance section asserts sourcing that the file itself does not carry. The series authoring spec (Federal_AAN_Series_Authoring_Spec.md) requires 'Vendor sources:' links for vendor claims.
findings.fix: Add the actual Microsoft Learn 'Vendor sources:' links (Sentinel scheduled-rule schema, repository connections, KQL geo_distance_2points/prev, SigninLogs schema) or reword Provenance to say the vendor sourcing lives in the kit/Vol III book.

findings.claim: Vendor-capability claims: Sentinel deploys via 'repository connection (GitHub / Azure DevOps), a PowerShell module, or ARM conversion'; commercial pipeline offers 'sub-second session revocation' and Identity Protection ML impossible-travel/atypical-IP/spray detections (lines 46, 101, 115, 117).
findings.problem: These are claims about an external product's current capabilities that no in-repo SSOT covers; they must be verified against Microsoft documentation before the document is treated as reviewed. Not judged true or false here.
findings.fix: Verify each against Microsoft Learn and attach the vendor-source links per the series spec (this also resolves the Provenance finding).

findings.claim: "Set the standing token-lifetime bound in the identity policy (Book VI-02)" and cross-reference "Book VI-02 — the token-lifetime standing control" (line 108); the 60–90 min short-token-lifetime config is also claimed as part of the AC-12 closure (line 96).
findings.problem: Book VI-02 (Vol_VI_Book_02_FedAAN_Identity_Access_as_Code.qmd, read in full) contains no token-lifetime artifact, control, deployment step, or even the word 'token'/'lifetime'/'session'. The 60–90 min bound exists only in this book, yet this book classifies it as a config artifact whose deployment home is VI-02. The standing control is load-bearing — it is the 'exposure ceiling under which the playbooks operate' and half of the AC-12 closure — and an assessor following the pointer finds nothing. Grep across all series .qmd confirms no other book carries it.
findings.fix: Either add the token-lifetime standing control (e.g., a sign-in-frequency / token-lifetime policy artifact) to Book VI-02's artifact table and deployment steps, or move the artifact fully into this book and drop the VI-02 attribution in deployment step 3 and the Cross-References section.

findings.claim: Promote to auto-action "only after the triggering rule's false-positive rate is measured (Book VI-08)"; Honest Limits calls "the alert-only ramp (Book VI-08)" mandatory (line 102); cross-reference says "Book VI-08 — false-positive measurement that gates auto-action" (line 111).
findings.problem: Book VI-08 (Vol_VI_Book_08_FedAAN_Validation_Test_Harnesses.qmd, read in full) contains no false-positive measurement, no alert-only ramp, and no auto-action gate. Its three harnesses are detection-efficacy (known-bad replay), telemetry-completeness, and deploy smoke tests, and its own Honest Limits state the efficacy tests 'bound false-negative regression' — the opposite failure axis. The mandatory safety mechanism this book relies on to prevent auto-containment denial-of-service is attributed to a book that does not carry it.
findings.fix: Add a false-positive / alert-only measurement harness to Book VI-08 (with the promotion criterion), or re-home the ramp into this book's own Deployment section and remove the VI-08 attribution from lines 81, 102, and 111.

findings.claim: "the sub-second Continuous Access Evaluation revocation the boundary removes" — repeated as "CAE sub-second revocation" in the ladder table (line 39), playbook table (line 47), and pseudocode notes (line 70).
findings.problem: Two external claims with no vendor source and no support elsewhere in the corpus: (a) that CAE enforcement is 'sub-second' — Microsoft characterizes CAE as near-real-time, and 'sub-second' is a quantitative vendor-capability claim this series states nowhere else (Book VI-03 says only 'real-time'); (b) that the GCC Moderate boundary removes CAE — 'Continuous Access Evaluation' appears in no other book, so this boundary-availability premise, on which the whole book's substitute framing rests, is asserted only here and unverified. Not judging either true or false; both need verification against Microsoft documentation and the series boundary analysis.
findings.fix: Verify CAE availability/latency in the GCC Moderate boundary against Microsoft documentation; add a 'Vendor sources:' citation per the series authoring spec, and soften 'sub-second' to Microsoft's own characterization (near-real-time) unless a source supports sub-second.

findings.claim: Pseudocode calls "PATCH /identityProtection/riskyUsers/confirmCompromised" (while using POST for revokeSignInSessions).
findings.problem: The Microsoft Graph confirmCompromised action is documented as a POST action, not PATCH; the inconsistent verb inside otherwise realistic Graph paths invites a reviewer nit even though the block is disclaimed as pseudocode. Needs verification against current Graph documentation.
findings.fix: Verify the HTTP verb against Microsoft Graph docs and align (POST), or strip HTTP verbs from the pseudocode entirely since it is declared non-deployable.

findings.claim: Medium-confidence row: enrich + open ticket with a human in the loop "Substitutes for: Vendor auto-remediation".
findings.problem: A human-in-the-loop ticket is a downgrade of, not a substitute for, automated remediation — the row asserts functional equivalence with no mechanism, unlike the High row which honestly annotates its latency degradation ("→ minutes"). A hostile reviewer will ask what property of auto-remediation the ticket preserves.
findings.fix: Annotate the degradation as the High row does (e.g., "Vendor auto-remediation (→ human-speed, ticketed)") or reword to "replaces" / "compensates for" with the human-review trade-off stated.

findings.claim: "Book VI-01 — the key-vault placement inside the authorized boundary."
findings.problem: Book VI-01 (Vol_VI_Book_01_FedAAN_Landing_Zone_Network_as_Code.qmd) contains no key-vault content at all — no mention of 'vault', 'Key Vault', or KMS anywhere; its module topology is platform/network/ddi only. A reviewer following this pointer to find where the key vault sits inside the boundary finds nothing.
findings.fix: Reword to what VI-01 actually provides (e.g. 'Book VI-01 — the landing zone and authorized boundary the key vault is deployed inside') or add key-vault placement to VI-01.

findings.claim: "Set the audit tier and export so retention meets the high-impact bar" (also in fig-03 alt text, line 75).
findings.problem: 'High-impact bar' is an undefined benchmark that appears nowhere else in the corpus and cannot be reproduced from any SSOT. Vol III Book 05 justifies retention as 10-year for privileged users / 1-year default 'per AU-10' — it never states a high-impact retention requirement. In a series that must never claim FedRAMP High, 'high-impact bar' as the stated compliance target reads as a High-baseline requirement being met; this file has no baselined High mentions in aan-high-claim-baseline.yml.
findings.fix: Name the actual driver: cite Vol III's AU-10 10-year/1-year retention rationale, or the specific authority (e.g. OMB M-21-31 tier) if that is what is meant, and drop 'high-impact bar'.

findings.claim: Provenance states "Vendor claims cite vendor documentation."
findings.problem: The document contains zero links or citations of any kind (grep for 'http' returns 0) while making multiple vendor-capability claims: BYOK label encryption with agency rotate/revoke, Purview Audit premium tier with immutable export, and the whole multi-CSP substitution column. The provenance assertion is contradicted by the document's own content, and the series authoring spec requires vendor-source links for vendor claims.
findings.fix: Either add the vendor-documentation sources for the Purview/Key Vault/AWS claims or soften the provenance line to say sources are carried in the Vol III architecture book this deploys.

findings.claim: Multi-CSP substitution column: 'AWS Macie classifications' substitutes for the sensitivity-label taxonomy; 'Symantec/Forcepoint DLP policy-as-code'; 'CloudTrail Lake retention config' substitutes for the AU-10 audit-retention artifact.
findings.problem: These are product-capability equivalence claims that require verification against vendor documentation. In particular, whether Macie (a discovery/classification service) provides a protection-carrying label equivalent to encryption-enforcing sensitivity labels, and whether CloudTrail Lake retention provides the immutability/non-repudiation property the AU-10 row depends on, are not judged here — but a 3PAO will ask, and no source is cited.
findings.fix: Add vendor-source citations for each substitution cell, or annotate the column as mechanism-preserving analogues rather than capability-equivalent substitutions.

findings.claim: Label encryption binds to agency-held keys so the agency can rotate or revoke them, e.g. after an administrator with access departs (also fig-02 alt text, line 62).
findings.problem: The rotate/revoke semantics of Purview/AIP BYOK — specifically that key revocation cuts off a departed administrator's access to previously protected content — is a vendor-capability claim with no cited source in this book. Not judged true or false; flagged for verification against Microsoft documentation.
findings.fix: Cite the Microsoft Learn BYOK/tenant-key documentation for the revocation behavior, or point to where Vol III carries that citation.

findings.claim: Fig-02 alt text tags card 1 'Agency rotates and revokes' as SC-12(1).
findings.problem: Per the SSOT catalog, SC-12(1) is 'Availability' — maintaining availability of information in the event of key loss (Vol III maps it to soft-delete/recovery accordingly). Rotation and revocation belong to base SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management); tagging the rotate/revoke card with the availability enhancement is a mapping imprecision.
findings.fix: Tag card 1 as SC-12 (or SC-12/12(1) if recovery is also meant) and reserve SC-12(1) for the key-recovery/soft-delete content.

findings.claim: Controls Operationalized row: 'MP-2..5 | Media Protection'.
findings.problem: 'Media Protection' is the MP family name, not the title of any of the four controls in the range; the SSOT titles are MP-2 Media Access, MP-3 Media Marking, MP-4 Media Storage, MP-5 Media Transport. The column header is 'Title', so a strict reviewer will flag the cell as not matching the catalog.
findings.fix: Either list the four controls with their catalog titles (as Vol III Book 05 lines 860-863 already does) or relabel the cell 'Media Protection family'.

findings.claim: "the retention-cliff fix the detection layer depends on for long-tail forensics" (also fig-03 alt text, line 75).
findings.problem: The term 'retention cliff' is defined nowhere in the corpus outside this book and its spec, and Book VI-03 (the detection layer) never states a dependency on extended audit retention for long-tail forensics — its Honest Limits cover fidelity, threat intel, revocation latency, and rule rot only. The dependency claim cannot be traced.
findings.fix: Either define the retention cliff inline (Vol III Book 05 line 859 carries the underlying fact: standard audit retention is 90 days) or add the retention dependency to VI-03 so the cross-claim resolves.

findings.claim: "CM-6 is satisfied only when the baseline is machine-enforced and drift is detected and dispositioned" (also line 31: "the loop CM-6 actually requires: an enforced configuration, a detection of deviation, and a documented reconciliation").
findings.problem: Base CM-6 (Configuration Settings) requires establishing/documenting/implementing settings and identifying, documenting, and approving deviations — it does not require machine enforcement or automated drift detection. Automated management/verification is control enhancement CM-6(1) 'Automated Management, Application, and Verification' and automated response to change is CM-6(2) 'Respond to Unauthorized Changes' (verified against reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json). Stating base CM-6 is satisfied ONLY with machine enforcement is a requirement the control text does not impose; a hostile assessor will flag the overstatement.
findings.fix: Reword to position machine enforcement as this book's implementation standard rather than a CM-6 requirement — e.g. 'this book satisfies CM-6 the strong way: machine-enforced, drift detected and dispositioned — and reaches CM-6(1)/(2) enhancement territory' — or explicitly cite CM-6(1)/CM-6(2) as what the automation operationalizes.

findings.claim: Illustrative YAML labeled "deployed example: Azure Machine Config" uses `enforcementMode: AuditThenRemediate` and per-rule `onDrift: remediate|report` dispositions.
findings.problem: Azure Machine Configuration assignment types are Audit / ApplyAndAutoCorrect / ApplyAndMonitor, set per assignment, not per rule; 'AuditThenRemediate' is not a real mode and per-rule drift disposition is not a native Guest Config capability. The Provenance section does disclaim the YAML as 'an illustrative pattern to adapt, not a drop-in pack,' which mitigates, but the inline comment '# Guest/machine-config baseline (deployed example: Azure Machine Config)' invites a reviewer to read it as product syntax. Needs external verification against current Azure docs — do not treat as judged true/false here.
findings.fix: Either drop the product label from the code block (keep it generic pseudo-policy) or add a one-line note that mode names and per-rule dispositions are abstracted and map to Azure Machine Config assignment types plus a remediation pipeline.

findings.claim: Controls Operationalized table says CM-7 (Least Functionality) is deployed via "Host hardening roles; admission control".
findings.problem: "Admission control" appears nowhere else in the book — no deployable artifact, deployment step, or cross-reference covers it (admission control belongs to Vol III Book 04 / the container posture lane). The table claims a deployment mechanism this book never describes, which a reviewer tracing the row will not find.
findings.fix: Either drop 'admission control' from the CM-7 row or add a cross-reference cell pointing at the book that actually deploys it (e.g. Vol III Book 04 realization in Vol VI).

findings.claim: Deployable Artifacts table asserts product equivalences: ScubaGear for SCuBA assessment; AWS SSM State Manager and GCP OS Config as substitutes for Azure Machine Config; Chef/Puppet as equivalents to Ansible/DSC STIG/CIS roles.
findings.problem: These are external product-capability claims (that each named substitute delivers the same guest-config baseline + drift-detection mechanism). They are plausible and framed under the mechanism-not-product doctrine, but their current capability parity cannot be verified from in-repo SSOTs — flagged for external verification only, not judged true or false.
findings.fix: No text change required; ensure these rows are covered by whatever vendor-source verification pass the series applies to 'Vendor sources:' claims.

findings.claim: Controls Operationalized table row: 'CA-7 / CA-7(1) | Continuous Monitoring | Telemetry→evidence→KSI→package pipeline'
findings.problem: The catalog SSOT (reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json) titles CA-7(1) 'Independent Assessment', not 'Continuous Monitoring'. An automated evidence pipeline does not deploy assessor independence, so the row claims a control the mechanism cannot operationalize. CA-7(1) also appears nowhere in aan-compliance-spine.yml — the spine's CA-7 closures (book-evidence-fabric line 283, book-sn-attestation line 314) never bind the enhancement. A 3PAO would reject this row as-is.
findings.fix: Drop CA-7(1) from the row (leaving CA-7, whose title and spine closure both match), or split it into its own row with the correct title 'Independent Assessment' and a mechanism that actually addresses assessor independence — and add a matching spine entry if the claim is kept.

findings.claim: Illustrative evidence-contract record binds a CM-6 machine-config record to "ksi": ["KSI-CM"] (also in fig-01 alt text, line 37)
findings.problem: The spine SSOT's KSI vocabulary is KSI-CNA/IAM/MLA/SVC/CMT/PIY/SCR — 'KSI-CM' never appears in aan-compliance-spine.yml, and the spine's own CM-6 closure (book-cloudnative-posture, ~line 288) binds CM-6 to [KSI-CMT, KSI-SVC]. The example presents the field as 'FedRAMP 20x KSI theme(s)', so a reviewer validating the record against the KSI schema would flag an identifier the series' own registry does not recognize. (Vol III Books 03/04 also use KSI-CM, so this is a corpus-wide spine-vs-books vocabulary split, but this book's example inherits it into the load-bearing contract definition.)
findings.fix: Change the example to a KSI id the spine recognizes for CM-6 (e.g. ["KSI-CMT"]), or reconcile the spine's KSI vocabulary with the Vol III books' KSI-CM usage in one direction and regenerate.

findings.claim: Controls Operationalized table titles AU-12(1) 'System-Wide Time-Correlated Trail'
findings.problem: Catalog SSOT title is 'System-wide and Time-correlated Audit Trail' — the table drops 'Audit'. The spine (line 282) uses the exact catalog title, so the book diverges from both.
findings.fix: Use the exact catalog title 'System-wide and Time-correlated Audit Trail' in the title column.

findings.claim: Deployable Artifacts table (line ~50) lists 'Baseline conformance re-check' realizing 'CM-6 verification', but the Controls Operationalized table (lines ~95-99) lists only CA-2, CA-7(3), and SI-4 — CM-6 is absent.
findings.problem: The book claims a deployed artifact realizes CM-6, and the spine (aan-compliance-spine.yml lines 271 and 288) names 'Vol VI Book 08 — baseline conformance re-check' as the test mechanism for both CM-6 rows, yet the book's own controls table omits CM-6. The baseline conformance re-check is also the only one of the four artifacts with no step in the Deployment section (steps 1-4 cover completeness, efficacy, smoke tests, and evidence emission only). A reviewer reconciling the book against the spine will ask which list is authoritative.
findings.fix: Add a CM-6 | Configuration Settings row to the Controls Operationalized table (and a deployment step for the scheduled baseline re-scan), or remove/re-scope the CM-6 artifact row and update the spine test fields accordingly.

findings.claim: Closure Necessity callout: 'CA-7(3) [requires] that monitoring detect degradation' (line ~90).
findings.problem: CA-7(3) is 'Trend Analyses' (confirmed in reference/nist-800-53r5-controls.json): employing trend analyses to determine whether monitoring implementations/frequency need modification. 'Detect degradation' is a loose paraphrase that overstates the enhancement's requirement; the book's own Controls Operationalized table titles it correctly. A pedantic 3PAO could flag the mismatch between the callout's characterization and the official enhancement intent.
findings.fix: Rephrase to something like 'CA-7(3) requires trend analyses that reveal when monitoring is degrading' so the claim tracks the official enhancement language.

findings.claim: 'A rebuild fails silently far more often than it fails loudly' (line ~29).
findings.problem: An empirical frequency claim ('far more often') presented as fact with no source or mechanism. It is rhetorical framing, but a hostile reviewer can ask for the basis.
findings.fix: Soften to an argued position ('the failures that matter most are the silent ones') or drop the frequency comparison.

findings.claim: "Ten of the twenty-nine CR26 KSIs are attestable by ScuBA-class tooling alone; the other nineteen..."
findings.problem: Labels the 29 as "CR26 KSIs". The series' own evidence contract (inbox/Application Aware Networking/AAN_Evidence_Contract_Spec.md, section 8, line 165) states the "29 KSI rules" are an INTERNAL rule decomposition, explicitly NOT the published FedRAMP CR26 Moderate KSI catalog, and that the reconciliation is the series' #1 open evidence-layer item. Vol 0 Book 00 (Executive Summary, line 80) — the very source this sentence attributes the claim to — likewise calls the 29 "the series' internal 29-rule KSI decomposition". A 3PAO checking the count against the actual CR26 indicator list would find a different number and reject the sentence as factually wrong. The 10/19 split itself is reproducible against Vol 0 Book 00 ("10 of 29 KSI rules attestable by conformance tooling alone"); only the CR26 attribution is the defect.
findings.fix: Rephrase to match the source it cites, e.g. "Ten of the series' twenty-nine internal KSI rules (its decomposition of the CR26 KSI surface) are attestable by ScuBA-class tooling alone; the other nineteen..." — same fix pattern the Executive Summary already uses.

findings.claim: "Volume V is the only volume that depends on all of the others — it teaches them, referencing each Vol I–IV book..."
findings.problem: Stale against the spine. aan-compliance-spine.yml (Date Code 2026-07-13, after this book's 2026-07-09 date code) registers Volumes VI–IX (Implementation, ServiceNow Automation, Multi-Cloud DDI, Day-2 Operations). Volume V's two tracks, per this same file, cover only Volumes 0–IV; it neither teaches nor depends on Vols VI–IX, so "depends on all of the others" cannot be reproduced from the current volume registry. The subtitle ("teaches Volumes 0–IV") is accurate; the superlative is not.
findings.fix: Scope the claim: "Volume V depends on every architecture volume it teaches (Volumes 0–IV)..." or explicitly state the training corpus is Vols 0–IV and that later volumes (VI–IX) are out of curriculum scope.

findings.claim: Volume V "produces the one evidence artifact the other volumes cannot generate for themselves: proof that the people running the program are trained" (restated at line 83 as producing the training-effectiveness-record that "no other volume can supply").
findings.problem: Exclusivity is contradicted by the cross-referenced books: Vol IV Book 06 line 405 attributes the Training Effectiveness Record schema to "(Vol IV Book 05)" and line 651 exports `governance.training-effectiveness-record` via the LMS adapter (Viva Learning Graph API) — i.e. Volume IV's AT-4 LMS program generates the record whether or not the Volume V academy exists. The file's own callout (line 75) concedes Vol IV Book 05 specifies the program and its closure; the absolute "cannot generate for themselves" / "no other volume can supply" is rhetoric a hostile reviewer would puncture with Vol IV Book 05's AT-4 completion-record evidence chain.
findings.fix: Soften to the defensible division already stated in the callout: Volume V operationalizes the training program at manuscript depth and is the intended production path for the training-effectiveness-record; drop "the one artifact the other volumes cannot generate" and "no other volume can supply".

findings.claim: Module B1's IPAM inventory export binds as "slot-02 addressing" evidence (also line 85 "slot-02 verdict" and the line 247 table row "slot 2 (addressing)").
findings.problem: The spine SSOT (aan-compliance-spine.yml, slots registry) defines slot-02-data = "Data", and the spine actively binds closures to slot-02-data (e.g., AC-4 and SI-12 under book-sn-saas). Vol 0 Book 00 (Executive Summary, line ~676) likewise calls slot-02 and slot-04 "the data and telemetry slots". Under the spine, addressing/inventory evidence (CM-8, SC-20/SC-21) maps to slot-03-network. An assessor tracing the B1 artifact into the fedramp_aan_catalog slot mapping would find slot-02 is the Data slot, not an addressing slot — the module's evidence-landing instruction points at the wrong slot per the registry. Note Vol V Book 01 (Module A2 "Addressing Control Plane (Slot 2)") shares the divergent taxonomy, so this is a Volume V-wide conflict with the spine, but it is load-bearing here because this book instructs engineers where to bind evidence.
findings.fix: Reconcile the Volume V eight-slot taxonomy with the spine slots registry: either rename B1's landing slot to match the spine (addressing/inventory evidence lands per the spine's CM-8/SC-20/SC-21 slot assignments, slot-03-network) or, if "slot 2 = addressing" is the intended catalog surface, update the spine slots registry and Book 00 usage in the same change; fix line 78, line 85, and the module table row together with Vol V Book 01.

findings.claim: The book's stated purpose is "how to build the architectures Volumes I–IV describe" (subtitle and line ~41), with eight modules covering the corpus; Module B6 reads "Vol III Books 02, 04–07".
findings.problem: Vol III Book 03 (Patch & Systems Management, spine id book-patch-sysmgmt — SI-2/SI-2(2)/SI-2(3)/CM-2/CM-6/CM-8/RA-5 closures, including a Closure-Necessity anchor for SI-2 and the CM-8 IPAM join-key anchor) is built by no module B1–B8. The compliance track (Vol V Book 01, Module A5) does cover it, so the implementation track is the only Volume V surface that silently drops a spine-registered closure book. A reviewer checking module coverage against the spine's Volume III book list (intro, 01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 06, 07) can reproduce the gap.
findings.fix: Either add Vol III Book 03 to Module B6's read/build list (with its remediation-actuation lab landing slot-05 evidence per the spine's SI-2 closures) or state explicitly why the patch/systems-management build is out of the track's scope.

findings.claim: Vendor/product claims: customer-owned edge gear "(Cisco / Palo Alto / Juniper) accredited through NIAP / DISA STIG / FIPS 140-3 / DoDIN APL" (B3); "The reference stack is Infoblox" with "UIAO modernization adapters for BlueCat and Infoblox" (B1); and vendor training catalogs (Infoblox education, BlueCat learning, AZ-700, SC-300, SC-401, SC-200, DP-300, AZ-500, Cisco U, SailPoint Identity University, Fortinet/Palo Alto SASE, AWS Skill Builder Amazon Connect, Splunk/Elastic, SANS, CISA Learning, NIST NICE).
findings.problem: These are external-product facts not verifiable in-repo. The training-catalog names are backed with source links in Vol V Book 04 (verified: AZ-700, SC-401, SailPoint Identity University, AWS Skill Builder rows carry vendor URLs), but this file itself carries no "Vendor sources:" links, and the blanket claim that specific Cisco/Palo Alto/Juniper gear holds current NIAP CC / DoDIN APL / FIPS 140-3 listings is model- and version-specific — an assessor would ask for the certificate/APL entry numbers. Not judged true or false here.
